"I understand that this news may cause fear and uncertainty for members of our community, particularly for immigrant families who may be directly or indirectly impacted," Smyth said in the statement. "Let me be clear: Norwalk is a city that welcomes and values all of our residents, regardless of immigration status. Our immigrant communities are an important part of the fabric of Norwalk, and no one should feel alone or without support during this difficult time."

In her statement, Smyth said federal immigration enforcement is the responsibility of the federal government.

"The city of Norwalk and the Norwalk Police Department are separate from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and our local government does not control federal immigration enforcement activities," Smyth said. "The actions of the officers of the Norwalk Police Department are aligned with the TRUST Act of the State of Connecticut, which prohibits cooperation or the sharing of any intelligence or information for immigration enforcement operations."

"Norwalk is a city built by people from many backgrounds, cultures and countries," Smyth said. "We will continue to be a welcoming, inclusive community, and we will continue to stand with our immigrant neighbors during these challenging times."

ICE activity has also recently been reported in some nearby Connecticut communities, including Danbury and Stamford.

In a statement sent to Patch, an ICE spokesperson said they "will not disclose or discuss law enforcement operations" for operational security and the safety of their officers.

The agency added: "Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, if you break the law, you will face the consequences. Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the U.S."

Smyth and Norwalk Public Schools Interim Superintendent Sandra Faioes released a joint statement Wednesday as students returned to school across the city.

"As the new school year begins, we want to reaffirm something that should never be in doubt: Norwalk's schools are safe, welcoming places where every child has the opportunity to learn, grow, and thrive," the statement reads. "We recognize that recent changes to immigration policies, including changes to Temporary Protected Status (TPS), as well as increased immigration enforcement activity around the country, have created uncertainty and concern for some families in our community. We want our students and families to know that you belong here, and your schools are here for you."

Smyth and Faioes noted the district does not ask students or families to provide information about their immigration status as a condition of attending school.

"Student privacy is protected by federal and state law," the statement reads, "and the district has established protocols for responding to requests for student information and to any law enforcement activity involving our schools."

They also emphasized the safety and well-being of students will always be their highest priority.

"We will continue to work closely with our school leaders, staff, families, and community partners to ensure that our schools remain safe, supportive, and welcoming environments for every student," the statement reads. "We also encourage families to make sure their emergency contact information is current with Norwalk Public Schools and to familiarize themselves with the resources and information available to them."

Families who have questions or concerns are encouraged to reach out to their school or the district, who can help connect them with appropriate resources, the statement notes.

"Norwalk is a community built on the strength of its families, its diversity, and its commitment to one another," the statement reads. "Every child deserves to feel safe walking into school each morning, and every family deserves to know that their community stands with them. We are proud to stand together — as a city, as a school district, and as a community — in support of all of our students and families."

Top state officials say that they are highly concerned about immigrant families after multiple arrests by federal ICE agents in Stamford and Danbury.

Gov. Ned Lamont traveled to Danbury to meet with U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy and local officials to talk about residents who have been detained in recent days by agents from the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency. Lamont went to the city’s Kennedy Park, where day laborers had been arrested. He also spoke with state Attorney General William Tong earlier in the day before heading to Danbury.

“It’s clear that this has moved well beyond targeting violent criminals or gang members and is just indiscriminate terror sweeps, basically, to pick up whoever they can pick up and scare whoever they can scare,” Tong said in his Hartford office. “Whenever you raise the temperature like this and put people in harm’s way, the potential for violence increases exponentially. So that’s what I’m most concerned about.”

Citing cases in Minneapolis and elsewhere, Tong said he is worried about potential violence.

If the situation escalates, Tong said he is not ruling out a civil lawsuit against the federal government as he has filed in the past concerning other actions by President Donald Trump’s administration.

“If there are broad-based violations of civil rights of people here in Connecticut, and if there are broad-based violations of our law that rise to the level of me needing to file a lawsuit, I will do that,” Tong said when asked by The Courant. “I don’t want to speculate, but if ICE does something that violates our law and violates federal law, yes, potentially the state could take action.”

Tong, Lamont, and other officials advised immigrant families to be cautious and aware of the recent activities.

“The one thing I would say to people is be careful, don’t take any unnecessary risks,” Tong said. “Have the conversation with your children. It is similar to the conversation you hear about Black parents having to have with their African-American children. Know that there is a target on everyone’s backs.”

He added, “I’m saying, go to school. Go to work. Be careful. If you man the front desk of a construction company or of a public school, you should know what the process is and what the plan is if ICE shows up. You should have a phone tree and somebody in authority should be ready to engage with the authorities and assert the rights of individuals and organizations.”

ICE officials could not be reached for comment Wednesday, but the agency has said in the past that it does not offer details on law enforcement operations.

In a developing situation, Lamont was obtaining more details throughout the day.

“It’s ramped up, really aggressive ICE enforcement all over the country,” Lamont said. “Right now, we’re trying to find out who these folks are and get them legal representation.”

Lamont added, “Stop picking up people because you think they look suspicious and taking them away on the grounds you think that’s keeping us safe. We work with everybody to get dangerous people off the streets. They’re not reaching out to us. They’re not trying to coordinate with us. They’re just picking up people.”

Later, he warned ICE agents to “stay away. Let our kids get to school safely.”

But state House Republican leader Vincent Candelora of North Branford said he was concerned that Lamont quickly released written guidelines on what immigrants should do if they are stopped in their car or asked about their status.

“It took a week and reporters’ questions to get Democrats to tell police officers whether standing near a polling place could get them charged with a felony,” Candelora said. “A how-to guide from Governor Lamont for people here illegally went out in hours. Their priorities are out of whack, and taxpayers are paying for it. Connecticut has real problems tied to illegal immigration, and both the governor and legislative Democrats keep pretending their sanctuary state policies and their refusal to work with federal officials have nothing to do with what is happening in Danbury.”

U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who has raised concerns about ICE in the past, criticized the actions by federal agents.

“ICE’s cruelty and craven brutality has no limit,” Blumenthal said. “Snatching people off the streets as they walk their children to school or wait for a ride to work — such tactics are abusive, abhorrent, and illegal. I am in touch with state and local authorities and am ready to assist in any way possible.”

Danbury Mayor Roberto Alves released a video on Facebook that showed him in a car returning to the city after celebrating his grandmother’s 100th birthday outside of the country.

“We are driving around Danbury right now — first day of school and a lot going on and a community that is scared,” Alves said in the car. “A community that is scared to go to work, a community that’s scared to send their kids to school, a community whose kids are scared to come home and have a parent missing because of the ICE operations yesterday and today throughout our state, but more heavily here in Danbury.”

Alves rejected the notion that the Trump administration was only looking for criminals in a policy that “is fear-driven” and is “meant to divide us” in Connecticut.

“They weren’t going after folks with judicial warrants or deportation orders. It looks like they were just pulling random people,” Alves said. “They are specifically targeting folks who are Latino. … A lot of folks knew this was going to happen eventually. We have to be stronger. We have to stay together. … There are ‘know your rights’ cards. Make sure your neighbors know what their rights are. … They’re not just deporting serious criminals. … Let’s not get overwhelmed. Let’s stay together. Let’s understand the true way to beat this is at the polls.”

During a news conference that was televised live, Alves said, “The Danbury police department does not partner with ICE. … We’re now seeing racial profiling, random people being picked up off the streets. … To the activists here, you’re the reason why we know what is going on. That’s how we know that ICE is pulling people after they put their kids on a school bus, where kids are seeing this happen. Operations in front of a daycare where 3 to 5-year-olds are looking out the window, asking folks what is going on.”

He added, “This isn’t coincidence. This is intentional. … The folks doing it the right way are also getting deported.”

Alves added that “masked agents in unmarked vehicles” were making the arrests.

“What I need you to do is understand that these are dangerous actors who have killed people,” Alves said, cautioning activists to be careful. “Videotape them.”

text:
A Cheyenne-based judge on Tuesday dismissed a lawsuit filed by a church, barbershop, and immigration advocacy group in May against Laramie County Sheriff Brian Kozak.

With the help of the American Civil Liberties Union, the coalition had accused Kozak of exceeding his authority when establishing three agreements to work with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

The advocacy group Juntos, the Unitarian Universalist Church of Cheyenne, and Drew’s Barbershop alleged that Kozak never got permission or expense authorization from the Laramie County Commission to work with ICE, and that he didn’t follow Wyoming’s administrative procedure laws.

Those entities haven’t shown how any specific harms they suffered from Kozak’s immigration enforcement entitled them to defend the County Commission’s authority in court, Laramie County District Court Judge Robin Cooley ruled in a Tuesday order.

Drew’s Barbershop lost an employee because the sheriff’s deputies worked with ICE to deport him to Nicaragua, the original complaint says.

Juntos had to shift its events to online rather than in person because the immigration community harbored fears of being detained if they ventured out to travel to the events, the complaint says.

And the church had to redirect around $10,000 from its charity and donation coffers to bolster its ministry for immigrants, adds the complaint.

“Although Plaintiffs allege concrete harms arising from immigration enforcement, they have not alleged a particularized injury arising from the alleged infringement of the Commissioners’ authority,” says the order.

The harms the plaintiffs described, rather, stemmed from the enforcement activities, not the county’s approval process, which was challenged in the case.

Then quoting from an earlier Wyoming case, the judge added, “It is not the function of the judicial branch to pass judgment on the general performance of other branches of government. Instead, it is our function to resolve specific controversies between adverse parties and determine whether those parties, in the context of that controversy, have complied with the law.”

Cooley dismissed the case. She specifically avoided answering the question of whether Kozak exceeded his authority, because the groups that brought the suit didn’t show they have standing to press that question in the first place, Cooley wrote.

The plaintiffs’ attorney Elizabeth Bartels Lance did not immediately respond to a Thursday-morning text message request for comment and inquiry about potential appeal.

Meanwhile...

Meanwhile, Kozak faces another immigration-advocacy suit that Colorado-based Lichter Immigration, its investigator Kevin Lewis, and its attorney Drake Hill are waging against him.

The Lichter suit accuses Kozak's office of withholding important records from the firm while it represents an immigrant who needs those records to fight his own case.

Kozak has called that case a political maneuver, pointing to his investigation of one of Lewis' and Hill's political allies.

Lewis, conversely, said Kozak's assertions are "ridiculous" excuses.

title: One Nation's immigration policy is clear as mud – but that ambiguity could be a secret ...
description:
Officially, the policy listed on the party’s website is a promise to cap visas at 130,000 per year.
Whether that would mean a net overseas migration (Nom) target or a permanent visa ceiling is unclear.
“So, if you have 130,000 people coming in, that’s a net migration of minus 90,000.
So that’s a totally different matter.” If the 130,000 figure One Nation commits to is, indeed, a Nom target, it would mean a permanent population increase of 130,000.
Assuming that figure remains consistent, a Nom of 130,000 would mean 330,000 arrive in the country.
text:
One Nation has experienced a swell in popular support in the past year, and has primarily done so off the back of tough talk on immigration – a policy area almost synonymous with its leader, Pauline Hanson.

But a series of blunders this week show a party unable, or unwilling, to clearly articulate what it would actually do about immigration levels.

Does it want “net zero” immigration, as it boasted for many years? Or does it want a small increase – a net gain of up to 130, 000 people per year – as Barnaby Joyce said emphatically this week?

Let’s step through what key figures have said – and what the party’s policy says.

Officially, the policy listed on the party’s website is a promise to cap visas at 130,000 per year. Whether that would mean a net overseas migration (Nom) target or a permanent visa ceiling is unclear.

Joyce has said this is the party’s Nom cap. On Thursday, Hanson reiterated this.

Nom is the overall gain or loss of population through long-term arrivals and departures. It measures people coming into or leaving the country for a period of at least 12 months over 16 months and thus excludes tourists.

This week David Farley said One Nation’s Nom was 130,000 but that it wouldn’t include an additional 100,000 skilled workers, backpackers and Pacific and Timor-Leste labour through the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (Palm) scheme.

Joyce said that wasn’t right. The former Nationals MP, who defected to One Nation last December, said there were no additional visas hidden from the policy’s headline figure, ruling Farley’s comments out as a rookie mistake.

“When people are new in parliament, they can sometimes get things incorrect,” Joyce said.

The messaging was further muddied after the contribution of the Queensland senator Malcolm Roberts. In a brief interview with the far-right influencer Andre Mamet, known as Ausmaxx, on Tuesday, Roberts appeared to say he supported “net negative migration” – when fewer people enter the country than leave – but he also supported a cap on net migration of 130,000, which implies more people coming than leaving.

“What we’re saying is, every year about 220,000 people leave. I didn’t realise it was so high. And what we’re saying is, we will cap the number of people, net people, [that] come in at 130,000,” Roberts said.

“So if 220,000 people leave … and we allow in 220,000, then that’s – we can’t do that migration. Net migration is complex because it talks about, in 12 months out of only 16 months, the number of people who come in minus the number of people to leave.

“So, if you have 130,000 people coming in, that’s a net migration of minus 90,000. In other words, you lose your population by 90,000. So what we’re saying is the cap on net is 130,000.”

Both Roberts and Hanson have made numerous social media posts supporting “net zero” and net negative migration in the years leading up to 2026.

Hanson confused things further on Thursday when she said the 130,000 figure target was for Nom but didn’t include Pacific labour workers. When asked if that meant there would be more than 130,000 migrants allowed each year under One Nation, she responded: “Correct.”

“Correct, because your Palm workers, rural and regional Australia would die if they didn’t have the workers coming in, and especially the abattoirs and the farmers. So that’s a different program,” she told a News Corp Bush Summit panel.

“These people are given accommodation by the farming sector and the businesses that employ them. So that is not the big impact here. But with immigration, you can’t just tie it to your housing, because infrastructure is another big thing and hospitals and schools and the nursing homes – that has to be all accounted for so it’s just not about houses.”

Hanson added Farley “didn’t understand” and “got confused” when discussing the Palm workers over the weekend.

“As I’ve always said, Palm workers is, the visa-holders that can come into the country. They’re provided accommodation, usually by those on the farms. They’re not taking up the housing. So that’s a totally different matter.”

If the 130,000 figure One Nation commits to is, indeed, a Nom target, it would mean a permanent population increase of 130,000. Each year, about 200,000 people leave the country, including Australians leaving to study and work abroad. Assuming that figure remains consistent, a Nom of 130,000 would mean 330,000 arrive in the country.

However, if One Nation’s policy is a hard cap offering 130,000 visas each year, as the party’s policy says and as Hanson and Roberts argued for less than a year ago, the result would probably lead to negative migration.

The problem with various explanations and interpretations is that it’s impossible for voters to determine which are accurate, and whether others are misleading.

But for a party trying to appeal to its more extreme supporters who argue for hardline policies, it’s a beneficial political tactic, whether intentional or not.

Farley’s comments, which included the suggestion that One Nation’s Nom target was “not too different” from the Albanese government’s, drew a lot of criticism from a number of far-right figures.

Roberts’ interview with Mamet this week could be viewed as an attempt to bring some of them back.

Policy ambiguity has long been Hanson’s secret weapon.

Whether it remains that way under increasing scrutiny of the party, especially under the spotlight of an election campaign, remains to be seen.

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement is planning to buy a device able to stop a car from moving.

A federal contract to purchase a “vehicle arresting devise (sic)” is dated Aug. 14, weeks after ICE agents shot and killed two drivers in Maine and Texas who failed to stop for the unmarked vehicles conducting immigration enforcement operations. In both cases, the driver was not ICE’s intended target.

RELATED STORY | ICE officers kill 1 in Maine while executing a warrant for a different person

After the shootings, the Department of Homeland Security put a temporary suspension on ICE vehicle pursuits but President Trump quickly reversed the pause.

Now ICE is set to spend $29,286 for a system from Stock Enterprises, LLC, a company based in Phoenix.

A representative from the company tells Scripps News it makes one product that fits the description of a vehicle arresting device. It’s known as The Grappler police bumper.

Here is how it works: Officers with a Grappler mounted to the front of their car get directly behind a suspect vehicle, then use a switch to launch a nylon net around one of the back tires, aiming to slow and stop the fleeing car.

An increasing number of police departments are using the Grappler. That includes the Aurora Police Department in Colorado, with 13 of the devices.

"It captures the vehicle and slows it down to a speed where our other vehicles come in, pin in the vehicle, and make contact with the driver in a safer manner,” said Aurora Deputy Chief Michael Gaskill.

Aurora police have been using the tool since March, with a success rate of about 65 percent. Officers go through a day of training on the system before using it on the road.

It is not meant for use in busy traffic, Gaskill said.

"When the suspect vehicle is being captured, it can still move side to side,” he said.

DHS did not answer questions about its contract for a vehicle arresting device, including what level of training ICE agents would receive.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Deportation crackdown accelerates with highest ICE arrest total in months

ICE’s potential use of The Grappler to carry out civil immigration enforcement is troubling, said Jared Keenan, executive director of the Arizona Center for Law in the Public Interest.

"It seems that they'll probably overuse it and be violently stopping automobiles on mere suspicion of an immigration violation,” Keenan said. “They are mostly going after folks who have no criminal record, pose no threat to the public.”

DHS declined to say how many Grapplers the agency wants to buy, or where they would be deployed. The relatively low dollar figure would not be enough for widespread use of the product on ICE vehicles.

text:
U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Richard Durbin, U.S. Representative Mike Quigley, and Illinois General Assembly members joined children’s legal service providers yesterday to raise the alarm about severe due process violations currently targeting unaccompanied immigrant children at the Chicago Immigration Court.

The press conference took place after an immigration judge, presiding via video at the Chicago Immigration Court, ordered the deportation of nine out of about 20 unaccompanied children who appeared in person for their removal hearings. During one of the final cases in the proceedings, after spending hours watching other children receive removal orders, one Indigenous child courageously asked the judge directly: “Why are you sending me back to Guatemala? What did I do?”

The children who received deportation orders had been deemed by a state court to have been abused, abandoned, or neglected in their home countries, and had applications pending for legal protection known as Special Immigrant Juvenile Status (SIJS). Congress created SIJS protections in 1990 for abandoned children whom the U.S. government determined could not safely return to their home countries.

“What I witnessed today illustrated President Trump and Stephen Miller’s ruthless agenda: they will go so far with their cruel immigration operation to target terrified children, forcing them to articulate their fears in front of a judge and explain why they must remain in this country,” said Senator Durbin in a statement. “As a father and grandfather, I cannot fathom the cruelty this Administration has inflicted on immigrants—including children across the country. I will continue to work with the National Immigrant Justice Center and Children’s Legal Center to end this administration’s disgusting attacks on children and relegate their actions to the dustbin of history where they belong.”

“Children are being seen in immigration court without lawyers, without parents, and facing a language barrier, and being asked to explain why they deserve to stay in this country,” said Representative Quigley. “These are kids young enough to be playing with toys while they wait for their turn in front of a judge. A judge who couldn’t even show up to the courtroom to look these children in the eye. As always, the cruelty is the point. Using children to instill fear and intimidate immigrant communities is beyond the pale. I’m going to keep working with the National Immigrant Justice Center, the Children’s Legal Center, and Senator Durbin to protect immigrant kids and families.”

The children who appeared in the Chicago court on Thursday were some of the hundreds nationally who have been scheduled for expedited hearings with little notice in recent months, as the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda has increasingly targeted children. On July 31, the administration ended federal contracts that for years had ensured unaccompanied immigrant children had access to legal advice and representation. Since then, hundreds of more children have been scheduled for USCIS interviews, which advocates fear could result in coming weeks in even more children being put into deportation proceedings before a court that has been turned against them.

Illinois General Assembly members and legal services providers who attended Thursday’s court hearings provided the following statements:

Michael Hoyt, managing attorney, National Immigrant Justice Center:

“The Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda is escalating its attacks on children. The administration has weaponized a court system against them. It’s violated their due process. It’s put children with pending and approved protections into the deportation pipeline. Throughout 2026, the average time in custody at government shelters for immigrant youth has skyrocketed. At the same time, court hearings for these youth have dramatically accelerated. Our children in detention often have loved ones here in the community ready to receive them, yet this morning, even in cases where children are eligible or have been approved for protection under law, immigration courts entered removal orders against those children.”

Illinois Senator Cristina Castro:

“When I attended proceedings involving unaccompanied minors, I expected to see Ashley’s Law, which I helped pass, in action. Instead, I witnessed a process seemingly designed to speed cases through court, contrary to due process and the law’s protections. This only strengthens my commitment to safeguarding the rights of our most vulnerable.”

Laura Smith, executive director, Children’s Legal Center:

“Today, the Chicago Immigration Court ordered six of our children removed from the United States without due process. These children fled to the United States seeking safety and protection from the horrors that no children should have to endure. Instead of following the law, instead of adjudicating these children’s applications, instead of protecting abandoned children, the Department of Justice has directed immigration judges to order the removal of these children from the United States. The law is clear, and we will continue to fight to hold this administration accountable for their violations of the law.”

Danielle DeWinter, legal director, The Immigration Project:

“What we are seeing in court is kids being removed with approved relief, kids fearing whether or not they’ll be able to have their day in court or have representation because of cut funding. That is exactly what is happening not only in Illinois but nationwide. We need continued support, we need continued change, and we need continued funding to be able to help support these children to make sure that they have their day in court and can have due process.”

Illinois Representative Lilian Jimenez:

“While Illinois is finding ways to protect children, creating hope and pathways to legalization for unaccompanied minors with our work on Ashley’s Law, this administration is hell bent on traumatizing families and young people. It’s got to stop and we will continue to work with partners to protect children in Illinois.”

text:
TROY — The state attorney general’s office on Thursday filed a lawsuit against Rensselaer County Sheriff Kyle Bourgault asking a judge to vacate an agreement the county has with the federal government to coordinate on immigration enforcement.

The lawsuit, which also names Rensselaer County as a defendant, was filed in state Supreme Court after Bourgault became the only sheriff in New York to defy a new law that took effect earlier this week and bans formal agreements involving civil immigration enforcement coordination between local, state and federal agencies.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Although there is no indication that Rensselaer County — or other county sheriff’s departments — have participated in civil immigration enforcement matters, the agreements are still banned under the law that was passed as part of the state budget this year.

The lawsuit was filed a day after Bourgault and 14 other New York sheriffs filed a federal lawsuit challenging the new statute. That lawsuit noted that many local police departments in New York have multiple types of written agreements with federal immigration agencies; the complaint alleges that New York’s various new laws restricting that collaborative law enforcement work with federal agencies are a constitutional overreach.

The Times Union reported Wednesday that multiple sheriffs provided affirmations in their federal lawsuit noting that their departments have not participated in any matters with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement concerning only civil immigration proceedings, which is what the state law was intended to ban. Their departments have worked with ICE to process or serve warrants on immigrants charged with crimes, they said, which is something that Gov. Kathy Hochul this week acknowledged that she supports.

“Once they’re convicted and do their time, we work with ICE to ensure they’re deported,” Hochul said Tuesday, referring to immigrants who are in the U.S. illegally and have committed crimes.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

When asked for comment on the state attorney general’s lawsuit, Rensselaer County Executive Steve McLaughlin said, “We’ll see them in court in 14 days.”

He was apparently referring to an order U.S. District Court Judge Mae A. D’Agostino issued this week directing the state to file a response by Sept. 9 to the 15 sheriffs' request for a temporary restraining order that would suspend enforcement of the new law. But D’Agostino’s order said that she would determine whether to conduct a hearing in the case after receiving the state’s opposition papers and any replies.

The war of words between McLaughlin and state leaders that include Hochul and state Attorney General Letitia James has intensified over the past month after the attorney general’s office demanded in a letter sent to multiple New York sheriffs on July 24 that they confirm what steps they were taking to terminate their agreements with ICE.

Rensselaer County, according to the attorney general’s office, was the only department that did not respond to their request and apparently chose not to end its agreement with ICE. In a news release announcing their lawsuit against the county, the attorney general’s office cited public statements McLaughlin had made about his intent to defy the state law, including saying that the governor and attorney general “could take that letter, crumple it up and shove it.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“All law enforcement agencies are expected to uphold New York’s laws,” James said. “The Rensselaer County Sheriff’s Office has been given every opportunity to follow the law, yet has chosen not to. My office is suing to enforce New York’s laws and ensure that local law enforcement agencies remain focused on their most fundamental responsibility: keeping New Yorkers safe.”

The attorney general’s lawsuit seeks a court order directing the county to terminate its agreement with ICE and also an order declaring that agreement is “void and unenforceable as a matter of law.”

It’s unclear whether the county could face any penalties for defying the state law.

Nearly a dozen sheriff’s departments in New York terminated their agreements with ICE in recent weeks. But many of those sheriffs noted their agreements were narrow in scope and only allowed designated officers only to serve warrants and complete custodial transfers of migrants who are in jailed on local criminal charges at the time of their release.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Some police departments in the U.S. have agreements with ICE that allow their officers to be deputized as federal immigration officers “to question, arrest, and detain people for suspected violations of federal civil immigration law,” according to the attorney general’s office. But the sheriffs challenging New York’s law banning the agreement said their agreements only involved enforcement actions such as serving immigration warrants — and only on individuals who were already in their jails for unrelated crimes.

The federal statute that authorizes the various types of agreements — Section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act — was added to the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, which was adopted during the administration of President Bill Clinton. The congressionally approved legislation was amended in 2002 to authorize the secretary of the Department of Homeland Security — which was created after the 9/11 terrorist attacks — to enter into written agreements with state and local agencies “so that qualified personnel can perform certain functions of an immigration officer.”

Other federal contracts, including some that may fall under the umbrella of section 287(g), also have enabled local and state law enforcement agencies to house people who are being held in custody on behalf of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Broome County Sheriff Fred Akshar, a former state senator, said in an affirmation filed in the federal lawsuit filed this week that his department’s agreement with the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is part of what’s known as a Warrant Service Officer Program — which is one of the most limited forms of 287(g) agreements under the section of federal law that created the programs.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Like other sheriffs, he said their agreement had not resulted in the department assisting with any cases involving only civil immigration proceedings.

“It operates only inside the jail. Its purpose is to allow designated officers to serve immigration warrants and complete custodial transfers of people who are already in local criminal custody at the moment of scheduled release,” Akshar wrote in his affirmation. “Our designated officers did not make civil immigration arrests in the community, did not conduct traffic stops for immigration status, and did not question people on the street about their papers.”

But Hochul and other state officials have implied in their public statements that the agreements have led to local sheriff’s departments participating in ICE raids or helping round up migrants who may be facing only deportation proceedings.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

In a related case, D’Agostino, the federal judge, last month rejected the U.S. Justice Department’s request for a temporary injunction to block the portion of the law that bans the 287(g) agreements. D’Agostino concluded that the law prohibiting those agreements does not impede federal immigration enforcement activities.

title: ICE officer's release from Texas jail opens a new front in the escalating fight over extradition
authors: MICHAEL GONZALEZ, VALERIE GONZALEZ and SUDHIN THANAWALA, MICHAEL GONZALEZ, VALERIE GONZALEZ, SUDHIN THANAWALA, Associated Press

text:
BROWNSVILLE, Texas (AP) — The release of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer from a Texas jail on Thursday despite Minnesota’s request for his return could set a dangerous precedent, increasing friction between states and helping criminal defendants avoid justice, legal experts said.

Christian Castro was released from a detention center in Brownsville after Texas Gov. Greg Abbott declined to immediately sign his extradition warrant. A federal judge also declined to block Castro’s release or order Abbott to sign the warrant.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Minnesota officials say they believe Castro could flee to Mexico to avoid prosecution on charges he shot a man and lied about it during an immigration crackdown in Minneapolis in January. Extradition from Mexico would require action by the Trump administration, which opened an investigation into Castro's actions but also has argued ICE agents have “absolute immunity” for their actions on duty.

The standoff between the two states is highly unusual. Under federal law, states have little discretion to reject extradition requests from fellow states. Thousands of fugitives are sent to other states each year as a matter of routine.

But Abbott, a Republican, said last week he would not respond to Minnesota’s extradition request, citing the ongoing investigation into fraud in government social service programs in the state, which President Donald Trump used to justify his immigration crackdown there.

The decision is alarming because it injects politics into the extradition process, said Marsh Halberg, a criminal defense attorney and former prosecutor in Minnesota.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“Something that’s been a routine process may now turn into a political card,” he said in a phone interview.

In recent months, California and New York have rejected extradition requests from Louisiana for doctors accused of mailing abortion pills.

But legal scholars say those cases are different because the doctors weren’t in Louisiana and never fled the state and became fugitives.

Under federal law, the New York and California governors had no duty to turn over the doctors, Georgetown University law professor Stephen Vladeck wrote on Substack.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“Abbott is just refusing to perform his,” he said.

An email to Abbott's office was not immediately returned, but he wrote in a Wednesday post on the social platform X that Minnesota's attorneys did not know the law.

Castro is charged in Minnesota with assault and falsely reporting a crime in the Jan. 14 shooting of 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis. Prosecutors in Hennepin County, where the county attorney is a Democrat, say he fired a gun through the front door of a Minneapolis home, shooting Sosa-Celis in the leg, and then falsely accused Sosa-Celis and another man of attacking an ICE officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel.

The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that “the officer in question has been suspended without pay" while the U.S. Attorney's Office investigates statements by officers involved in the Minneapolis altercation.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“Upon conclusion of the investigation, the officers may face disciplinary action, including termination of employment, as well as potential criminal prosecution,” the DHS statement said.

After a Minnesota judge issued a nationwide warrant for Castro’s arrest in May, authorities, including Minnesota’s Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, arrested him in Texas' Cameron County on May 29. Minnesota authorities have sought his extradition since then, but he remained in custody in Brownsville, a city bordering Mexico.

Under Texas law and barring extradition, Castro had to be released Thursday after 90 days in detention. Though he is free, he remains a fugitive subject to arrest in Minnesota and other states.

Abbott has exposed one of several loopholes in extradition laws that are likely to lead to more conflict between states in the future, said Ethan Lowens, a fellow at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Texas attorneys have argued that Abbott's extradition decision is still pending, as he awaits the outcome of an internal state investigation considering whether Castro was legally a fugitive.

U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. wrote Wednesday that the court couldn’t intervene without a final decision by Abbott. Minnesota had asked him to compel Castro’s extradition.

Lowens said other governors could make similar arguments to avoid extradition requests they oppose. As states diverge on laws over abortion, gender-affirming care and other issues, he said he expects such extradition conflicts to “come up more and more.”

___

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Gonzalez reported from McAllen, Texas, and Thanawala from Atlanta. Associated Press writer Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire, contributed to this story.

___

This story was corrected to fix the spelling of Gov. Abbott in one reference.

text:
The U.S. Department of Justice is suing Washington over state laws that allow undocumented immigrants to access in-state tuition and other financial assistance at public universities and colleges.

The lawsuit alleges Washington has for over two decades “ignored” federal laws that bar immigrants without legal status from being eligible for state postsecondary education benefits like grants and student loans.

Under a landmark state law passed in 2003, undocumented students can receive “resident student” status if they have a high school diploma or equivalent, live in Washington for at least a year, and file an affidavit declaring they either have already or will apply for permanent residency.

“Washington denies this same financial assistance to U.S. citizens from other states,” the Department of Justice's complaint reads. “These statutes constitute blatant unequal treatment favoring illegal aliens over U.S. citizens. Such preferential treatment is squarely prohibited and preempted by federal law.”

In a statement, a spokesperson for the Washington State Attorney General’s Office called the lawsuit “politically motivated” and said the agency looks forward to defending “longstanding Washington laws that recognize the potential and promise of all our residents regardless of citizenship status.”

The online database The Higher Ed Immigration Portal estimates roughly 15,000 undocumented students are enrolled in higher education in Washington state.

The Department of Justice on Thursday also announced similar lawsuits targeting three other states — Arizona, New Mexico, and Oregon. That brings the total number of states the Trump administration has sued over these policies to 21.

In each of the lawsuits, the Department of Justice seeks to block the states from enforcing these laws. Courts have already declared these laws unconstitutional in five states: Texas, Kentucky, Nebraska, Oklahoma, and Illinois.

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has granted a $16.7 million no-bid contract for 6,000 gloves that can deliver electric shocks, a new use-of-force tool that the agency claims will help officers control resisting detainees and avoid using more serious or lethal weapons.

Dubbed the G.L.O.V.E., or Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, the device operates as a conventional patrol glove until an officer activates its "electrical mode." Once activated, the device must make direct contact with a person's skin to deliver a painful shock designed to force compliance.

In contract paperwork released on a federal database Thursday, ICE describes the gloves as "conductive distraction and de-escalation devices," and says the new technology will offer personnel a lower-impact option during arrests, detainee transports and disturbances surrounding detention facilities. According to the agency's procurement rationale, the gloves may be used when a person is "actively or passively resisting" and an officer needs to gain control quickly.

Federal records show ICE signed the contract Wednesday with a Kentucky-based company known as Compliant Technologies LLC, but formally posted the award Thursday. The six-month deal includes the gloves, support equipment and services. The gloves themselves cost $2,495 apiece.

The agency argues the devices reduce agency reliance on physical force and, in more dangerous encounters, grant officers an alternative to resorting to a firearm.

"ICE does not currently have an empty hand use of force device to provide to the field amidst unprecedented levels of threats and violence against ICE officers and agents to help ensure they can de-escalate tense situations before they turn violent," the agency wrote in procurement documents.

ICE said the gloves would be deployed under approved policies, training requirements and accountability standards, though procurement documents do not account for those safeguards in detail.

Compliant Technologies' instruction manual says users of the gloves should "always give the subject(s) a reasonable opportunity to comply before force is used." It suggests using them for up to 15 seconds, unless the subject becomes more violent or endangers people. The company also states that the devices should not be used to punish people, and shouldn't be used on the elderly, pregnant women, small children or "the severely handicapped."

ICE first announced the planned purchase earlier this month. The plan has drawn opposition from congressional Democrats and civil rights advocates who question how the gloves will be used and whether ICE has adequate safeguards in place to prevent abuse.

Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada and 15 other Democratic senators urged ICE on Thursday to abandon the purchase, warning that a device capable of inflicting an electric shock during civil immigration arrests raises questions about proportionality, medical safety, constitutional rights and oversight.

"A device capable of delivering an electrical shock through direct contact with an individual presents substantial risks if deployed during civil arrests," the senators wrote, adding that the risks would be heightened without clear limits, adequate training and comprehensive oversight. Lawmakers demanded that ICE disclose its rules for authorized uses, safeguards and procedures for reviewing deployments moving forward.

The Department of Homeland Security has defended the purchase, accusing critics of trying to deny federal law enforcement officers safety equipment. In a statement to CBS News, a DHS spokesperson called the pushback from Democrats "despicable and a deliberate attempt to undermine and endanger our officers."

"ICE is constantly assessing the needs of our officers in the field to ensure they have the tools and equipment necessary to safely arrest and remove criminal illegal aliens from our country. Every decision is made with careful consideration and appropriately reviewed to ensure that any technology ICE utilizes is consistent with all applicable law enforcement policies and standards," the spokesperson said, adding that personnel are "highly trained in de-escalation tactics."

CBS News has reached out to Compliant Technologies for comment.

The contract marks a meaningful expansion for the glove technology that up until this point has been used primarily by local police departments and jails. Critics argue the new tactic could make it easier for immigration officers to inflict pain during routine law enforcement encounters, with use of force even less visible to the public.

text:
Takeaways

The State Department is pausing immigrant visa interview appointments while consular officers receive updated public-charge training. The agency has not publicly announced the duration or precise scope of this pause.

The pause follows an August 21 federal court decision vacating the State Department’s separate suspension of immigrant visa issuance to nationals of 75 countries.

Employers should monitor affected employees’ appointments and account for potential delays when planning start dates, relocation, or international travel.

The State Department has paused immigrant visa interview appointments at U.S. embassies and consulates to accommodate a global training initiative for consular officers. A State Department spokesperson stated that visa appointments would be adjusted to facilitate training on updated public-charge guidance. The agency has not publicly indicated the duration of the pause or whether all consular posts and immigrant visa applicants will be affected in the same manner.

Court Vacated Earlier 75-Country Immigrant Visa Suspension

The pause follows the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York’s Aug. 21, 2026, decision in Catholic Legal Immigration Network, Inc. v. Rubio, No. 26-CV-00858. The court vacated a State Department policy, which went into effect Jan. 21, that suspended immigrant visa issuance to nationals of 75 countries.

Under that policy, consular officers were directed to refuse immigrant visas under Section 221(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) based solely on an applicant’s nationality when no other ground of ineligibility applied, even when an individualized assessment did not support a public-charge finding.

The court held that the policy violated the INA’s prohibition against nationality-based discrimination in immigrant visa issuance, conflicted with the statutory and regulatory framework governing visa refusals, and exceeded the secretary’s authority. The court vacated the policy and refusals that were based solely on it. Refusals supported by an independent ground of ineligibility were not vacated.

USCIS Changes Adjustment of Status Adjudications

Separately, DHS rescinded its 2022 public-charge regulations, effective Sept. 18, 2026. In subsequent guidance, USCIS confirmed that officers will evaluate adjustment-of-status applicants subject to public-charge review.

USCIS officers will consider the following five statutory factors, along with other relevant information:

Age;

Health;

Family status;

Assets, resources, and financial status; and

Education and skills

For benefit requests received on or after Sept. 18, 2026, officers may consider any means-tested public benefit. The guidance applies to covered Forms I-485 postmarked or electronically submitted on or after that date.

Practical Implications

While USCIS adjudicates adjustment-of-status applications within the United States, the State Department administers immigrant visa processing abroad. Both developments reflect increased public-charge review across permanent residence pathways.

Applicants abroad should monitor communications from the applicable consular post and confirm appointment status before making travel arrangements.

text:
A federal district court judge on Thursday heard arguments in a class action lawsuit in which petitioners held in federal detention on civil immigration charges allege they have been unlawfully detained.

The lawsuit, filed by Helena-based Upper Seven Law on Aug. 2, was instigated by the arrest of Jesus Verde Hernandez, who lives in Worden, a small farming community in Yellowstone County, with his partner and three children, who are U.S. citizens.

According to court documents, U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) agents stopped Hernandez on July 30 when he was driving in Lewistown. The agents arrested Hernandez on civil immigration charges and detained him in Lewistown before transferring him to facilities in Jordan, Malta, Havre, and eventually the Cascade County Detention Center in Great Falls.

Upper Seven alleges that Hernandez was arrested without probable cause or a warrant and was detained unlawfully. Attorneys allege that federal officers did not conduct a required flight risk assessment or evaluate whether Hernandez posed a danger to his community before detaining him. Chief United States District Court Judge Brian Morris on Aug. 7 ruled in favor of Hernandez individually and ordered the government to release him from detention.

Class members include individuals who, like Hernandez, are or have been detained by the federal government on civil immigration charges, and who allege they are or were wrongfully detained. As of Aug. 21, approximately 41 plaintiffs had joined the class, according to Upper Seven. Lawyers representing the class allege that the petitioners’ continued detention violates their constitutional rights and have asked Morris to grant their immediate release or, alternatively, order bond hearings.

A lawyer representing the respondents — who include Cascade County Sheriff Jesse Slaughter, Acting Attorney General of the United States Todd Blanche, Department of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and several CBP and Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials — argued Thursday that the judge does not have legal authority to grant the requested relief.

The case comes amid a national rise in habeas petitions, or petitions for release, as the Trump administration deploys federal immigration agents in multiple American cities to enact mass deportation policies, sometimes without clear processes. There have been five habeas cases in Montana since Jan. 2025, according to ProPublica.

COURT HEARING

Arguments in Thursday’s hearing were highly technical, involving primarily whether the judge has authority to grant a certain type of relief.

Randy Tanner, a lawyer representing the federal government who appeared via Zoom, argued that the court does not have authority in this case to grant injunctive relief, which Tanner said could include an order requiring the government to provide bond hearings. Injunctive relief refers to a court order requiring an entity to take a certain action.

Upper Seven attorney Andres Haladay argued that the petitioners are not seeking injunctive relief, but rather declaratory relief, or a statement that an action is unlawful, and habeas relief, or release from detention, which he said the court has authority to rule on.

Tanner also alleged that the petitioners have not satisfied certain criteria necessary to define their class. He said there is “no evidence that the circumstances of Mr. Hernandez’s arrest are indicative, typical or common of the other class members.”

Haladay argued that the record reveals a pattern of individuals being arrested and detained without individual assessments of flight risk.

“The government is not doing what it is supposed to do under statute,” he said.

Morris said he would issue an order “as soon as I can.”

CLASS MEMBERS

While most members of the class are unnamed, court documents include details regarding at least three people who allege they’ve been wrongfully detained. Each alleges having been arrested without being served a warrant. They describe poor conditions in detention and allege that federal immigration agents pressured them to sign documents, according to court filings.

Jonny Hernandez Antunez, a 26-year-old who lives in Butte, was arrested and detained by CBP agents on Aug. 5 in Billings, according to court documents.

“A CBP agent put me in his car and told me that he wanted me to run so that he could use his gun on me,” according to Antunez’s declaration. “… I was terrified.”

Antunez also alleges that agents asked him to sign a document written in English, which he cannot read, and later told him the document was a “voluntary departure form.” Antunez alleges that after he was arrested, Border Patrol agents put him and other detainees in “the back of a truck that was like a box.”

“I began hitting the wall of the box, asking for more air,” according to his declaration. “At some point, my heart began to beat really fast. I felt the guy sitting next to me pour water on my head. I’m not sure exactly what happened, but I believe that I passed out from the heat.”

Antunez, who as of Aug. 27 was still detained in Cascade County, alleged in court documents that he shares a cell with two people detained on criminal charges.

“They do not speak Spanish, so I cannot speak to them,” he wrote in a declaration. “There are only two beds. I sleep on a pad on the floor.”

Irving Alonso Acosta, 26, lives in Phoenix, Arizona, with his wife and son, who are both U.S. citizens. He and his family were on vacation in North Dakota on Aug. 10 when they drove to Sidney for medical care. Acosta alleges they took a wrong turn, and while they were parked at a gas station, a local sheriff’s deputy arrested him and took him to a local sheriff’s office. There, according to court documents, a CBP agent arrested Acosta and took him to Plentywood and then to a nearby CBP office, where he was detained. He alleges that while he was resting in his cell in a Border Patrol office near Plentywood, a Border Patrol agent “kicked me in my back to get my attention.” He alleges the agent “threatened me and told me that if I talked to anyone, such as an attorney, I would have to stay in the jail.” Acosta alleges the agent pressured him to sign a document without speaking with his wife, and said, “if you don’t sign, I’m going to sign it for you.”

Acosta alleges that Border Patrol agents transferred him to the Cascade County Detention Center, where he remains detained, between the night of Aug. 13 and the morning of Aug. 14. He alleges that he is allowed out of his cell one hour a day, sometimes at 3 a.m., making it difficult to contact his wife or lawyer.

Jose Alfredo Martinez Alaniz lives in Denver, but had been staying with his brother in Missoula. He alleges that he and his brother, Margarito Martinez Alaniz, were driving to Missoula from Denver when a Montana Highway Patrol trooper pulled them over on Aug. 3. Jose’s declaration alleges that a Border Patrol agent was in the state trooper’s car. A Border Patrol agent, according to court documents, arrested Alaniz and his brother and transported them, along with other detainees, to a Border Patrol station near the Canadian border. There, Alaniz alleges in court documents, Border Patrol agents asked him questions without advising him that he could talk to a lawyer. Alaniz wrote in his declaration that he signed paperwork assenting to voluntary departure “because I thought it meant I could get out of detention faster.” He signed several other documents, though he alleges that agents did not explain their contents. On Aug. 5, Border Patrol agents transported Alaniz and his brother to Cascade County Detention Center, where they remain detained, according to court documents.

“I want to remain in the United States with my family,” Alaniz wrote in his declaration. “I feel exhausted and scared being in detention and not knowing what will happen to me.”

text:
On Aug. 21, 2026, in Catholic Legal Immigration Network (CLINIC), et al. v. Rubio, a federal district court vacated the State Department policy requiring consular officers to pause issuance of immigrant visas to nationals of 75 designated countries, ruling that “the Policy is contrary to law and was issued in excess of Secretary Rubio’s statutory authority.”

Key takeaways:

The immigrant visa issuance suspension policy violated the INA. The policy, announced Jan. 14 and effective Jan. 21, 2026, directed consular officers to pause issuance of immigrant visas to nationals of 75 countries if no other ground of ineligibility applied. The U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York concluded that the policy violated the Immigration and Nationality Act’s (INA) prohibition on nationality discrimination in immigrant visa issuance.

Under the APA, the policy exceeded the Secretary of State’s authority. The court held that under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), Congress reserved decisions on granting or refusing visas for consular officers and excluded those decisions from the secretary’s administrative authority.

Visa refusals based solely on the suspension policy are to be set aside and remanded. The court directed consular officers to reconsider those applications without relying on the vacated policy, stating, “In remanding these applications for adjudication by the consular officers, the Court does not direct any particular outcome or process so long as any refusal is not based upon the Policy.” The order does not disturb refusals based on other statutory grounds of ineligibility, even if the suspension policy was also cited. The ruling does not guarantee visa issuance, and consular officers retain authority to determine eligibility under applicable law.

Additional information: Separate presidential actions regarding travel restrictions or proclamations for certain countries are not part of this case and remain in force, unless impacted by other court orders.

The government may appeal the decision, and yesterday plaintiffs asked the court to enforce its judgment. BAL is monitoring the litigation and will provide updates. BAL clients are encouraged to work closely with their BAL teams to assess case-specific next steps.

This alert has been provided by the BAL U.S. Practice Group.

text:
By Kanishka Singh

WASHINGTON, Aug 27 (Reuters) – The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency granted a $16.7 million contract to buy 6,000 pairs of electric shock gloves for officers ​in the field despite human rights advocates having raised ‌alarm about the plans when they were revealed earlier this month.

• A notice on a federal database said that ICE, which has been the face of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, entered into a no-bid contract ‌to ​purchase the gloves from Kentucky-based firm Compliant ⁠Technologies.

• The notice said ⁠6,000 of the devices, which can give painful electric shocks and aim to disrupt an individual’s capacity to respond, will be bought with support equipment and services over the next ​six months.

• The website of the Department of Homeland Security, of which ICE is a part, said this month ⁠ICE planned to buy CTG-5 Generated ⁠Low Output Voltage Emitter, or GLOVE units.

• The ​American Civil Liberties Union said that giving immigration agents “a concealed means ​of delivering terrible pain is a recipe for more ‌harm to the public and less accountability.”

• DHS described the gloves as “a Conductive Distraction and De-escalation Device which will be issued to Homeland Security Investigations and Enforcement Removal Operations officers and ⁠agents.”

• Fatal shootings by ICE agents of two U.S. citizens in Minnesota earlier this year and concerns by rights groups about conditions in ⁠ICE detention have ‌sparked protests.

• Over 50 people have died ⁠in ICE custody nationwide since Trump took office ​early ‌last year.

• Trump says his immigration crackdown aims ​to improve ⁠domestic security.

• Rights groups call it discriminatory, saying it violates free speech and due process rights while also creating an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.

(Reporting by Kanishka Singh and Christian Martinez; Editing by Muralikumar Anantharaman ​and Lincoln Feast)

From Palo Alto to Washington D.C., RNs condemned Palantir’s support of ICE kidnappings and imprisonment

On Thursday, Aug. 27, hundreds of registered nurses – joined by patients and community allies – mobilized to demand hospitals and elected officials immediately cut ties with artificial intelligence giant Palantir. The nurses, who are members of National Nurses United, the nation’s largest union of registered nurses, stopped traffic in an act of civil disobedience in eight cities: Palo Alto, California; Los Angeles, California; Chicago, Illinois; Washington, D.C.; Portland, Maine; Asheville, North Carolina; Austin, Texas; and New Orleans, Louisiana.

The actions included visual displays of the deadly costs of Palantir’s products, including its development and operation of ELITE, an application used by federal agents that identifies people for arrest using, in part, improperly obtained Medicaid data.

In each city, nurses placed 50 pairs of baby shoes in the street – one pair of shoes representing every 10 babies who have been detained since President Trump took office. Passersby could also see large images of the heart-wrenching notes written by some of the 6,000 children who have been imprisoned by federal agents since the second Trump term began.

The nurses also held large red umbrellas emblazoned with eyes, symbolizing that nurses are keeping an eye on Palantir’s harmful activities.

“Union nurses cannot be silent when our most vulnerable people, babies and children, are being detained by federal immigration agents,” said NNU President Jamie Brown, RN. “While our patients and neighbors are living in fear of immigration raids enabled by Palantir, our hospitals are facing huge cuts and our patients are facing mounting health care costs because of H.R. 1. Nurses aren’t just saying no to Palantir, but we’re calling for our public resources to go toward the benefit of working people, not billionaires and their corporations.”

While the U.S. government and corporations award the company billions of dollars in contracts to Palantir, the U.S. health care system faces a dire threat. H.R. 1 is the 2025 budget bill, pushed through by Republicans and President Trump, that cut more than $1 trillion in Medicaid and Medicare funding to give billionaires tax breaks, militarize immigration enforcement, and fund endless wars abroad. Not only will these cuts threaten health coverage for millions of people, they risk closures and service cuts at more than 600 hospitals nationwide, according to new NNU research.

NNU President Brown continued: “What we know is the money spent on ICE detention could fund health care for at least 12 million children every single year. Nurses and our allies condemn these unjust, misguided political choices. Everyone deserves health care, education, and housing. Our politics should not be controlled by billionaires.”

Purge Palantir allies join RNs nationwide.

Across the eight cities, NNU nurses were joined by community allies in their calls to “Purge Palantir!”.

“Palantir makes money by enabling mass violence in the U.S. and around the world,” said Kenny Morris, campaigns strategist for the American Friends Service Committee. “The surveillance company has no place in our hospitals, our utilities, our investments, or our government. This day of action shows just how many communities are organizing to push our institutions to cut ties with Palantir.”

“It is critical times like these, where Palantir brings us together across movements, crystallizing a common enemy,” said Olivia DiNucci, D.C. organizer for CodePink. “The fight for Medicare for All, the fight to end the genocide in Gaza, the fight to end mass surveillance and deportations are unified to cut ties and influence of Palantir and its profiting on mass deportations, genocide and war, and a for-profit healthcare system."

“In a moment where Big Tech is attempting to become the final decision maker of what is democracy, freedom, and what is the definition of privacy, we see it essential for all sectors of labor and organizing to come together against this common evil,” said Cathy Carrillo, organizer for Mijente. “Palantir is at the forefront of the chaos happening to immigrant communities and the attempt to expand surveillance and AI in all other sectors. We are united in the call to Purge Palantir.”

“Palantir is a secretive data and AI company whose technology facilitates ICE terror and enables the Israeli military’s genocide on Gaza,” said Dani Noble, campaigns organizer for Jewish Voice for Peace. “Palantir should have no place in our hospitals — it’s designed to control and to harm. It is a company built on unlawful surveillance deeply embedded in policing and war, all to generate profit for right-wing billionaires.”

“Palantir’s AI technology is used to harm our communities by putting patient care in the hands of a machine, identifying and tracking immigrants for ICE abduction, and targeting Palestinians in Gaza for assassination,” said fatima mohammadi, director of organizing at U.S. Campaign for Palestinian Rights (USCPR). “The well-being and safety of our loved ones and neighbors are at stake. Palantir out of hospitals! Every institution must cut ties with Palantir now.” [Note: the lowercase name is intentional.]

Nurses say: “Palantir Out!”

Palantir’s growing notoriety – fueled by a growing wave of grassroots protests organized by nurses and criticism from employees, clients, and elected officials – have threatened its business and made its brand politically toxic in the United States and abroad. However, Palantir continues to benefit from its close relationship with the Trump administration, and, increasingly, with the U.S. hospital industry.

From 2009 to 2025, Palantir received $2.5 billion in federal government funding, but this number has grown tremendously in just the past year. Last July, the Department of Defense announced a $10 billion agreement with Palantir to use its technology to share data across federal agencies, enabling unprecedented surveillance power. This followed a $30 million contract awarded to Palantir by the Department of Homeland Security to build an AI-powered system that would identify immigrants for deportation. In Feb. 2026, the Department of Homeland Security and Palantir signed a $1 billion contract.

In the hospital industry, already, Palantir manages more than one-fifth of U.S. hospital beds. For nurses, this marks a dangerous threat to the nursing profession, which is seeing a glut of untested and unregulated technology introduced into patient care settings.

The firm’s technology is already being used for automated scheduling and staffing in the largest for-profit hospital group in the country, Hospital Corporation of America (HCA). Timpani, otherwise known as HCA Inspire, is used for nursing staff scheduling, removing hospitals’ local managers from staffing decisions and replacing them with an anonymous office in Nashville.

Even these limited applications are already exacerbating the nationwide staffing crisis, as executives are rushing to use untested and unregulated technology to replace clinical judgement and make critical health care decisions like how many nurses are on a unit to take care of patients on a shift.

Other hospitals represented by NNU, like MaineHealth, are also using Palantir technologies. As with HCA, MaineHealth has refused to disclose the extent of the hospital’s cooperation with Palantir, including how patients’ and health care workers’ data are being protected. That lack of transparency only underscores the importance of demanding hospitals purge Palantir out of their operations.

text:
On Aug. 21, 2026, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York issued a decision in Catholic Legal Immigration Network (CLINIC), et al. v. Rubio, striking down a Department of State policy that suspended immigrant visa issuance to nationals of 75 countries based on generalized public charge concerns and vacated the policy.

Background

In January 2026, the Department of State announced a policy directing U.S. consular officers to refuse immigrant visas to nationals of 75 designated countries. The policy was based on concerns that individuals from those countries were more likely to rely on public benefits in the United States. As a result, applicants could be denied immigrant visas regardless of their personal circumstances or whether they were otherwise eligible for visa issuance.

Countries Affected by the Immigrant Visa Ban

The ban applied to nationals of the following 75 countries: Afghanistan, Albania, Algeria, Antigua and Barbuda, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Bahamas, Bangladesh, Barbados, Belarus, Belize, Bhutan, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Brazil, Burma, Cambodia, Cameroon, Cape Verde, Colombia, Cote d’Ivoire, Cuba, Republic of the Congo (Congo-Brazzaville), Democratic Republic of the Congo (Congo-Kinshasa), Dominica, Egypt, Eritrea, Ethiopia, Fiji, The Gambia, Georgia, Ghana, Grenada, Guatemala, Guinea, Haiti, Iran, Iraq, Jamaica, Jordan, Kazakhstan, Kosovo, Kuwait, Kyrgyzstan, Laos, Lebanon, Liberia, Libya, Moldova, Mongolia, Montenegro, Morocco, Nepal, Nicaragua, Nigeria, North Macedonia, Pakistan, Russia, Rwanda, Saint Kitts and Nevis, Saint Lucia, Saint Vincent and the Grenadines, Senegal, Sierra Leone, Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, Syria, Tanzania, Thailand, Togo, Tunisia, Uganda, Uruguay, Uzbekistan, and Yemen.

The policy was based on an individual’s nationality rather than their country of residence. As a result, a citizen of one of the listed countries might be subject to the ban even if they reside permanently in another country or apply for a visa from a third country.

The Court’s Decision and Its Impact on Applicants

The court found that the policy was inconsistent with U.S. immigration law because it exceeded the secretary of state’s statutory and regulatory authority, and imposed a blanket nationality-based restriction rather than requiring the individualized review of each applicant’s eligibility. The court held that visa applicants must be assessed on a case-by-case basis and that the Department of State exceeded its authority by categorically denying visas based solely on nationality. Accordingly, the court vacated the policy and directed the Department of State to restore individualized processing of visa applications.

This decision reaffirms that immigrant visa applications must be evaluated based on each applicant’s individual circumstances rather than broad assumptions tied to nationality. However, the ruling does not eliminate public charge screening or other visa eligibility requirements, and applicants must still satisfy all applicable requirements for immigrant visa issuance.

The government may appeal the decision.

text:
PHOENIX — The Trump administration is suing the Arizona Board of Regents for allowing certain people living in the country illegally, known as “Dreamers,” to pay the same tuition as all other Arizona residents.

In legal papers filed in federal court, the Department of Justice says the policy, approved by Arizona voters in 2022, violates a 1998 federal law.

It also runs afoul of a sweeping executive order issued last year by President Donald Trump directing the agency to take action against any state that gives benefits to people living in the country illegally that are not available to all American citizens. That, the order says, includes “state laws that provide in-state higher education tuition to aliens but not to out-of-state American citizens.”

Similar lawsuits have been filed against more than a dozen other states, according to Assistant Attorney General Garrett Greene, who signed the new lawsuit. He said judges in five states have voided those policies.

Proposition 308, the 2022 ballot measure, allows certain Arizona high school graduates who meet other conditions to pay the same tuition available to state residents, regardless of immigration status. At the same time, U.S. citizens from another state can be required to pay the higher non-resident tuition.

In fact, one provision in that voter-approved law specifically says that “persons without lawful immigration status are eligible for in-state tuition.”

Attorney General Kris Mayes, anticipating such a lawsuit, issued a legal opinion last year contending that the wording of the 2022 ballot measure is sufficiently different from what federal law forbids.

That opinion states that in-state tuition eligibility is not based on Arizona residency. Instead, to qualify, someone needed to have attended an Arizona high school “while physically present in this state for at least two years” and having obtained a diploma in Arizona.

That, Mayes said, means residency does not trigger eligibility. Therefore, it does not run afoul of the federal law that prohibits states from offering in-state tuition to their Arizona residents, regardless of legal status, while denying the same benefit to U.S. residents from elsewhere.

“Although many people who meet the eligibility requirements will also be residents, not all will be,” she said.

“For example, a student could meet the statute’s attendance and graduation requirement, move to another state, and then plan to return to Arizona for college,” Mayes wrote in her legal opinion. “That student would not be a current Arizona resident, but would be eligible for in-state tuition.”

She also said the law allows in-state tuition for someone who crosses into Arizona every day from another state to attend school here despite being a legal resident of that other state.

Conversely, she said, some Arizona residents will not be eligible for in-state tuition because they did not attend high school for the two years required by the law and did not graduate from high school here.

Justice Department lawyers, however, say the result is the same: Arizona residents in this country without legal status pay a tuition rate lower than U.S. citizens who are residents of other states.

The new lawsuit also asks a federal judge to overturn Prop. 308 as violating the supremacy of federal laws on immigration. And, according to federal attorneys, that would also override policies at Maricopa and Pima community colleges that mirror those of the universities.

The issue of tuition for those who are not citizens traces its roots back to the Obama administration, which created the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program in 2012. It allows people who arrived in this country illegally as children before 2007 — colloquially called “Dreamers” — to remain and even to work if they meet certain conditions.

Based on that, the Maricopa Community College system and, later, the Arizona Board of Regents agreed to let DACA recipients pay in-state tuition. But the Arizona Supreme Court ruled in 2018 that is precluded by Proposition 300, a 2006 ballot measure that denies various public benefits to those not in the country legally — including any form of subsidized tuition.

Prop. 308, approved by a margin of 51.2% to 48.8%, was crafted to create an exception.

In a prepared statement, Mayes took a swat at the administration for filing suit, not just here but against other states.
