title: ICE is arresting a record number of immigrants — a majority have no criminal history
description:
The share of arrests of immigrants with past violent criminal convictions fell to less than 4 percent.
Those immigrants, as well as immigrants already in the custody of local law enforcement, then become easy targets for arrest and removal.
Spikes in removal flights to third countries Deportation flights are also increasing.
Deportation flights on U.S. military aircraft also resumed in June, with at least 25 removal flights to Honduras by the end of July.
Removal flights to so-called “third” countries — where immigrants have no connection — also reached a record high last month.
text:
Donald Trump’s administration hit record highs of monthly immigration enforcement arrests this summer, with more than 43,000 people arrested in June and another 50,000 arrested in July.

But last month, for the first time since Trump took office, more than half of all people arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement had no prior criminal convictions or pending charges.

A growing majority of immigrants targeted by federal law enforcement officers have no criminal history whatsoever, as officers increasingly target immigrants whose legal status has lapsed or been stripped by the Trump administration, according to new reviews of federal data. The share of arrests of immigrants with past violent criminal convictions fell to less than 4 percent.

The administration has instead shifted its focus to legal immigration pathways, including people seeking asylum, the spouses of U.S citizens stuck in legal limbo, and refugees with temporary legal status whose humanitarian protections were revoked, forcing them to return to volatile countries they fled.

Those immigrants, as well as immigrants already in the custody of local law enforcement, then become easy targets for arrest and removal.

Earlier this year, ICE officials told Congress that the agency plans to deport one million people — and hold at least 99,000 people on any given day in ICE detention centers — in the 2026 and 2027 fiscal years.

To meet those goals, the administration has pumped billions of dollars into the Department of Homeland Security, with ambitious plans to scale up detention space and hire more officers. Secretary Markwayne Mullin has been hoping to avoid damning images of militarized officers storming through cities that plagued his predecessor Kristi Noem, but the administration is now confronting scrutiny over the fatal shootings of two immigrants by ICE officers during traffic stops and a surge of arrests targeting immigrants who have been in the country for years without issue.

More money for officers

As ICE shifts away from arresting people with criminal records, the percentage of ICE “arrests” at prisons and jails has steadily fallen, according to data reviewed by the American Immigration Council.

Instead, a growing share of ICE arrests are being carried out “at large,” or by officers who track down and arrest people at work, in their homes or in traffic stops. Roughly 63 percent of all ICE arrests were performed “at large” by an officer or through state and local police, according to the American Immigration Council. Those arrests are often supported by state and local authorities through the 287(g) program, which effectively deputizes local police to carry out federal immigration enforcement.

The number of people brought into ICE custody through the 287(g) program is now roughly 14 percent, according to data collected by the Deportation Data Project and reviewed by The New York Times.

Florida police have tallied at least 15,000 such arrests under Trump, according to The Times review. But the program has seen heavier impacts in states without a significant ICE footprint, including Wyoming and West Virginia, where 287(g) arrests in both states have hit more than than 50 percent.

Immigrants stuck in legal limbo

The administration also doesn’t appear to be targeting people with final orders of removal, decisions by immigration court judges requiring immigrants to leave the country. In the first week of August, roughly one quarter of arrests targeted people with final orders of removal.

Instead, the administration is increasingly arresting people stuck in bureaucratic hurdles.

ICE is arresting people with lapsed legal status while their paperwork is pending, including immigrants who overstayed their visas while awaiting extensions or green cards. Under previous administrations, those immigrants were rarely detained while in legal limbo, but the president’s mass deportation campaign has labeled any misstep — even if the lengthy wait times are the government’s fault — as illegal or criminal.

The administration is also working to rapidly remove roughly one million people in the U.S. with humanitarian protections after fleeing disaster and violence in their home countries.

In June, the Supreme Court allowed Homeland Security to revoke Temporary Protected Status for Haiti and Syria, two nations rocked by political instability and humanitarian crises. That decision opened the door for the administration to begin stripping protections for tens of thousands of other immigrants from a dozen other nations with the designation.

Following the ruling, administration officials said they intended to begin removing 350,000 Haitians and roughly 6,000 Syrians whose protections have now been revoked.

Spikes in removal flights to third countries

Deportation flights are also increasing.

Domestic transfer flights between ICE detention centers peaked in July, reaching an “alarming” monthly record of 1,363 flights across 61 U.S. cities, according to data collected by Human Rights First’s ICE Flight Monitor project.

Those flights amount to the most domestic shuttle flights since at least 2020 when the group first began tracking them.

Deportation flights on U.S. military aircraft also resumed in June, with at least 25 removal flights to Honduras by the end of July.

Last month, ICE performed at least 329 removal flights to 37 countries, an increase of 14 percent from the previous month, Human Rights First found.

Removal flights to so-called “third” countries — where immigrants have no connection — also reached a record high last month. Human Rights first tracked 18 flights to 10 countries, with first-time flights to Belize and Dominica, and repeated flights to Central African Republic, Costa Rica, Equatorial Guinea, Eswatini, Ghana, Panama, Paraguay and Sierra Leone.

Within just 24 hours this month, from August 20-21, Human Rights First tracked third country transfers to Liberia, Equatorial Guinea, Cameroon and Paraguay, as well as flights deporting Mexicans to Guatemala, Honduras and Costa Rica.

“We are extremely concerned about the egregious violations of people’s due process rights when they are summarily removed to a third country,” as well as the conditions they face upon arrival and the “very real risk people face of being sent onward from those countries to the very places from which they fled,” according to Savi Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First.

Homeland Security provided arrest photos of six men taken into custody, including Alexei Marti-Martinez, who was convicted of grand theft. ICE filed a detainer against him in April 2025 and recently arrested him.

Carlos Cortez-Aquino, who pleaded guilty in 2020 to aggravated assault with a deadly weapon and served a year in jail, was also arrested by ICE six years after his release. Antonio Cordova-Sajic, arrested in 2020 for lewd and lascivious conduct and later violating probation in 2022, was taken into custody four years after his initial arrest.

"All of these cases that were administratively closed five, six, ten years ago, people are getting picked up. So no, they haven't committed a new crime," DeMine said.

DeMine explained that previous administrations did not prioritize these cases, but the second Trump administration has changed that policy. "I believe what we're seeing is these ICE officers have quotas they have to meet," DeMine said.

In a statement, ICE said, "Every day, DHS is conducting law enforcement activities across the country to keep Americans safe. DHS does not discuss ongoing or future operations."

ICE arrests in Lee County are expected to continue through Friday.

DANBURY, Connecticut (WABC) -- People in Connecticut are reporting an uptick in ICE raids and there's growing concern among immigrant communities.

A woman says she spoke briefly with her husband who was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement on Monday morning in Stamford.

"He didn't say much. I don't know if it's because he doesn't want me to worry about it or I'm not sure."

According to the woman who did not want to be identified, Fidel Romero has no criminal record and is the father of three children.

Her employer Chloe Layman, said the detention reflects a growing concern among residents about immigration enforcement activity in the area.

"I think there's a kind of like naivete. You live in a blue state and you think these things aren't going to happen. That it's a horrifying news story you're going to read in the news from several time zones away," Layman said.

The detention comes amid what residents and activists described as an increase in ICE activity across Fairfield County this week.

In Danbury, an estimated 50 people have been taken into custody this week, according to community activists.

"A part of the reason why they're having this uptick right now is because school is starting and parents are letting their kids back in and to make the community and the people feel unsafe," said "Julio" of Danbury Unites for Immigrants.

Gov. Ned Lamont and other elected officials have pledged support for immigrants, reminding community members of their rights and of limits on ICE access to private property.

Activists said they plan to continue monitoring enforcement activity and notifying residents.

"We believe in justice. We believe in the rule of law. We believe in human rights and constitution rights. And none of those things are being followed by ICE at the moment," community activist Margaret Henderson said.

Community activist Fran O'Rourke added: "They're not here to protect our community. They're making it unsafe. And that's why we're here."

In a statement, an ICE spokesperson said: "For operational security and the safety of our officers, ICE will not disclose or discuss law enforcement operations. Every day, DHS enforces the laws of the nation across the country including in Connecticut."

authors: Michael Gonzalez, Valerie Gonzalez, Sudhin Thanawala, apnews.com, valerie-gonzalez, sudhin-thanawala

text:
BROWNSVILLE, Texas (AP) — Thursday’s release of an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer from a Texas jail despite Minnesota’s request for his return could set a dangerous precedent, increasing friction between states and helping criminal defendants avoid justice, legal experts said.

Christian Castro was released from a detention center in Brownsville after Texas Gov. Greg Abbott declined to immediately sign his extradition warrant. A federal judge also declined to block Castro’s release or order Abbott to sign the warrant.

Minnesota officials say they believe Castro could flee to Mexico to avoid prosecution on charges he shot a man and lied about it during the January immigration crackdown in Minneapolis. Extradition from Mexico would require action by the Trump administration, which opened an investigation into Castro’s actions but also has argued ICE agents have “absolute immunity” for their actions on duty.

The standoff between the two states is highly unusual. Under federal law, states have little discretion to reject extradition requests from fellow states. Thousands of fugitives are sent to other states each year as a matter of routine.

But Abbott, a Republican, said last week he would not respond to Minnesota’s extradition request, citing the ongoing investigation into fraud in government social service programs in the state, which President Donald Trump used to justify his immigration crackdown there.

The decision is alarming because it injects politics into the extradition process, said Marsh Halberg, a criminal defense attorney and former prosecutor in Minnesota.

“Something that’s been a routine process may now turn into a political card,” he said in a phone interview.

In recent months, California and New York have rejected extradition requests from Louisiana for doctors accused of mailing abortion pills.

But legal scholars say those cases are different because the doctors weren’t in Louisiana and never fled the state and became fugitives.

Under federal law, the New York and California governors had no duty to turn over the doctors, Georgetown University law professor Stephen Vladeck wrote on Substack.

“Abbot is just refusing to perform his,” he said.

An email to Abbott’s office was not immediately returned, but he wrote in a Wednesday post on the social platform X that Minnesota’s attorneys did not know the law. ICE also did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Castro is charged in Minnesota with assault and falsely reporting a crime in the Jan. 14 shooting of 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis. Prosecutors in Hennepin County, where the county attorney is a Democrat, say he fired a gun through the front door of a Minneapolis home, shooting Sosa-Celis in the leg, and then falsely accused Sosa-Celis and another man of attacking an ICE officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel.

After a Minnesota judge issued a nationwide warrant for Castro’s arrest in May, authorities, including Minnesota’s Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, arrested him in Texas’ Cameron County on May 29. Minnesota authorities have sought his extradition since then, but he remained in custody in Brownsville, a city bordering Mexico.

Under Texas law and barring extradition, Castro had to be released Thursday after 90 days in detention. Though he is free, he remains a fugitive subject to arrest in Minnesota and other states.

Abbott has exposed one of several loopholes in extradition laws that are likely to lead to more conflict between states in the future, said Ethan Lowens, a fellow at the University of Pennsylvania Carey Law School.

Texas attorneys have argued that Abbott’s extradition decision is still pending, as he awaits the outcome of an internal state investigation considering whether Castro was legally a “fugitive.”

U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. wrote Wednesday that the court couldn’t intervene without a final decision by Abbott. Minnesota had asked him to compel Castro’s extradition.

Lowens said other governors could make similar arguments to avoid extradition requests they oppose. As states diverge on laws over abortion, gender-affirming care and other issues, he expects such extradition conflicts to “come up more and more,” he said.

___

Valerie Gonzalez reported from McAllen, Texas. Thanawala reported from Atlanta. Associated Press writer Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire, contributed to this story.

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has awarded a $16.7 million contract to purchase 6,000 pairs of gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks, saying officers would use them to control detainees and protesters who resist.

ICE moved forward with the purchase despite opposition from civil rights advocates and Democratic members of Congress, who said ICE officers cannot be trusted to use them appropriately.

A notice published in a federal database Thursday said ICE entered into a no-bid contract to purchase the gloves from Compliant Technologies LLC, a Kentucky-based firm that manufactures them. The deal includes acquiring 6,000 of the devices along with support equipment and services over the next six months.

Civil rights advocates have said ICE officers already face criticism for their use of force with little oversight or accountability while enforcing President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.

ICE published the notice hours after a group of U.S. senators, led by Democrat Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada, urged the agency to cancel its plan to buy the gloves. In a letter to ICE's acting director Thursday, Cortez Masto and 15 of her colleagues in the Democratic caucus questioned ICE's need for the devices.

“The blatant and tragic misuse of force in Los Angeles, Chicago, Minneapolis, Houston, Maine, and other locations around the country raises significant skepticism about the agency’s professional capability to safely deploy a new tool that could be used to harm Americans without cause,” the letter said.

The senators were the latest to express opposition to the plan, which became public this month when ICE published a notice outlining its intent to purchase thousands of “conductive distraction and de-escalation devices” for officers and investigators.

The devices are normal patrol gloves until an officer presses a button to activate the electrical mode. They must be applied directly to someone’s skin to produce a shock that causes pain, which is promoted as a way to gain compliance from people who are resisting. They have been used by some local jails and police departments in recent years.

ICE's notice said officers would use them in “high-tension environments,” including while making arrests, transporting combative detainees and responding to civil disturbances outside detention facilities.

“It will be used when a subject is actively or passively resisting and an officer needs to gain control quickly to prevent injuries to both parties,” the document said.

It said that the shocks would help “maintain control over inmates and prevent aggression or escape attempts,” allow officers to handcuff people hiding their hands, and assist in crowd control. The goal would be to avoid using “more severe force,” including firearms. The notice said the gloves would be used with “approved policy, training, and accountability standards,” but it did not elaborate.

Cortez Masto and the other senators said in their letter that the device “presents substantial risks if deployed during civil arrests — even more so if it is deployed without clear limits, appropriate training, and comprehensive oversight.” They said ICE must make public details about how officers will be trained and how use of the gloves will be documented and reviewed internally to avoid misuse.

ICE's parent agency, the Department of Homeland Security, reacted defiantly Thursday to critics of the purchase.

“Sanctuary politicians attempting to ban our federal law enforcement from any safety equipment is despicable and a deliberate attempt to undermine and endanger our officers,” the agency said in a statement.

text:
A federal judge on Wednesday halted the Trump administration’s plan to overhaul a decades-old grant program targeting housing discrimination, siding with fair housing groups that argued the changes hindered their ability to work.

U.S. District Judge Myong Joun, who was appointed by former President Biden, ruled that the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) failed to explain the reasoning behind moving forward with “sweeping changes” that would take away money from more than 100 nonprofit recipients and narrow the recipient pool.

The Fair Housing Initiative Program (FHIP) run by the agency has provided funding to nonprofit organizations that investigate complaints of housing discrimination and assist tenants and homebuyers under the Fair Housing Act.

According to attorneys representing the fair housing groups, HUD has historically distributed more than 100 grants, providing funding that ranged from $75,000 to $425,000.

The administration instead proposed distributing $46 million of the $56 million appropriated by Congress toward five larger grant awards. One grant, worth $25 million, was designated for a law school, while another $10 million would be available to a state or local agency.

The move was challenged by the National Fair Housing Alliance and the Massachusetts Fair Housing Center in court in July. The nonprofit groups argue the trimmed funds would be detrimental to the housing enforcement work of many organizations that depend on the funds.

Joun sided with the plaintiffs, agreeing HUD had not shown why such a major shift in funding distribution was necessary.

“The effect of HUD’s restructure effectively bars the very housing organizations that have been effectuating FHIP’s mission year after year since its enactment,” Joun wrote in his ruling.

The judge ordered the agency to return to its original framework for distributing the funds.

The administration defended the changes as an effort to modernize the program and attract a wider range of participants.

It also sought to add new policy requirements to receive funding, including requiring applicants to comply with the administration’s positions on “gender ideology” and immigration.

Lila Miller, an attorney representing the groups, praised the decision, telling Reuters it “rightfully recognizes the stakes at issue and protects the rule of law.”

text:
New York State Attorney General Letitia James is asking a state court judge to terminate an agreement between the Rensselaer County Sheriff's Office and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

In a lawsuit filed Thursday, James accused Rensselaer County Sheriff Kyle Bourgault of violating the recently passed Local Cops, Local Crimes Act. The law bars law enforcement agencies in New York from maintaining 287(g) agreements with ICE.

“The Rensselaer County Sheriff’s Office has been given every opportunity to follow the law, yet has chosen not to," James said in a statement Thursday. "My office is suing to enforce New York’s laws and ensure that local law enforcement agencies remain focused on their most fundamental responsibility: keeping New Yorkers safe.”

The lawsuit comes two days after Bourgault and 14 other sheriffs sued New York State in federal court. Nassau County is also expected to join the lawsuit.

"This isn't just about 287(g)," Bourgault said during a press conference Tuesday. "This is about tools being taken away from law enforcement to safely protect the people they are closest to. I was elected by the people of Rensselaer County to serve as their sheriff and to make the difficult decisions on how we keep this county safe, and that is why I will continue to advocate for the independence of the office of sheriff."

Rensselaer County has had a 287(g) agreement since 2018, which allows sheriff's deputies to identify immigrants in the county jail and initiate immigration proceedings against them on behalf of ICE. Court documents indicate that Rensselaer County has removed nine immigrants under the program.

Rensselaer County's agreement was unique among those in New York State. Other 287(g) agreements were enacted during President Donald Trump's second term and allowed officers to make immigration-related arrests and/or serve and execute warrants on immigrants in their custody.

Twelve other jurisdictions had 287(g) agreements with ICE, but the Rensselaer County Sheriff's Office is the only one that refused to terminate their contract.

name: Human Rights
title: The War on Immigrants - Race, Racism and the Law
description:
Like the War on Drugs and the War on Crime that preceded it, this War on Immigrants invokes the specter of criminality, here coded through racialized tropes of immigrant invasion, to recast migration as crime and transform the criminal system into a primary instrument of immigration enforcement.
Overall, this new War on Immigrants marks a stark departure from established legal norms and poses serious threats to constitutional principles.
Part III critically examines how this deployment of criminal law in the War on Immigrants violates constitutional principles that limit state authority and vitiates protections under federal and state constitutional law.
The new War on Immigrants challenges established constitutional principles defining the federal government’s authority to regulate immigration and the limitations on state police power.
This Article has articulated four legislative models that make up an emerging state crimmigration regime--the Crimmigration Loop, Short-Circuiting Crimmigration, Collapsing Crimmigration, and Muscular Proxy Criminalization--collectively reshaping both criminal law and immigration enforcement to wage a War on Immigrants.
text:
Abstract

Excerpted From: Erika Nyborg-Burch, The War on Immigrants, UCLA Law Review 416 (July 2026) (356 Footnotes) (Full Document)

The intersection of state criminal law and federal immigration enforcement--part of a phenomenon termed “crimmigration”--has entered a new and contentious phase. Traditionally, the federal government has held exclusive authority to set immigration policy and enforce immigration law. Yet state criminal law has increasingly influenced who is subjected to federal removal proceedings, through local arrests, state court convictions, and referrals to federal law enforcement. While these developments blur jurisdictional lines between federal and state enforcement authority, the U.S. Supreme Court has continued to demarcate immigration regulation as federal civil law. Now, a surge of state legislation is radically challenging this paradigm. These new state laws criminalize mere immigration status and authorize criminal courts to impose unprecedented punishments that neither the federal nor state criminal systems had previously sanctioned. This shift toward state criminal enforcement raises profound constitutional concerns.

Consider the following scenarios. In Oklahoma, Jane was pulled over for driving with a broken taillight. Officers arrested her for “impermissible occupation,” a new state offense that criminalizes mere presence without formal immigration status. After months in pretrial detention separated from her family, Jane was sentenced to a year in prison and ordered to leave the state within seventy-two hours of her release. Jane is unsure if Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers will be there waiting to arrest her. Jane now faces banishment from the community she calls home.

In Texas, John was arrested while at a work site and charged with “illegal entry.” The arrest separated John from his spouse, a lawful permanent resident, and their three children. If convicted, state law mandates his removal from the United States even though, under federal immigration law, he could qualify for cancellation of removal and potentially obtain a green card. These federal protections are not available in state criminal court.

In Tennessee, Jay was charged with driving under the influence and reckless endangerment with a deadly weapon (Jay’s car). The arresting officer noted Jay’s foreign license and accent, and the prosecutor escalated the charge by introducing evidence that Jay was not lawfully present in the United States. If established, this fact authorizes the judge to impose a life sentence without the possibility of parole--a significant sentence enhancement--solely based on Jay’s lack of formal immigration status.

These three scenarios highlight a troubling trend in immigration federalism, where multiple states are now using state criminal law to enforce their own immigration policies. This Article is the first to identify and systematically examine how state criminal enforcement of these newly enacted immigration crimes destabilizes immigration federalism, distorts criminal law, and erodes individual rights.

Since the late nineteenth century, the Supreme Court has consistently struck down state efforts to directly regulate immigration, deeming such laws an impermissible overreach into core federal authority. Just over a decade ago, in Arizona v. United States , the Court reaffirmed that the federal regulatory framework preempts states from creating parallel state crimes for federal immigration law violations, or policing those immigration violations without federal authorization. Despite this well-established precedent--and perhaps emboldened by recent shifts in the Court’s composition--several states have begun to directly regulate immigration through their criminal legal systems. By enacting criminal laws that impose incarceration and banishment on noncitizen defendants, these states challenge the federal government’s longstanding authority over the admission, exclusion, and removal of noncitizens. In purporting to transform violations of federal civil law into state criminal offenses or sentence aggravators, these laws single out immigrants for unprecedented and disproportionate punishments. Like the War on Drugs and the War on Crime that preceded it, this War on Immigrants invokes the specter of criminality, here coded through racialized tropes of immigrant invasion, to recast migration as crime and transform the criminal system into a primary instrument of immigration enforcement.

This Article is the first to unpack the emerging crimmigration regime by identifying four legislative models that each use criminal law to formally or effectively control immigration and banish noncitizens. First, the ““Crimmigration Loop” laws criminalize immigration status itself, using prosecution for immigration crimes to trigger federal enforcement. For instance, Oklahoma’s House Bill 4156 criminalizes “impermissible occupation”-- presence without federal immigration authorization--and imposes incarceration followed by banishment from the state. Second, “Short-Circuiting Crimmigration” laws bypass federal authority, with states enforcing their own immigration policies. Texas’s Senate Bill 4, for example, requires state courts to issue removal orders against undocumented noncitizens independent of federal action. Third, “Collapsing Crimmigration” laws enhance penalties for non-immigration crimes based solely on immigration status, as seen in Tennessee’s Senate Bill 2770, which imposes the state’s second harshest sentence on undocumented individuals, leading to de facto banishment through lifetime incarceration. Finally, “Muscular Proxy Criminalization” laws target offenses disproportionately committed by undocumented immigrants. For example, Florida’s House Bill 1589 imposes heightened penalties for second or subsequent convictions for driving without a license in a state where undocumented noncitizens cannot obtain one.

This Article demonstrates, first, that each legislative model poses a direct challenge to federal supremacy in immigration law. What began in the 1990s with federal legislation authorizing state cooperation with federal enforcement--through screening for civil immigration violations during arrest and post-conviction--has evolved into states asserting independent criminal authority over immigration. Many of these laws go beyond “mirroring” federal immigration crimes, imposing criminal penalties that include exile, deportation, and banishment where federal law does not. They also prevent noncitizens from accessing federal protections, including those enshrined in international obligations like asylum and protections under the Convention Against Torture. By authorizing enforcement outside of or even contrary to federal law, these state laws challenge federal authority to a greater degree than the laws the Court struck down in Arizona v. United States .

Second, and beyond federalism concerns, this Article shows how these laws undermine core criminal law principles and contravene constitutional protections. Although the Court has ruled that entering the country without permission is not an ongoing federal crime, states have criminalized mere presence in their jurisdiction after crossing U.S. national borders without federal authorization. By making undocumented presence a state crime, these laws violate Eighth and Fourteenth Amendment constitutional prohibitions against imposing criminal liability for status offenses and run afoul of the principle of concurrence. Their penalty structures also depart from existing sentencing frameworks, imposing disproportionate punishments like actual or effective banishment--through state removal orders and extreme sentences--where state law would otherwise be more lenient.

Third, enforcing these laws transfers discrimination based on immigration status to state prosecutors and judges, sanctioning racialized law enforcement as a matter of law and practice. These prosecutions violate defendants’ equal protection rights, while policing these offenses threatens the Fourth Amendment rights of entire communities.

Overall, this new War on Immigrants marks a stark departure from established legal norms and poses serious threats to constitutional principles. By framing migration as a legitimate basis for state criminal enforcement, it shifts the traditional balance between federal immigration authority and state criminal law while emboldening discriminatory state criminal enforcement. By targeting noncitizens for prosecution and punishment, these statutes undermine defendants’ constitutional protections, with parallels to other regulatory realms where state criminal law increasingly constrains individual rights. As states continue to push the boundaries of their authority to criminalize and punish, it becomes critical to identify, unpack, and rigorously examine this expanding crimmigration frontier.

This Article takes up that challenge in three parts. Part I traces the federal immigration system’s increasing reliance on the criminal legal system as a gateway to civil immigration enforcement. As states were given a larger role in screening for immigration enforcement, they began leveraging their criminal legal systems to shape federal immigration outcomes. Still, Arizona v. United States curtailed more direct attempts by states to control immigration policy through criminal law, limiting their role in immigration enforcement. Part II argues that the new wave of state criminal laws destabilizes this understanding of the relationship between state criminal law and immigration enforcement. It categorizes four legislative models that usher in a new crimmigration regime by harnessing state criminal law to more directly effectuate removal of noncitizens. Each model turns immigration status into a basis for criminal liability and introduces new forms of punishment that differentially burden noncitizens. Part III critically examines how this deployment of criminal law in the War on Immigrants violates constitutional principles that limit state authority and vitiates protections under federal and state constitutional law. It raises concerns under the Eighth Amendment, Fourteenth Amendment, and Fourth Amendment regarding the criminalization of status, differential liability for noncitizens, disproportionate punishments, and the sanctioning of discriminatory policing.

[ . . . ]

The new War on Immigrants challenges established constitutional principles defining the federal government’s authority to regulate immigration and the limitations on state police power. Despite the Court’s rejection of state efforts to directly enforce federal immigration laws in Arizona , a new wave of state legislatures is testing these constitutional boundaries. By enacting laws that criminalize immigration status and impose unprecedented and disproportionate punishments on noncitizens, these state laws undermine fundamental constitutional rights and fracture immigration policy. This Article has articulated four legislative models that make up an emerging state crimmigration regime--the Crimmigration Loop, Short-Circuiting Crimmigration, Collapsing Crimmigration, and Muscular Proxy Criminalization--collectively reshaping both criminal law and immigration enforcement to wage a War on Immigrants.

This evolution in crimmigration threatens the constitutional rights of individuals subjected to prosecution by criminalizing status itself. The punishments it purports to authorize, including de jure and de facto banishment, contravene the Eighth Amendment’s prohibition against cruel and unusual punishment and erode the principle of proportionality in sentencing. Despite the promises of equal protection under the law, the new crimmigration embeds discrimination into the criminal code and sanctions discriminatory policing practices. This targeted enforcement disproportionately impacts people of color, exacerbates existing inequalities, and threatens the Fourth Amendment rights of entire communities. It also undermines the coherence of federal immigration law by fracturing immigration policy across state and county lines. The resulting patchwork of state enforcement mechanisms often conflicts with federal statutory protections, including protections designed to advance humanitarian values and fulfill international obligations. Finally, this crimmigration regime empowers state law enforcement to levy both state criminal punishment and state immigration enforcement against noncitizens prosecuted under these new state statutes.

These constitutional and human costs compel a critical reevaluation of crimmigration law. In some sense, the War on Immigrants that states are waging is the natural consequence of decades of policymaking framing immigration regulation as necessary for national security and public safety. To address this latest manifestation of that stigmatizing discourse, policymakers should work toward decoupling immigration enforcement from criminal law. Efforts could include repealing the federal statutes that criminalize border crossing and limiting state and local participation in immigration enforcement. These changes must be accompanied by a deliberate shift in the discourse surrounding immigration--challenging narratives that dehumanize migrants, acknowledging the complex factors driving migration, and recognizing that those without formal status are members of communities throughout the country. Only by dismantling the conditions that have given rise to the War on Immigrants can we hope to protect the rights of all individuals within our borders through a coherent, just approach to immigration policy.

Assistant Professor, Florida State University College of Law. J.D., Yale Law School; B.A., Brown University.

text:
28 August 2026

Amnesty International Australia urges the Australian Government to not fall short in fulfilling its obligations it owes in offering pathways to protection and safety. The Government’s immigration policy review should be an opportunity to strengthen Australia’s commitment to people seeking safety.

Andrew Witheford, Amnesty International Australia’s International and Crisis Campaigner says:

“We remind the Government that Australia holds both a moral responsibility and obligations under international law to people seeking protection from persecution and grave human rights violations.

“Having been involved in Afghanistan for two decades, Australia has a particular responsibility to ensure that people at risk in Afghanistan are not abandoned as the country continues to experience a devastating human rights crisis.

“Australia should be expanding its commitment to people fleeing persecution, not shrinking it.”

Andrew Witheford, Amnesty International Australia’s International and Crisis Campaigner

“This must include dedicated places for women and girls who have endured five years of the Taliban’s systematic repression, as well as human rights defenders and members of marginalised and persecuted groups.

“Australia should be expanding its commitment to people fleeing persecution, not shrinking it. The Government must ensure that Australia remains a country where people facing grave human rights abuses can find safety, protection and the opportunity to rebuild their lives and futures.

“Amnesty International Australia reiterates its calls to the Australian Government to establish dedicated pathways for people seeking safety from Afghanistan, with priority and expedited processing for women and girls at risk, human rights defenders and minority communities. These pathways must include meaningful access to family reunion and adequate settlement support, recognising that protection does not end when a person reaches Australia.

“Amnesty International Australia reiterates its calls to the Australian Government to establish dedicated pathways for people seeking safety from Afghanistan, with priority and expedited processing for women and girls at risk, human rights defenders and minority communities.”

Andrew Witheford

“The Government should also commit, in the May 2027 Federal Budget, to a multi-year allocation of humanitarian places for the following three years. A predictable, adequately resourced humanitarian program would provide greater certainty for people seeking protection and ensure Australia is able to meet its international obligations.”

Amnesty International is a global movement of more than 10 million people who take injustice personally. We are campaigning for a world where human rights are enjoyed by all – and we can only do it with your support.

text:
A second Roman Catholic priest from the Diocese of Des Moines has filed a lawsuit against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security over alleged delays in work authorization permits.

Father Nipin Thakidipurathu Scaria, a citizen of India who now resides in Des Moines, is suing Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services Director Joseph Edlow, and Thomas Schuurmans, the director of CIS’s Nebraska Service Center, in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa.

According to the lawsuit, Scaria — known to parishioners as “Father Nivin,” was admitted to the United States several years ago on an R-1 visa, which is a temporary visa for foreign nationals entering the country to work in a religious capacity.

According to court records, Scaria’s employment authorization to work in the United States was initially set to expire on March 30, 2025, but in October 2024, he received notice of an automatic 540-day extension — meaning his authorization would expire on Sept. 21, 2026, unless U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services first acted on his application for a work permit.

Since then, no action has been taken, the lawsuit asserts.

“If Father Nivin loses work authorization, he will be unable to perform his religious duties to his parish as a priest of the Roman Catholic Church,” the lawsuit states. “If Father Nivin loses work authorization, he will be required to stop work at the Roman Catholic Diocese of Des Moines in his position as rector of St. Ambrose Cathedral in Des Moines. This abrupt halt to his work authorization will interfere with religious services for the diocese.”

Federal law suggests the processing of such an application should be completed no later than 180 days after the initial filing of the application.

“Clearly, Congress did not contemplate an adjudication time of over a year,” the lawsuit states. “There is no reasonable justification for these delays and inactions… It is unreasonable for (Scaria) to abruptly stop his work for the Catholic Church and this impairs the free exercise of religion for the church (and its) parishioners.”

The lawsuit asks the court to assume jurisdiction over the matter, set the matter for an expedited hearing, and order U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to process his application.

The U.S. Department of Justice has yet to file a response to the lawsuit on behalf of the defendants.

Other priest’s lawsuit is dropped

In July, a priest from Nigeria, Father Sylvester Okoh, filed a similar lawsuit against the same defendants.

According to that lawsuit, Okoh was initially admitted to the United States on an R-1 visa. In November 2022, with his previously granted employment authorization set to expire on January 25, 2025, Okoh allegedly filed an application to adjust his residency status. In September 2024, CIS issued a notice indicating Okoh’s work authorization would be automatically extended 540 days to July 19, 2026.

With that expiration date only three days away, Okoh sued, citing the threat to his religious duties as a priest in the Roman Catholic Diocese of Des Moines.

That lawsuit contended that CIS had delayed action on Okoh’s application based on the agency’s December 2025 policy memoranda placing an indefinite hold on pending benefit applications from nationals of Nigeria and 38 other countries the Trump administration designated as “high risk.”

Earlier this week, Okoh’s attorney dismissed the lawsuit, informing the court that the defendants, without ever responding to the lawsuit itself, had processed Okoh’s application.

text:
A group of mostly Democratic senators pressed for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to not use gloves that can electrically shock people in a Thursday letter.

In the letter addressed to ICE acting Director David Venturella, the senators said they were writing “to express deep concern about U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) plans to spend up to $20 million on gloves that deliver electric shocks.”

“Over the past year, ICE personnel have been involved in numerous well-documented incidents of excessive force and civil rights violations. These incidents have shown the American people that ICE personnel are not adequately trained or accountable for their interactions with civilians,” the senators wrote.

The letter was signed by Sens. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.), Angus King (I-Maine), Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.), Peter Welch (D-Vt.), Patty Murray (D-Wash.), Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.), Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), Angela Alsobrooks (D-Md.), Andy Kim (D-N.J.), Adam Schiff (D-Calif.), Jack Reed (D-R.I.), Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) and Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.).

Earlier this month, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) published a notice outlining plans to give ICE officers gloves producing painful electric shocks. The agency was planning to pay up to $20 million for the new devices, also known as the Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter (G.L.O.V.E.), which could be used by officers in the field amid immigration operations.

“ICE is constantly assessing the needs of our officers in the field to ensure they have the tools and equipment necessary to safely arrest and remove criminal illegal aliens from our country,” a DHS spokesperson previously told NewsNation.

The senators wrote in their letter that “the American people have made it clear that ICE must de-escalate its immigration enforcement operations.”

“ICE must refrain from deployment of the G.L.O.V.E. and instead invest in de-escalation tools, training, and accountability,” they added.

The Hill has reached out to ICE for comment.

text:
After an outcry from immigrant and civil rights advocates over plans to equip immigration officers with gloves capable of delivering electric shocks, California lawmakers on Thursday unveiled a bill that would ban the use of shock gloves by any law enforcement agent in the state.

The gloves deliver can an electrical shock strong enough to drop a strong man to his knees in an instant, and proponents say the gloves provide a fast and non-lethal way to subdue a person.

Two weeks ago, the Associated Press reported that the Department of Homeland security planned to use $10 million to $20 million to procure the gloves from Compliant Technologies of Lexington, Ky., for Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents. The department defended its decision, saying it was “made with careful consideration” and that other law enforcement agencies in the country already use the technology.

Civil rights organizations including the American Civil Liberties Union accused the department of attempting to intimidate the public by arming agents with another use-of-force option. They noted that ICE already is contending with criticism for multiple deaths in custody and during arrests.

Assembly Bill 2760, authored by state Assemblymember LaShea Sharp-Collins (D-San Diego), would prohibit local, state and federal agencies from possessing, using or procuring electric taser gloves in the state or with state funds.

“We cannot spend state money or tax dollars on technology that is not to better our state,” Sharp-Collins said during a news conference with other lawmakers in Sacramento. “It cannot be used on our children, it cannot be used on our teachers, our business owners, it cannot be used on anyone.”

The CTG-5 G.L.O.V.E — standing for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter — resembles a thick work glove and can be activated to emit a 380-volt shock upon contact with a body. Compliant Technologies has maintained that the gloves are weaker than traditional tasers, but critics say they can be life-threatening in the hands of ICE.

“Many people try to say weapons like this are about de-escalation, but I don’t know how many people have put hands on someone and said that’s de-escalation,” state Assemblymember Alex Lee (D-Alameda) said. “There’s already a spectrum of non-lethal, less-than-violent weapons out there that exists… ICE and law enforcement don’t need another tool.”

The gloves have been adopted in detention centers, law enforcement agencies and jails across the country, though apparently none in California. Last week, AP reported that Omaha police agreed to stop using the shock gloves after parents realized they’d been adopted by departments that monitored schools.

Sharp-Collins said she prepared the legislation in consultation with the state attorney general’s office and legislative council to ensure it would withstand a challenge from the Trump administration if it became law.

The Senate voted 30-9 on Monday to approve a rule change that would allow for the bill to pass quickly before the end of the legislative session on Aug. 31.

text:
BROWNSVILLE, Texas -- An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer charged with shooting a man and lying about it during the immigration crackdown in Minneapolis was released from a Texas jail Thursday, after a judge refused to order his return to Minnesota.

Christian Castro was released at the break of dawn from a detention center in Brownsville. He motioned his hand toward a few camera operators and a reporter crowding around him and quickly got into an SUV that drove off.

A day earlier, U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. wrote in an order that said he couldn't prevent a county sheriff from releasing Castro or order Texas Gov. Greg Abbott to sign his extradition warrant.

Castro is charged in Minnesota with assault and falsely reporting a crime in the Jan. 14 shooting of 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis.

Castro is accused of firing a gun through the front door of a Minneapolis home, shooting Sosa-Celis in the leg. Prosecutors say Castro also falsely accused Sosa-Celis and another man of attacking an ICE officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel.

After a Minnesota judge issued a nationwide warrant for Castro's arrest in May, authorities, including Minnesota’s Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, arrested Castro in Cameron County on May 29. Minnesota authorities have sought his extradition since his arrest, but he remained in custody in Brownsville, a city bordering Mexico.

Under Texas law and barring extradition, Castro had to be released after 90 days of detention, which was Thursday.

Minnesota officials believe Castro could flee to Mexico.

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison filed a request for a temporary restraining order last week seeking to block Castro’s release or to order his return to Minnesota.

Texas attorneys on Tuesday argued the judge could not rule on a decision that’s still pending. Abbott has not denied the extradition. Instead he is waiting for the outcome of an internal state investigation considering whether Castro was legally a “fugitive” under the Extradition Clause, the lawyers said.

The judge wrote in Wednesday’s order that the court couldn't yet step in.

“The Court concludes that it lacks subject matter jurisdiction because the case is not ripe for adjudication,” the order read. “Minnesota cannot premise its causes of action on the allegation that Governor Abbott may violate those authorities in the future; it must prove that a violation has already occurred.”

The judge said in his order that the extradition laws do not outline how long the Texas governor can take to make that decision.

Abbott said last week he would not respond to the extradition request, citing the ongoing investigation into fraud in government social service programs in Minnesota, which President Donald Trump used to justify his immigration crackdown there.

After the judge's decision, Ellison posted online that the Texas governor had an obligation to extradite Castro. And by refusing to extradite him, “Greg Abbott is turning Texas into a sanctuary state for violent criminals.”

Abbott responded to Ellison.

“You guys are such bad lawyers. You showed up unprepared, uninformed & unpersuasive,” Abbott wrote online. “You don’t know the law & it showed.”

The Texas governor accused Minnesota of refusing to enforce immigration laws and threatened to send immigrants in the future to their state as he did with New York City, when thousands were released into Texas under President Joe Biden's administration.

A message seeking reaction from Ellison was sent to his office Thursday.

Minnesota officials say Castro could flee the country, citing calls he made from jail to a woman in Mexico, talking “about marrying her and buying a house in Mexico when he is released,” according to the lawsuit.

The judge conceded that Castro could flee the country but added that “the threat of injury by itself does not create an issue ripe for adjudication.”

___

Valerie Gonzalez reported from McAllen, Texas. Associated Press writer Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire, contributed to this story.

title: ICE is arresting a record number of immigrants in a summer surge - Yahoo
description:
The share of arrests of immigrants with past violent criminal convictions fell to less than 4 percent.
Those immigrants, as well as immigrants already in the custody of local law enforcement, then become easy targets for arrest and removal.
Spikes in removal flights to third countries Deportation flights are also increasing.
Deportation flights on U.S. military aircraft also resumed in June, with at least 25 removal flights to Honduras by the end of July.
Removal flights to so-called "third" countries — where immigrants have no connection — also reached a record high last month.
text:
Donald Trump's administration hit record highs of monthly immigration enforcement arrests this summer, with more than 43,000 people arrested in June and another 50,000 arrested in July.

But last month, for the first time since Trump took office, more than half of all people arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement had no prior criminal convictions or pending charges.

A growing majority of immigrants targeted by federal law enforcement officers have no criminal history whatsoever, as officers increasingly target immigrants whose legal status has lapsed or been stripped by the Trump administration, according to new reviews of federal data. The share of arrests of immigrants with past violent criminal convictions fell to less than 4 percent.

The administration has instead shifted its focus to legal immigration pathways, including people seeking asylum, the spouses of U.S citizens stuck in legal limbo, and refugees with temporary legal status whose humanitarian protections were revoked, forcing them to return to volatile countries they fled.

Those immigrants, as well as immigrants already in the custody of local law enforcement, then become easy targets for arrest and removal.

Earlier this year, ICE officials told Congress that the agency plans to deport one million people — and hold at least 99,000 people on any given day in ICE detention centers — in the 2026 and 2027 fiscal years.

To meet those goals, the administration has pumped billions of dollars into the Department of Homeland Security, with ambitious plans to scale up detention space and hire more officers. Secretary Markwayne Mullin has been hoping to avoid damning images of militarized officers storming through cities that plagued his predecessor Kristi Noem, but the administration is now confronting scrutiny over the fatal shootings of two immigrants by ICE officers during traffic stops and a surge of arrests targeting immigrants who have been in the country for years without issue.

More money for officers

As ICE shifts away from arresting people with criminal records, the percentage of ICE "arrests" at prisons and jails has steadily fallen, according to data reviewed by the American Immigration Council.

Instead, a growing share of ICE arrests are being carried out "at large," or by officers who track down and arrest people at work, in their homes or in traffic stops. Roughly 63 percent of all ICE arrests were performed "at large" by an officer or through state and local police, according to the American Immigration Council. Those arrests are often supported by state and local authorities through the 287(g) program, which effectively deputizes local police to carry out federal immigration enforcement.

The number of people brought into ICE custody through the 287(g) program is now roughly 14 percent, according to data collected by the Deportation Data Project and reviewed by The New York Times.

Florida police have tallied at least 15,000 such arrests under Trump, according to The Times review. But the program has seen heavier impacts in states without a significant ICE footprint, including Wyoming and West Virginia, where 287(g) arrests in both states have hit more than than 50 percent.

Immigrants stuck in legal limbo

The administration also doesn't appear to be targeting people with final orders of removal, decisions by immigration court judges requiring immigrants to leave the country. In the first week of August, roughly one quarter of arrests targeted people with final orders of removal.

Instead, the administration is increasingly arresting people stuck in bureaucratic hurdles.

ICE is arresting people with lapsed legal status while their paperwork is pending, including immigrants who overstayed their visas while awaiting extensions or green cards. Under previous administrations, those immigrants were rarely detained while in legal limbo, but the president's mass deportation campaign has labeled any misstep — even if the lengthy wait times are the government's fault — as illegal or criminal.

The administration is also working to rapidly remove roughly one million people in the U.S. with humanitarian protections after fleeing disaster and violence in their home countries.

In June, the Supreme Court allowed Homeland Security to revoke Temporary Protected Status for Haiti and Syria, two nations rocked by political instability and humanitarian crises. That decision opened the door for the administration to begin stripping protections for tens of thousands of other immigrants from a dozen other nations with the designation.

Following the ruling, administration officials said they intended to begin removing 350,000 Haitians and roughly 6,000 Syrians whose protections have now been revoked.

Spikes in removal flights to third countries

Deportation flights are also increasing.

Domestic transfer flights between ICE detention centers peaked in July, reaching an "alarming" monthly record of 1,363 flights across 61 U.S. cities, according to data collected by Human Rights First's ICE Flight Monitor project.

Those flights amount to the most domestic shuttle flights since at least 2020 when the group first began tracking them.

Deportation flights on U.S. military aircraft also resumed in June, with at least 25 removal flights to Honduras by the end of July.

Last month, ICE performed at least 329 removal flights to 37 countries, an increase of 14 percent from the previous month, Human Rights First found.

Removal flights to so-called "third" countries — where immigrants have no connection — also reached a record high last month. Human Rights first tracked 18 flights to 10 countries, with first-time flights to Belize and Dominica, and repeated flights to Central African Republic, Costa Rica, Equatorial Guinea, Eswatini, Ghana, Panama, Paraguay and Sierra Leone.

Within just 24 hours this month, from August 20-21, Human Rights First tracked third country transfers to Liberia, Equatorial Guinea, Cameroon and Paraguay, as well as flights deporting Mexicans to Guatemala, Honduras and Costa Rica.

"We are extremely concerned about the egregious violations of people's due process rights when they are summarily removed to a third country," as well as the conditions they face upon arrival and the "very real risk people face of being sent onward from those countries to the very places from which they fled," according to Savi Arvey, director of policy, refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First.

The State Department did not specify details on the training and its timeline, beyond saying the training aimed to help consular officers screen out applicants deemed likely to become dependent on US public benefits and to ensure evaluation of visa applicants “comprehensively and consistently.”

The pause on visa appointments was reported earlier by the Financial Times, which said immigrant visa applicants with scheduled interviews at US embassies and consulates have received emails that their appointments were being rescheduled and that they would receive future notice of a new date.

Trump’s immigration crackdown has been widely condemned by human rights groups as being discriminatory and in violation of free speech and due process rights. text:
A 5-year-old child and his father, who were arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Texas last week, have been deported to Mexico, the family’s attorney confirmed to MS NOW on Thursday.

Liam Tadeo and his father, Victor Martinez Nieto, were detained by ICE officers in Austin on Aug. 16 and held at the Dilley Immigration Processing Center, which houses a majority of children in federal custody. In a video of their arrest that went viral, Liam is crying and holding on to Martinez Nieto’s hands, which are cuffed behind his back, as they are escorted into an ICE vehicle.

Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, the family’s attorney, confirmed to MS NOW that Liam, who is not a U.S. citizen, and his father have since been deported together. Martinez Nieto had asked the Department of Homeland Security to allow his child to stay in the United States with his mother, to no avail.

“Liam should be completing his second week in kindergarten in the United States,” Lincoln-Goldfinch said in a statement. “This case highlights the cruelty of our immigration policies where a young child who has spent more than half of his life in the United States is unnecessarily detained with his father and deported without being able to say goodbye to his mother. None of this was acceptable or necessary.”

More articles

DHS previously said in a statement that Martinez Nieto did not have legal status in the U.S. He was arrested by immigration officers in late 2025 and removed to Mexico in February, but re-entered the U.S. at an unspecified time, the department said.

Liam is far from the first — or the youngest — child to have been arrested by ICE officers and held in detention facilities. Research conducted by MS NOW and The Marshall Project shows that at least 500 babies and toddlers have been detained by ICE in President Donald Trump’s second term.

In Dilley, which Trump reopened in 2025 and is now being run by for-profit prison operator CoreCivic, conditions are abysmal, according to detainees.

title: ICE has grabbed hundreds of Maine immigrants in 2026, only one was convicted of a violent crime
description:
The data puts lie to the Trump administration’s central justification for its enforcement campaign: that ICE is targeting dangerous criminals.
In 2026, 98% of the people ICE seized in Maine had no criminal conviction at all.
“Behind every data point is a person, a family, and a community living with fear and uncertainty,” said Mufalo Chitam, executive director of the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition.
Making this information public helps communities name what is happening, demand accountability, and act together.” The pace of arrests is accelerating.
“They’re really stalking people,” Lisa Parisio of the Immigrant Legal Advocacy Project told Maine Public.
text:
Federal immigration agents have apprehended more people in Maine in the first seven months of 2026 than in the two previous years combined. Only one of them has ever been convicted of a violent crime, according to government records.

Newly-released Immigration and Customs Enforcement administrative data — obtained through Freedom of Information Act litigation by the Deportation Data Project and analyzed for Maine by the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition (MIRC) — shows 482 apprehension events in Maine so far this year, compared to 168 in all of 2024 and 308 in 2025.

The data puts lie to the Trump administration’s central justification for its enforcement campaign: that ICE is targeting dangerous criminals. In 2026, 98% of the people ICE seized in Maine had no criminal conviction at all.

“Behind every data point is a person, a family, and a community living with fear and uncertainty,” said Mufalo Chitam, executive director of the Maine Immigrants’ Rights Coalition. “These numbers show the scale of ICE enforcement, but they cannot capture the tears shed by families torn apart, or the pain community members share with us every day. Making this information public helps communities name what is happening, demand accountability, and act together.”

The pace of arrests is accelerating. After the January surge, when 200 people were detained in a single month during the operation ICE dubbed “Catch of the Day,” arrests settled to roughly one per day. But that rate has doubled since May and June’s total of 75 arrests was the highest monthly figure since January. The summer spike mirrors a national trend, with ICE arresting a record 49,571 people nationwide in July.

The geography of enforcement is expanding too. For the first time, the federal data includes the towns and cities where arrests occurred and it shows ICE operating in 50 different Maine communities in 2026, up from 20 in 2024. Portland, Scarborough, Lewiston, South Portland, and Biddeford top the list, but arrests also occurred in small towns from Machias to Bethel to Sandy River Plantation.

Nearly 80% of Maine apprehensions were “at-large” arrests, made at homes, workplaces and public spaces in Maine communities, rather than transfers from another agency’s custody.

“They’re really stalking people,” Lisa Parisio of the Immigrant Legal Advocacy Project told Maine Public. “We are seeing so many arrests of people near their homes. You know, so many people report to us that they were heading out to work, they were heading out to a necessary medical appointment, when ICE arrested them.”

More than one in five at-large arrests statewide were recorded in Scarborough, home to ICE’s Portland-area field office. MIRC’s analysis found Scarborough arrests cluster on Tuesdays, one of the two days the office holds routine check-in appointments. That means many immigrants doing exactly what the government asked of them, showing up for scheduled appointments, are being detained when they arrive.

The public may soon know less about ICE’s actions. The latest release no longer includes information on whether arrests were “targeted” or “collateral,” a field that previously revealed most Maine apprehensions were untargeted, people who were simply swept up randomly.

text:
For almost a year, immigrant advocates and attorneys have complained that federal agents are repeatedly detaining people in Colorado without warrants that would give them permission to take people into custody.

Now they have alleged in federal court filings that the behavior of some Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents working in Colorado goes far beyond simply detaining people without a judge's authorization: lawyers claim they are abusing them too and regularly violating Constitutional protections.

In 48 pages of testimony filed in the U.S. District Court for Colorado, American Civil Liberties Union lawyers and immigration attorneys allege that ICE agents are still not complying with a preliminary injunction issued earlier this year by a federal judge requiring them to get arrest warrants in most cases before taking people into custody.

And in five declarations filed with the court, immigrants identified by their initials furnished details about violent ICE detentions and arrests even when they were complying with their orders.

In each case, the allegations made by immigrants would surely lead to internal affairs investigations and review by citizens commissions if the acts described were committed by police in Colorado’s cities. But it’s not clear in any of the cases whether the Department of Homeland Security is aware of the allegations or has taken any action to investigate them. A spokesman for ICE did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

A declaration signed Aug. 14 by an immigrant identified as D.B.D.J said that federal agents broke his window when they approached him at a 7-11 store as he was grabbing breakfast on the way to work earlier this summer.

“Both men were yelling at us. I do not remember exactly what they were yelling besides open the door. I opened the door and while opening it, the man that was banging on my window broke it, the man grabbed the front of my shirt and I put my hands up,” D.B.D.J wrote in court documents. “He grabbed my left hand and put it behind my back, he then pulled me down from the front of my shirt to the ground. I put my right hand down to blunt the fall but the officer grabbed it and pulled it behind my back too. I felt a lot of pain.”

Last November, U.S. District Judge R. Brooke Jackson issued a preliminary injunction, ordering the federal government to comply with its own rules surrounding so-called warrantless arrests, which are prohibited unless the immigrant is deemed a flight risk or a public safety risk.

Advocates and attorneys say that since President Donald Trump was sworn in for a second term, immigration agents have wholly ignored that restriction, detaining people wherever they can find them, no matter whether they have a warrant, and no matter whether the person is a flight risk or has a history that would point to a public safety risk.

In May, when both sides were brought back to court, Jackson ordered the Trump administration to train every ICE officer who conducts arrests and detentions in Colorado on his preliminary injunction order and that the federal government produce monthly reports on their detentions and arrests to ensure compliance.

But the lawyers allege in filings this week that ICE agents in Colorado have continued to grab people off the street without warrants and are at times breaking windows, racially profiling and assaulting immigrants.

The number of people taken into detention by ICE in Colorado reached its second highest level of Trump’s second term in July, when 467 people were taken into custody, according to data obtained by the Deportation Data Project. That organization, affiliated with the University of California Berkeley and UCLA, uses Freedom of Information requests and lawsuits to obtain data from the federal government.

The month with the largest number of immigration detentions in the state was July, 2025, when 536 were taken into custody. But the number has been climbing steadily this spring and summer, from 247 in March to 467 in July, the data shows.

“Defendants (the federal government) make warrantless arrests under the guise of field warrants; Defendants do not accurately report to plaintiffs the number of relevant arrests made … Defendants’ June, July and August (reports) included evidence of ICE agents detaining, handcuffing and arresting individuals without conducting a flight risk analysis,” ACLU lawyers said in the court documents. “Defendants’ document production shows that ICE routinely arrests people in this manner.”

Advocacy attorneys say the government is out of compliance with the preliminary injunction and the required filings ordered by the judge earlier this year. They said, in court documents, they are missing documentation for at least nine individuals and ICE has produced “incomplete sets” of documents for some 20 or so people who may have been detained without a field warrant this summer.

They also said that since the enforcement order in May, only 10 of the people they were tracking remain in ICE custody in Colorado.

The declarations from immigrants also indicate that violent arrests occur regularly outside the view of cell phone cameras and protesters who have documented ICE abuses across the country.

S.N., who is 18, said in court documents he’s been in the United States since April 2023 and entered with his family on parole from Venezuela. He had a work permit, was the captain of his high school soccer team and worked on the weekends at SONIC and helped his mother deliver food.

He was arrested by ICE when he was helping deliver food to an apartment in Aurora. ICE officers swarmed the hallway. He put his hands on his head and officers pointed long guns at his chest. An officer grabbed him and shoved him against the wall and handcuffed him.

“I was yelling that I was only there delivering food and that I did nothing wrong. I asked them if they were blind because the food I had delivered was right there. Then an officer punched me in the face and I felt extremely dizzy,” he said, according to court documents.

S.N. said that the officers “asked if I was Mexican because of my clown tattoo,” and I told them no. They then accused S.N. of being a member of a Venezuelan prison gang, Tren de Aragua. He said he was not.

“While in the car to Centennial, I asked the driver if they had something to stop the bleeding from the punch … they said no,” S.N. wrote. “They said that I belonged in Venezuela.”

The next step in the case is not outlined in the documents, but the case remains open in U.S. District Court.

text:
Texas Border Business

Texas Border Business

Comparing deportations under former President Barack Obama and President Donald Trump seems straightforward until you account for differences in federal definitions, agencies, reporting periods, and enforcement practices.

During Obama’s final four full fiscal years — fiscal years 2013 through 2016 — U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement recorded 1,160,255 removals, according to ICE records.

The annual totals were 368,644 in FY 2013, 315,943 in FY 2014, 235,413 in FY 2015, and 240,255 in FY 2016.

ICE defines a removal as the compulsory and confirmed departure of an inadmissible or deportable person based on an order of removal. Historical ICE removal statistics also included certain returns handled through the agency.

The Department of Homeland Security has said the Trump administration deported 948,000 people through June 24, 2026, following President Trump’s return to office in January 2025.

That number, however, should not be directly compared with Obama’s ICE removal totals.

Independent researchers have cautioned that publicly available ICE and U.S. Customs and Border Protection datasets cannot currently be combined into a reliable government-wide deportation total because some records may overlap.

The Deportation Data Project, an academic research initiative that obtains federal immigration records through public-records litigation, has said it does not have a reliable count of total deportations during Trump’s second administration. Researchers have explained that combining separate ICE and CBP datasets could potentially result in some individuals being counted twice.

Enforcement Has Accelerated

Available federal data nevertheless shows that immigration enforcement has accelerated during Trump’s current term.

Government data obtained by the Deportation Data Project shows ICE recorded 49,571 arrests in July 2026, up from 43,021 in June.

Nearly 34,000 removals occurred in July, according to reporting based on federal data, making it the highest monthly removal total of Trump’s second term to that point.

The composition of immigration enforcement has also changed.

During Obama’s later years, ICE increasingly concentrated interior enforcement on people with criminal convictions. In FY 2016, 92 percent of ICE interior removals involved people previously convicted of a crime, according to ICE.

Under Trump, enforcement has expanded substantially among immigrants already living inside the United States. Deportation Data Project researchers found that deportations following ICE arrests and detention were approximately five times higher in January 2026 than the average monthly level during the second half of 2024.

That finding does not mean total annual deportations increased fivefold. It specifically measures deportations following ICE arrests and detention during the periods examined.

The most defensible comparison, therefore, is not simply 1.16 million under Obama versus 948,000 under Trump.

Obama’s 1.16 million represents four full fiscal years of published ICE removal statistics. Trump’s 948,000 is a broader DHS-reported administration figure covering roughly 17 months, and its underlying methodology has not been publicly documented in comparable detail.

What can be established is that Obama’s final four fiscal years produced 1.16 million documented ICE removals, while immigration enforcement during Trump’s second term has accelerated sharply, particularly through arrests and removals involving people living in the interior of the United States.

Any direct numerical comparison should identify these methodological differences rather than treating the two totals as equivalent measurements.

Disclosure: This comparison is based on the most reliable federal data and publicly reported figures available at the time of publication. The findings are not conclusive because federal agencies have used different definitions, reporting periods, and methodologies for immigration removals and deportations. Some datasets may overlap or may not be directly comparable across administrations. Texas Border Business presents these figures for informational purposes and will update them as more complete federal data becomes available.

The U.S. sanctions follow a U.K. appeals court ruling last June that found the British government acted lawfully when it banned Palestine Action under the Terrorism Act. Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori responded in a statement, “The fact that Trump is now taking inspiration from Britain’s repression of the movement for Palestinian freedom exposes just how dangerous this ban is and should be a wake-up call to anyone who cares about free speech and civil liberties.”
