text:
The Department of Homeland Security sent its second deportation flight in a week to Haiti on Thursday, returning dozens of Haitians to the unstable Caribbean country, including several children born in the U.S.

The children were among several families aboard the Immigration and Customs Enforcement charter flight scheduled to land in Cap-Haïtien, Haiti’s second-largest city and the main gateway for international flights since gang violence prompted restrictions on U.S. carriers flying into Port-au-Prince.

The youngest person aboard the ICE Air flight was 1-year-old born in the U.S., according to information shared with Haitian authorities ahead of the plane’s arrival.

The ICE Air deportation charter flight GXA6196 originated in Alexandria, LA and departed Opa-locka Executive Airport at 10:04 a.m. for Cap-Haïtien, where it was scheduled to arrive at 11:33 a.m.

Until now, deportation flights to Haiti have taken place an average of once a month. The previous flight was last Thursday and had 161 deportees. including over a dozen individuals with criminal records that included sex crimes involving children.

Last month, however, U.S. officials warned Haitian authorities to expect an increase in deportations following the Supreme Court’s decision to allow President Donald Trump to end Haiti’s Temporary Protected Status designation even while litigation challenging the termination continues in the courts.

More than 300,000 Haitians were enrolled in the humanitarian program, which allowed them to legally live and work in the United States because of conditions in their homeland. Haitian immigrant-rights groups and others have argued that Haiti remains far too dangerous for large scale returns, while DHS has maintained that conditions have improved enough to send Haitians back.

Of Haiti’s nearly 12 million people more than half need humanitarian assistance because of surging gang violence while also facing deepening poverty. Meanwhile, nearly 1. 5million people have been displaced by gangs — the same number displaced by the 2010 earthquake, which prompted the Obama administration to designate Haiti for TPS.

“Following its mass de-legalization efforts, this administration is knowingly sending people, including children, back into danger in Haiti. There is no limit to its cruelty and disregard for human life,” said Savi Arvey, director of policy refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First. “This is the 9th flight this year and on average we’ve seen one flight per month since December 2023.”

The flight comes amid ongoing gang attacks in Haiti and a broader immigration crackdown by the Trump administration, which saw nearly 50,000 arrests in July. It is the highest single monthly arrest total by the Department of Homeland Security since Trump began his second term, according to the recently released government data provided by ICE to the Deportation Data Project based at U.C. Berkeley and UCLA.

Among them are over 7,000 arrests in Florida and 500 in Ohio, two states with populations of Haitians who previously had TPS and now are in danger of detention and deportation.

In addition to being arrested at traffic stops, Haitians are also being outfitted with electronic ankle monitors by federal authorities in the Ohio-area. No one appears to be immune, not individuals with asylum applications pending or pastors, two of whom were recently arrested by ICE in Springfield.

This weekend, faith leaders are expected to travel to Springfield to request the immediate release of one of the pastors, Joubert Adrien, from immigration detention after he was detained while riding as a passenger in a car. A husband and father of two children, ages 15 and 7, he has lived in the United States for five years. Faith leaders also note that he has no criminal history, no prior immigration detention and no final order of removal. He also has not lived in Haiti for more than 20 years.

This week dozens of Haitian migrants for example, were brought to the Krome Detention Center in southwest Miami-Dade country after being arrested in front of grocery stores and shopping malls.

On Tuesday, the United States was among several foreign governments offering its “deepest condolences to the victims and their families” after armed gangs stormed the mountainside farming community of Kenscoff above the capital, killing dozens of people and kidnapping more than 50 others, including infants.

Some of the victims were massacred in a church that had become a place of refuge for those displaced by the repeated violence; others were shot as they fled or burned alive.

It was unclear where those aboard Thursday’s flight were from in Haiti or how long they had been in the U.S. As reflected in the birthplace of some of the younger passengers, some of those being deported had previously lived in Brazil, which is part of a broader migration route that had emerged after Haiti’s 2010 earthquake.

title: Trump administration's wage cuts for seasonal farmworkers is unlawful, federal judge in ...
description:
A Labor Department rule that cut wages for foreign guest workers is unlawful, a California federal judge ruled Wednesday.
Sherriff ordered the Labor Department to “promptly produce” a new methodology for calculating H-2A wage rates consistent with his decision.
He directed the agency to notify employers backpay may be owed to H-2A workers and U.S. farmworkers if the new applicable rates exceed what they were paid.
“This decision recognizes the important and essential work of the men and women who put food on our tables and that farm workers should get paid fairly,” Teresa Romero, president of the United Farm Workers, said in a statement.
“Now that the court has spoken, the Trump administration should do the right thing and work to protect farm worker wages.”
text:
A Labor Department rule that cut wages for foreign guest workers is unlawful, a California federal judge ruled Wednesday.

U.S. District Judge Kirk E. Sherriff in Fresno concluded that the Labor Department failed to reasonably consider whether it could satisfy its legal obligation “to ensure that the hiring of H-2A workers will not ‘adversely affect’ U.S. farmworkers’ wages.” But he allowed the Department of Labor rule to remain temporarily in effect while the agency develops a replacement.

Sherriff ordered the Labor Department to “promptly produce” a new methodology for calculating H-2A wage rates consistent with his decision. He directed the agency to notify employers backpay may be owed to H-2A workers and U.S. farmworkers if the new applicable rates exceed what they were paid.

The ruling is a win for farmworker advocates who sued the Trump administration last year, arguing that the rule would undercut wages paid to U.S. workers. More than a dozen farmworkers across the nation, along with the United Farm Workers of America and the UFW Foundation, sought to overturn the rule.

The plaintiffs alleged that the rule — which they said cut wages of H-2A workers between $3 and $7 per hour — was “unlawful” and would “put downward pressure on the wages of U.S. workers” who are in similar jobs, often on the same contracts as those with visas.

According to the UFW Foundation, after the rule went into effect, wages in California fell from $19.97 to $16.90 an hour — a 15% cut for both H-2A workers and U.S. farmworkers working beside them.

“This decision recognizes the important and essential work of the men and women who put food on our tables and that farm workers should get paid fairly,” Teresa Romero, president of the United Farm Workers, said in a statement. “The government must move quickly to issue new, legal, wage rates that protect the jobs and wages of local farm workers, and employers must be held accountable for paying back any difference between the new legal wage and the illegal wage rates still in effect.”

The Department of Labor and the Department of Justice did not immediately respond to requests for comment on whether the government plans to appeal.

The Department of Labor previously estimated that the rule, which went into effect Oct. 2, would save employers $2.46 billion yearly. The union argued in the lawsuit that it constituted “a transfer of wealth from the workers to their employers.”

In 2020, the Trump administration attempted to implement a similar rule but was blocked by a UFW and UFW Foundation lawsuit.

At a March hearing, Alexandra McTague Schulte, an attorney representing the U.S. Department of Labor, argued that the lower H-2A wage rates would not affect U.S. workers because growers already faced a labor shortage, with demand for farm labor exceeding the available supply, CalMatters reported.

Plaintiffs in the lawsuit, which was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of California, include farmworkers from Michigan, Georgia, California, Washington, Texas and Missouri.

Among the plaintiffs is Crisanto Serrano, a farmworker in Sunnyside, Wash., who said more growers “just want to hire H-2A workers, who they can keep trapped on their property, instead of us local workers, who live here and who pay taxes here and have decades of experience.”

“We don’t matter to the growers and to this President,” Serrano said in a statement. “They are happy to hire a new worker for less pay. But I am very happy that the court did take us into account. I hope this court decision will protect our wages and our jobs here in the Yakima Valley for a long time.”

Erica Lomeli Corcoran, chief executive officer of the UFW Foundation, hailed Sherriff’s ruling as “a much-needed victory for farm workers all over the country.”

“Farm workers deserve to be paid a fair day’s wage for a fair day’s work,” she said in a statement. “Now that the court has spoken, the Trump administration should do the right thing and work to protect farm worker wages.”

text:
Attorney General Todd Blanche has filed responses to two of three lawsuits brought against the Trump administration by fired immigration judges who have alleged their removals were due to discrimination.

More than 100 immigration judges have been removed from their jobs since President Donald Trump returned to office in January last year. Since then, the Trump administration has sought to reshape the immigration court system as it made immigration enforcement and mass deportations key priorities in his second term.

This week, Department of Justice (DOJ) attorneys filed motions, which Newsweek reviewed, seeking to dismiss lawsuits brought by two of the fired judges, arguing they lack merit and that the attorney general is permitted to remove immigration judges at will.

Read More on News

While the Department of Homeland Security is responsible for carrying out Trump’s mass deportation agenda, immigration courts fall under the purview of the DOJ. Federal courts have strict rules and give judges lifetime tenure, but the attorney general can fire immigration judges with fewer restraints.

Blanche’s filings are the latest episode in a legal battle over the administration's treatment of immigration judges, who play a central role in deciding asylum claims and deportation cases.

Critics have argued that the removals undermine judicial independence, while Blanche has said the department is working to root out judges who are ruling too slowly or aren’t following the law as it works to cut down on the backlog of millions of pending immigration cases.

Newsweek has contacted attorneys for the DOJ and the former immigration judges for comment via email.

Judges Challenge Firings

The three judges said in their lawsuits that after serving two-year probationary terms, they were not appointed to permanent positions. They note that per DOJ policy, immigration judges are initially appointed to serve two-year terms, after which their appointments are “routinely” converted to permanent positions.

The complaints allege that many of the immigration judges who have been terminated were people of color, ethnic minorities or had a history or representing or advocating for immigrants.

According to a lawsuit brought by Carla Espinoza, she was appointed to a two-year probationary term as an immigration judge in Chicago in July 2023 that was not converted to a permanent position in the summer of 2025 despite her “exemplary performance.”

The complaint alleges the DOJ discriminated against her because she has a Hispanic surname and because of her prior work representing immigrants.

In a motion to dismiss filed on August 25, DOJ attorneys representing Blanche asked a judge to dismiss the lawsuit.

The government argued the complaint “does not plausibly allege” that Espinoza is entitled to relief under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 or the First Amendment.

She “fails to plausibly allege that she was terminated because of her sex (female), race (Hispanic) or national origin (Mexican),” the filing said.

Her complaint “merely alleges that some immigration judges of the same sex were terminated months earlier and that the Department did not offer a permanent position to some non-white immigration judges of various races at the same time that her position was not made permanent,” it adds.

The attorneys also argued that because Espinoza “was an immigration judge—an inferior officer exercising significant executive power and discretion—she was removable at will by the Attorney General under Article II of the Constitution.”

A day earlier, DOJ attorneys filed a similar motion seeking the dismissal of a lawsuit brought by former California immigration judge Kyra Lilien. Lilien was notified in July last year that her two-year probationary term would not be converted to a permanent position despite her meeting or exceeding all performance standards, according to her complaint, which was also filed in May.

She alleges she was discriminated against because of her age, her sex, her political affiliation, her past association with Hispanic individuals and prior work for an immigrants’ rights nonprofit organization.

The motion to dismiss argues Lilien's complaint is “heavy on conclusory statements and speculation and light on allegations of fact.”

The DOJ attorneys also argue that she failed to establish that similarly situated judges outside her protected groups were treated differently or that her political beliefs played any role in her termination.

As in Espinoza's case, the attorneys argued that immigration judges serve as executive branch officers who may be removed without cause by the attorney general.

Blanche’s attorneys have not yet filed a response to a third lawsuit brought by George Pappas, who had served in immigration courts in Boston and Chelmsford, Massachusetts.

In his complaint, Pappas alleges he was denied a permanent appointment despite exceeding all performance standards and “consistently receiving the highest performance rating available.”

Pappas alleges he was discriminated against because of his Greek national origin, his age, his political affiliation, his past work representing immigrants and his advocacy for immigrants and immigrant rights.

The complaint said DOJ officials had issued memoranda that “laid bare DOJ management’s hostility to the utilization of diverse immigration judges and those whose legal backgrounds included the representation of immigrants.”

All three lawsuits seek jury trials.

Blanche's Push To Reshape Immigration Courts

The lawsuits come amid the Trump administration’s efforts to overhaul the immigration court system.

Blanche, who has led the DOJ since the ousting of Pam Bondi in April and was confirmed by the Senate earlier this month, defended the dismissal of immigration judges in an interview with The Associated Press in May, saying changes were necessary to make the courts more efficient and focused on carrying out immigration laws.

“If there’s judges that are just not applying the law in the way that it needs to be applied, delaying inappropriately, have backlogs that are just unacceptable, they’re the folks that we’re going to try to find somebody different to fill that spot,” he said.

Blanche added there were problems with judges repeatedly delaying cases and other cases where judges weren’t following the law “because of sympathy towards individuals.”

He also dismissed criticism that newly hired immigration judges do not meet standards.

“We have a very rigorous process to get people interviewed, approved and then trained up. And then we’ll watch them,” he said.

Fired Judges Speak Out

Several of the fired immigration judges have spoken out in interviews over the past year, calling their terminations unlawful.

Espinoza told the AP in July last year that she believes the firings have disproportionately affected women and ethnic minorities, including people with Hispanic-sounding surnames like hers.

In that interview, she also said another reason could be her decision to release Ramon Morales-Reyes, a Mexican immigrant who was falsely accused of threatening to assassinate Trump. Morales-Reyes was accused of a writing a threatening letter but Wisconsin authorities determined that he was actually framed by a man who had previously attacked him.

Pappas told CBS Evening News in July last year that he and other judges faced pressure to dismiss cases as the Trump administration ramped up arrests of immigrants at federal immigration courts.

“This is when ICE was roaming the courthouses,” he said. “Because if we dismissed a case, that person, that respondent, then leaves the court vulnerable to immediate apprehension and expedited removal.”

In that interview, he and Espinoza called their firings an attack on the rule of law.

“If you are attacking the very judges that adjudicate cases, there is not going to be a rule of law,” Pappas said. “That should concern everybody, not just immigrants, but U.S. citizens.”

title: She thought she had permission to be in the US. Then ICE arrested her on a jetway. | CNN
authors: Shimon Prokupecz, Meridith Edwards, Rachel Clarke
description:
Any certainty in her life had vanished when she was detained for three weeks this month after ICE officers stopped her while she was boarding a plane home from Atlanta.
Increasingly people with papers they thought allowed them to be in the US are being targeted.
If she encountered immigration officers, she thought she would be able to offer documents to show she is in the US with permission and be allowed to go on her way.
In theory, ICE officers would know who would be arriving at the airports for which flights, and that they are unarmed by the time they reach the gate because they have gone through airport screening.
“A week before that, month before that, I’m just figuring ICE is out there doing their job.
text:
Indi Veitia walked into the Immigration and Customs Enforcement field office on Tuesday not knowing whether she would be allowed to leave.

She was entering the nondescript building in a nondescript business park off the I-465 that encircles Indianapolis for the first time to comply with a court order. Any certainty in her life had vanished when she was detained for three weeks this month after ICE officers stopped her while she was boarding a plane home from Atlanta.

After 20 minutes, officers sent her to a location nearby, her stress rising as the morning dragged on. About two hours later, the Venezuelan asylum-seeker emerged from the office of a security firm contracted by the government. She fell into the embrace of friends and began to cry. She had a new weight of a tracking monitor strapped to her right ankle and a ton of stress, emotion and dread on her shoulders, too.

“I’m broken,” the 47-year-old corporate worker told CNN. “There is nothing I can do.”

Veitia’s detention highlights the confusing nature of US immigration enforcement and underscores the ratcheting up of the Trump administration’s efforts to deport non-citizens. Increasingly people with papers they thought allowed them to be in the US are being targeted.

Tackling immigration was a key promise of Donald Trump’s re-election campaign and a priority for his White House team, including deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, which has set a goal of 2,000 arrests a day

Tactics have evolved from taking undocumented immigrants already in custody, to targeting foreign students, workplace raids often in Democrat-run cities, to traffic stops and now to identifying people using information they give before taking a domestic flight.

The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not respond to specific questions from CNN but said in a statement: “DHS reversed the horrendous Biden-era policy that allowed aliens in our country illegally to jet around our country. Under President Trump, DHS will no longer tolerate this. This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.”

Jorge Gavilanes, a seasoned immigration lawyer, told CNN: “We’ve been describing the immigration system as broken for decades. Now it’s just complete chaos.”

Veitia decided to share her story because she said she had contributed to her community and her company, had never broken any law and still was put through what she calls “hell.”

“I thought that I was going to lose my mind. I never thought that I could experience something like this in a country where you believe that the people do the things by the book.”

Veitia is a self-described rule-follower, who came to the United States on a visa in 2019 and later applied for asylum. If she encountered immigration officers, she thought she would be able to offer documents to show she is in the US with permission and be allowed to go on her way. She has a driver’s license and work permit, and the receipt of her application for asylum from 2020 states: “You may remain in the US until your asylum application is decided.” She is still waiting to be called for an asylum interview.

She told CNN she thought she was doing everything correctly. She and her wife built a life in Indiana, making friends and raising puppies, as they waited for the government to adjudicate their claim. She worked her way from a warehouse job to a corporate position in a clothing firm that requires she travel on business around the country.

Earlier this month as she walked to her plane at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, she said she was slammed against the wall of the jetway to the cabin door by immigration enforcement officers who handcuffed her and hustled her down steps to unmarked SUVs.

When the men in plain clothes finally asked her status, she decided to say nothing.

“In any other circumstances, I probably will have answered those questions, but at that moment I felt that they were already being extremely rude and extremely aggressive to me,” she said. “That’s how kidnaps happen in my country.”

At the detention center in Lumpkin, Georgia, she was given threadbare towels, a sheet and a uniform. She said she was in a windowless dorm with more than 60 women, who shared four toilet stalls and four showers. One day there was no running water for 8 hours, another day power went out. “In that center, everything is awful. The treatment is awful. The guards are one ruder than another. They treat everyone like criminals. I wouldn’t treat an animal like that. It’s just inhumane.”

She tried to visualize happier moments and places with her wife but says she was breaking down emotionally and felt hopeless. “No one could guarantee that I was going to be safe and I was going to be allowed to be back home with my family. And that was heartbreaking.”

The detainees also tried to keep each other’s spirits up, and Veitia knew her friends and her employers were fighting on her behalf, writing supporting letters and finding lawyers in Georgia who represented her at a bond hearing where she was released after 21 days.

Friends from Indiana came to pick her up. “I said I don’t want to get in a plane,” Veitia recalled. “We went down to Alabama and didn’t touch Georgia anymore.”

Veitia wanted to put Georgia in the rear-view mirror.

In Venezuela, she had worked for a Japanese multinational company, rising through the ranks to lead its operations across Central America.

In the US, she said she was content to start over, confident she would rise again. “I started as a warehouse associate. Two weeks later, I was process lead. Three months later, I was supervisor,” said Veitia, who is now in a corporate role. She’s proficient in learning languages and finding solutions, making sense of things.

Still, the arrest and detention make no sense to her. “I have done everything that the government have asked me to do,” she said.

Gavilanes, a partner at the Kuck and Baxter law firm in Atlanta, represented Veitia in her Georgia hearing. A specialist in immigration law, he said he now advises clients not to fly, and for asylum seekers to take extra care everywhere.

“Yes, they have overstayed their visa, but also yes, they’re not unlawfully present,” he told CNN. “The government has given them a permit to work, get a driver’s license, and do whatever they need to do to take care of themselves while their application is pending. But now the same government is telling them, ‘Oh no, you’re not allowed to be here,’ which is contradictory.”

In DHS’ email to CNN, a spokesperson did not address the contradiction. “To be clear: a pending application does NOT confer legal status in the United States,” the email read. “The Trump Administration is utilizing all lawful options to carry out the largest deportation operation in history, just as President Trump promised.”

Gavilanes said that it used to take two to four years to get an interview where an asylum case could be determined, but that now it’s seven to 10 years. Immigration courts are backed up and judges have been purged.

Added to that, is the increased action against groups who have traditionally been left alone, Gavilanes said, like those with work permits or petitions for asylum.

“I’ve been practicing immigration for more than 10 years. I’ve never seen this level of enforcement, and it’s really disheartening.”

He has noticed the increase in arrests at airports — calling them “low-hanging fruit” for detention.

Passenger information is shared between ICE and the Transportation Security Administration, both of which come under the Department of Homeland Security.

In theory, ICE officers would know who would be arriving at the airports for which flights, and that they are unarmed by the time they reach the gate because they have gone through airport screening.

ICE records obtained and collated by the Deportation Data Project show just 13 immigration arrests at airports for the entirety of the last two years of the Biden administration. In 2025, the total jumped to at least 39 arrests, and that number is dwarfed by at least 77 detentions at airports just in July of 2026.

But mistakes are made. US citizen John Phillips is a regular traveler from Atlanta’s Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport, and has TSA PreCheck and frequent-flier status with his airline.

This month he was headed down the jetway to board a plane to Las Vegas when he was grabbed by three officers and handcuffed.

“In the moment, I was just thinking about, ‘Oh my gosh, what’s happening? Where am I going to be taken? What’s going on?’ But afterwards, you know, you start thinking about that, and you’re like, ‘Why do they think it’s necessary to do all of that for an obviously unarmed person,” he told CNN.

He said he was held back from the plane even as he said that he was a citizen. After a few minutes one of the men showed him an image on a phone of a man with apparently the same name and birthdate, but who clearly was not him.

The handcuffs were taken off, and he was allowed to board, shaking with shock.

“A week before that, month before that, I’m just figuring ICE is out there doing their job. They’re sending the criminals back, like I hear on the news,” he said.

His experience was a “big awakening,”, said the 54-year-old, adding that he has new empathy for immigrants who could be sought by ICE. “They have to feel like they’re being hunted, like a deer in deer season … They have to be thinking about this all the time, citizen or not, criminal or not, it’s got to be on their mind all the time. And now it’s on my mind all the time because I evidently share a name and a birthday with somebody that the government wants.”

Maria, a 22-year-old asylum-seeker from Venezuela, told CNN she, too, believed that immigration enforcement would be going after criminals. And like Phillips, her opinion has changed.

“It feels that they are slowly trying to get everybody that has come to this country,” she said, asking CNN not to use her real name for fear it might affect the handling of her case.

Her lawyer has advised her not to fly, but she said she is afraid everywhere she goes. Recently she saw police cars on the way to work. “I didn’t know if they were working to get people that were speeding, that were holding their phone (while driving), or if they were working to find people that don’t have a status,” she said.

“I’m already running from a country where you’re unlawfully detained for not having the same ideology as the government, and now I’m here trying to seek protection, and I’m also going to be scared to be detained again.”

Maria came to the US eight years ago on a tourist visa with her mother when she was 14. Once her asylum application was accepted for processing, she went to high school and has spent her entire adult life in the US.

“They do a really good job here in high school, teaching you the values of being an American, of always following the law, always filing for your taxes, doing the right thing,” she said. “I was hoping that by doing the right thing, I was going to get that future working and just having my life.”

But parts of her life are on hold. She’s a bridesmaid for a friend’s upcoming wedding but has decided not to go to the bachelorette party because it would involve a long drive.

“Every day, whenever I leave my house, it just feels like a gamble, if I’m going to make it to work or if I’m going to make it back home.”

In Indianapolis, those fears are impacting Veitia, too. She treasures being home and eating familiar food, but she tries not to look at her ankle monitor because it makes her cry.

“I do want to stay, but also I don’t know if I will be able to hold myself (together) if I have to be in a detention center ever again,” she said. “Those centers are built to break you down.”

text:
Christian Castro, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent charged with shooting Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in Minneapolis in January, was released from a Texas county jail early Thursday morning.

Castro has been the subject of a rare interstate extradition battle between Minnesota and Texas, as Texas Gov. Greg Abbott refused to sign paperwork facilitating Castro’s transfer to Minnesota, where he is charged with four counts of second-degree assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime.

U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. of the Southern District of Texas paved the way for Castro’s release in a Wednesday decision denying Minnesota’s request to force Abbott to facilitate the extradition, or at least keep Castro in custody until the matter is settled.

Castro was arrested by the Texas Rangers, a state law enforcement agency, on May 29. A Texas law prevents law enforcement agencies from holding fugitives with pending extradition requests for more than 90 days.

Cameron County Sheriff Manuel Treviño told the Reformer Castro was released at 6:59 a.m. Thursday.

Castro is accused of firing his gun through the closed front door of a Minneapolis home, hitting Cesar-Solis in the leg. Castro accused Sosa-Celis and another Venezuelan immigrant of assaulting him with a broom and a snow shovel before Castro opened fire, leading to assault charges against the two men that were dropped after surveillance footage proved Castro’s statements false.

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison submitted affidavits to the court showing that Castro was in a romantic relationship with a woman in Mexico, and owns property there, presenting a possible flight risk. Cameron County, where Castro was jailed, is on the U.S.-Mexico border.

Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, who charged Castro, said in a Wednesday press conference that the next steps in the legal process become much more complicated if Castro flees the country.

text:
The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent charged in a Minneapolis shooting during Operation Metro Surge has been released from a Texas jail, the Associated Press reports.

The release follows a federal judge's Wednesday denial of Minnesota's request for a temporary restraining order to halt Christian Castro's release.

The shooting occurred the night of Jan. 14, when a Venezuelan migrant was shot in the leg by officer Castro, and two others were arrested. Castro was charged in Minnesota with four counts of second-degree assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime. Castro accused the man of assaulting him with a broomstick and shovel before the shooting, but investigators say footage from a nearby camera helped prove that was a lie.

Castro was arrested in Texas on May 29, and has been held at the Cameron County Jail ever since, despite multiple extradition requests by Minnesota officials. The Cameron County sheriff said he would release Castro on Thursday morning.

In U.S. District Court Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr.'s 13-page ruling, he denied Minnesota's request because the "matter does not present an issue ripe for adjudication," saying Minnesota's case is based on claims that Republican Texas Gov. Greg Abbott has violated the Extradition Act by refusing to sign Castro's rendition warrant.

"The record reflects only that Governor Abbott has neither agreed nor refused to sign the rendition warrant as to Castro. Instead, Governor Abbott has requested that the Texas Secretary of State 'investigate [Minnesota's] demand and report to [the Governor] concerning Mr. Castro's situation and circumstances and whether he ought to be surrendered,'" Rodriguez wrote in his ruling.

Minnesota officials say Castro could flee the country, citing calls he made from jail to a woman in Mexico, talking "about marrying her and buying a house in Mexico when he is released," according to the lawsuit.

The judge conceded that Castro could flee the country but added that "the threat of injury by itself does not create an issue ripe for adjudication."

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison said that Castro "will not escape justice in Minnesota" regardless of the judge's ruling.

Abbott's press secretary, Andrew Mahaleris, welcomed the ruling and said it was the governor's duty to carefully consider the merits of extradition requests.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

text:
BIDDEFORD, Maine (WGME) -- The attorney for Johan Sebastian Duran Guerrero's family — the man shot and killed by an ICE agent in July — is speaking directly to CBS13 after Vice President JD Vance's remarks about the shooting.

During a speech in Brewer on Monday, Vance suggested people should "have a little bit of perspective" on the shooting and focus more on drugs coming into the country.

The family's attorney, Ben Gideon, is pushing back, saying the vice president misrepresented what happened.

Gideon says he spoke with Duran Guerrero's wife, Karolina, who was confused by Vance's remarks and felt they misrepresented who her husband was and had no connection to the circumstances surrounding the shooting.

Also read: Vance calls Canada a 'state' during remarks in Brewer, then corrects himself

"They were tone deaf, disrespectful and offensive," Gideon said.

Vance made the remarks while answering questions about the July shooting in Biddeford.

"My message to the Democrats who are so worried about that situation is to say, have a little bit of perspective," Vance said.

The vice president went on to suggest Democrats also consider the impact of drugs coming into the country and Maine.

Vance was also asked whether there would be a federal investigation into the shooting.

"Of course, the Trump administration, our Department of Justice — everybody investigates this stuff," Vance said.

Gideon says no federal agency has reached out to him or Duran Guerrero's family, which he believes indicates there is no active investigation.

"Vance can say whatever he wants, but the reality is there's no investigation because an investigation requires boots on the ground," Gideon said.

CBS13 asked the Department of Homeland Security whether it could confirm an investigation is underway and why no contact has been made with the family or its attorney.

DHS provided a statement it has previously shared, saying, "DHS OIG has been notified and, like all discharge of firearms, this will be investigated." The department provided no additional specifics.

Video from the scene of the shooting shows Duran Guerrero's car moving in circles as ICE agents surrounded the vehicle. DHS says an ICE agent fired because of a possible threat to public safety.

Vance defended the government's actions.

"I look at that case, what I see is inevitably a country that is trying to enforce its laws," Vance said.

Gideon argues the use of deadly force was unjustified.

"Under our legal system and our Constitution, driving off is not a legal basis or justified basis for the use of lethal force," Gideon said.

Also read: Family of ICE shooting victim demands answers during Congressional field hearing in Maine

Gideon is now calling on Vance to retract his statements.

"I think that the vice president of the United States, very sadly, is intentionally misrepresenting the circumstances for political gain," Gideon said.

Gideon says he is preparing to file a lawsuit against the federal government. He says the family is still in the investigation stage and working to gather all the facts it needs.

text:
Gov. Ned Lamont was joined at Kennedy Park by U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy, U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes, Lt. Gov. Susan Bysiewicz, Danbury Mayor Roberto Alves and representatives of Danbury Unites for Immigrants as ICE activity surged during the first days of school.

Bysiewicz said 50 people have been detained by ICE in Danbury this week. Danbury Unites for Immigrants said 16 people were detained Monday, 10 Tuesday and 25 Wednesday, bringing the group's estimate to 51 detentions over three days.

The agency added: "Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, if you break the law, you will face the consequences. Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the U.S."

Connecticut Officials Address ICE Activity

Lamont condemned the increased enforcement activity and questioned whether the operations were focused on people who pose a threat to public safety.

"I was on with Secretary Mullin, and I said, 'I'm outraged,'" Lamont said. "This is the first days our kids are back in school and you've got people patrolling around our courthouses, patrolling around our schools. Stay away."

The governor said Connecticut officials have limited authority to stop federal agents from carrying out immigration enforcement, but said the state would continue working to protect residents' rights and hold federal authorities accountable.

Lamont pointed to the November elections as a path toward changing federal immigration policy, urging voters to elect a Congress that could restrict ICE funding.

"Win in November. I'm telling you what the answer is," Lamont said. "Let's take back the House of Representatives."

U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy focused his remarks on reports of enforcement activity occurring around the start of the school year, accusing ICE of deliberately creating fear in the community.

“ICE is not here to protect Danbury,” Murphy said. “ICE is here to put Danbury into a state of terror.”

Murphy said he and U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes would demand information about the people detained and the legal basis for their arrests. He also called for Congress to withhold additional funding from the agency.

“Congress should not authorize a single additional dollar for ICE while this illegality continues,” Murphy said.

Hayes focused on steps families can take immediately if they fear a loved one could be detained.

Hayes said her office has received several calls from people trying to locate relatives detained by ICE and urged families to complete congressional privacy release forms in advance, which can allow her office to more quickly assist them.

She also urged parents to update their children's emergency contacts so another trusted adult can pick them up if a parent is detained.

“What I would hate to see is a snowball effect where a parent is detained and then a child goes into state custody because there's no one to pick them up,” Hayes said.

Hayes said she has also requested a meeting with regional federal immigration officials to determine the focus of the Danbury operation and how long it is expected to continue.

'They Were Taking People Everywhere,' Advocacy Group Says

Representatives of Danbury Unites for Immigrants, an immigrant advocacy group, described families separated by enforcement activity.

Clementina Lunar, a DUFI volunteer, said she spoke with a family whose child witnessed a parent being detained after putting the child on a school bus.

“When he handed the child to the bus helper, ICE came and took him,” Lunar said.

She said volunteers have delivered food to residents afraid to leave their homes and watched school bus stops to help children get home safely.

“There is fear, but there is also a lot of resilience and resistance,” she said.

Juan Fonseca Tapia, a Mexican immigrant and co-founder of DUFI, became emotional as he described what he said he witnessed during the operations.

“They were taking people everywhere,” Fonseca Tapia said. “They hurt them. They were bleeding. I saw the chains they put on them — not handcuffs, literal chains.”

He said one person was pepper-sprayed and another was hospitalized after being struck by an ICE vehicle.

ICE has not confirmed the group's detention figures or its accounts of the reported injuries.

Alves Calls For Transparency As Crowd Presses Officials

Mayor Alves called for greater transparency from federal authorities about who has been detained and why.

Alves said the city is demanding a public accounting of the number of people detained, the legal basis for the operations and prompt access to legal counsel for those taken into custody. He also called for an independent review of reported uses of force by federal agents.

Alves stressed that residents should continue to call Danbury police, firefighters and other emergency services when they need help, regardless of immigration status. He also urged people documenting federal agents to keep a safe distance and not interfere with operations.

Danbury was ranked the seventh-most diverse city in the United States in WalletHub's 2026 study of more than 500 cities.

“We have people from all over the world in this community,” Alves said. “We need to come together now. We may not always agree on the strategy or the tactic, but we agree that we want ICE out of our community.”

description:

There has also been a drop in legal migration arrivals, asylum claims and small boat arrivals to the UK compared to a year ago.

text:
There has been a significant fall in the use of hotels to house asylum seekers waiting for a Home Office decision, data shows.

In June 2025 there were more than 32,000 people in hotel rooms, but by June this year it had halved to more than 16,000.

There has also been a drop in legal migration arrivals, asylum claims and small boat arrivals to the UK compared to a year ago.

The Home Office said the figures showed that policies to control migration were having an effect - but said there was still more to do on the issue of small boat crossings.

There was also a fall in the number of family members coming to the UK to join someone already legally in the country, while asylum claims were also down by a fifth.

Some 38,000 illegal arrivals were detected in the year to June - 33,000 of them on small boats across the sea from France.

More up to date figures show the trend in small boat arrivals has continued to be lower than last year. Correspondingly, claims for asylum have also fallen.

Some 86,000 people sought asylum - down a fifth on the previous year. About half of those applications for help came from people who were already legally in the UK, rather than having arrived on a small boat.

The rise in the use of hotels coincided with an increase in arrivals across the English Channel from 2019 and a slowing down of Home Office decisions as to how many of these claimants had a genuine right to stay in the UK or should be told to leave.

One of the first decisions of the new Starmer government in July 2024 was to order officials to work faster in deciding these claims, with a target of ending the use of hotels within five years.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said: "A little over two years into office and the asylum backlog is down, the number of asylum seekers in hotels is falling, illegal working arrests are at record levels, and deportations and returns are up markedly.

"Small boats numbers are also now falling, but we are not complacent and there is more we must do."

"The surest way to empty the accommodation is to make plain that nobody who crosses the Channel gets to stay," he added.

Zia Yusuf, its home affairs spokesman, said "Under Reform, illegal boats in the Channel will be stopped by our Navy, and all those here illegally will be detained and deported."

The number of people in houses around the country paid for by the Home Office has gone up from 65,000 at the end of 2024 to 69,000 in June this year - arrangements that are part of a decade-long standing contract with private providers.

The number of asylum claimants waiting for an initial ruling on their case - meaning they are told whether they have a genuine case for protection or should leave the UK - was 40,000. That is down from the peak of 175,000 in June 2023.

Meanwhile some 40,000 found not to have a reason to be in the UK - either foreign offenders, visa overstayers or failed asylum applicants - were removed from the country in the year to June 2026, an 8% increase on the year before.

Officials say about a third were failed asylum seekers - the highest number for 16 years and double the rate of removals that occurred in 2021.

The statistics also show 235,000 work visas in the year to the end of June 2026 by the Home Office. That is down 18% on the previous year and 62% lower than the peak in December 2023.

That high related to policies followed by the former prime minister Boris Johnson to liberalise the work visa system - but in its dying months the Rishi Sunak government tightened the rules.

Significantly, the number of workers who could arrive on a specialist health and care worker visa fell by 90% - following progressive tightening of that route.

The data also reveals 383,000 foreign students came to the UK in the year to June 2026 - down 11% on the previous year and 41% down on the peak in June 2023.

Following the introduction of restrictions on how migrants could apply to bring family members to join them, only 58,000 such visas were granted in the year to June 2026 - 19% down on the previous 12 months.

Statisticians say that the fall was "largely driven" by new rules making it exceptionally hard for refugee families to come together in the UK. That policy - which has faced challenges in the High Court - remains in place with the government believing it has an impact on deterring illegal arrivals across the English Channel.

title: Trump Administration Pauses Immigrant Visa Appointments Worldwide Days After 75 ...
description:
The Trump administration has paused immigrant visa appointments at U.S. embassies and consulates worldwide, days after a federal judge struck down a separate policy that blocked immigrant visas for nationals of 75 countries.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio directed consular officers to refuse immigrant visas to nationals of 75 countries the department considered at heightened risk of becoming a public charge.
Federal immigration law already allows officers to deny an immigrant visa if, after reviewing an applicant’s circumstances, they conclude the person is likely to become primarily dependent on government support.
Applicants can still be denied immigrant visas under existing public-charge rules or for another legal reason.
The pause affects immigrant visa appointments for people seeking to move permanently to the United States through family-based, employment-based, and other categories.
text:
The Trump administration has paused immigrant visa appointments at U.S. embassies and consulates worldwide, days after a federal judge struck down a separate policy that blocked immigrant visas for nationals of 75 countries.

The State Department says the scheduling changes are temporary and needed to train consular officers on how to determine whether applicants are likely to become dependent on public benefits. It has not announced how long the training will last or when normal appointment scheduling will resume.

The timing has already returned the dispute to federal court. On Aug. 26, lawyers for the groups that successfully challenged the 75-country restriction asked U.S. District Judge Jeannette A. Vargas to enforce her Aug. 21 decision, arguing that the new global pause is preventing immigrant visa cases from moving forward.

The government opposes the request. The two measures are legally different: the earlier rule directed officers to refuse immigrant visas based on nationality, while the current pause applies worldwide and is described by the State Department as a temporary training measure. Vargas has not ruled that the new interruption violates her order or federal immigration law.

The dispute began with a policy announced Jan. 14 and put into effect a week later. Secretary of State Marco Rubio directed consular officers to refuse immigrant visas to nationals of 75 countries the department considered at heightened risk of becoming a public charge.

Federal immigration law already allows officers to deny an immigrant visa if, after reviewing an applicant’s circumstances, they conclude the person is likely to become primarily dependent on government support. The review can include age, health, family status, finances, education and skills.

The January policy went further by requiring refusals based on nationality even when an applicant was otherwise eligible and had not been found likely to become a public charge.

Vargas ruled Aug. 21 that the policy exceeded the Secretary of State’s authority and violated federal immigration law. In Catholic Legal Immigration Network v. Rubio, she found that Congress gave consular officers responsibility for deciding individual visa applications and did not allow the secretary to dictate those decisions solely because of an applicant’s nationality.

She also found that the restriction violated a federal law barring nationality discrimination in the issuance of immigrant visas, calling the 75-country policy “patently unlawful.”

The ruling set aside both the policy and visa refusals based solely on it. Those applications were returned to consular officers for another review, but the court did not require the government to approve them.

Applicants can still be denied immigrant visas under existing public-charge rules or for another legal reason. Vargas rejected the automatic nationality barrier, not the government’s authority to examine each applicant’s eligibility.

The State Department says the new training is intended to make those public-charge reviews more comprehensive and consistent.

Attorneys challenging the worldwide pause argue that canceling interviews prevents officers from conducting the individual reviews contemplated by the court’s ruling. Their emergency filing says immigrant visa appointments began being canceled around the world shortly after Vargas issued her decision and argues that training cannot leave applicants without a way to have their cases reviewed and decided.

The government maintains that the scheduling changes are temporary and apply equally to applicants worldwide rather than singling out particular nationalities.

The consequences extend beyond people who were covered by the earlier 75-country restriction. The pause affects immigrant visa appointments for people seeking to move permanently to the United States through family-based, employment-based, and other categories.

Temporary visas are not part of the announced pause. Nonimmigrant visas used for tourism, study, business, and other short-term purposes continue under separate processing rules.

Some applicants face deadlines that make even a temporary delay significant. The emergency motion points to people selected for fiscal year 2026 diversity visas, which generally must be issued by Sept. 30.

Anyone unable to complete the process before the fiscal year ends can lose the opportunity to receive a diversity visa even if otherwise eligible, making the length of the appointment pause especially important for those applicants.

text:
ALBANY — The immigration enforcement agreements that several New York sheriff’s departments have with federal agencies are narrow in scope and allow designated officers only to serve warrants and complete custodial transfers of migrants who are in jailed on local criminal charges at the time of their release, according to affidavits from several sheriffs filed this week in U.S. District Court.

The affidavits were included in a lawsuit that 15 New York sheriffs filed Tuesday challenging a new state law that took effect this week and bans congressionally authorized agreements governing civil immigration enforcement coordination between local, state and federal agencies.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

U.S. District Court Judge Mae A. D’Agostino signed an order Wednesday directing the state to file a response by Sept. 9 opposing the sheriffs' request for a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction that would suspend enforcement of the new law while the case is pending.

Gov. Kathy Hochul reiterated Tuesday, at a news conference touting “her new law to stand against ICE overreach,” that she believes the law applies only to “civil” immigration enforcement. She said: “Once they’re convicted and do their time, we work with ICE to ensure they’re deported.”

Some New York sheriffs were invited to the governor’s news conference, but none were in attendance. She was instead flanked by four police chiefs from cities led by Democratic mayors.

The governor’s public statements and the language of the new statute make clear that the law was intended only to prevent state and local police agencies — and other government workers — from conducting or assisting in civil immigration enforcement under the formal agreements with ICE. But according to the sheriffs' court filings, virtually none of the local sheriff’s departments conduct any type of civil immigration enforcement.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The federal statute that authorizes the agreements — Section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act — was added to the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, which was adopted during the administration of President Bill Clinton. The federal legislation was amended in 2002 to authorize the secretary of the Department of Homeland Security — which was created after the 9/11 terrorist attacks — to enter into written agreements with state and local agencies “so that qualified personnel can perform certain functions of an immigration officer.”

But the 287(g) agreements, which the state law mandated must be cancelled this week, are not the only contracts that police agencies in New York have with the U.S. Marshals Service. Other federal contracts also have enabled those local agencies to house people who are being held in custody on behalf of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Elected officials who support New York’s law have said little about the statute’s requirement that police departments must also cancel those contracts, which many agencies have had for decades with the Marshals Service. They have enabled their departments to house anyone who is in federal custody, including for criminal charges based on immigration violations. Those agreements were established under an appropriations law passed by Congress in 2001.

A subsequent memorandum issued by the Department of Justice noted that act had authorized the “U.S. Marshals Service and the Immigration and Naturalization Service … (to) frequently enter into (intergovernmental agreements) with state and local governments for the detention of persons in connection with federal criminal and immigration proceedings.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

But the new state law requires those agreements also must be cancelled by Nov. 25, according to the sheriffs' lawsuit. The result could cut off a significant funding stream for sheriff’s departments that rely on revenue they receive from temporarily housing federal prisoners, they said.

The Albany County Sheriff’s Office, which is not a plaintiff in the lawsuit, has had written agreements with the U.S. Marshals Service dating back years that produce millions of dollars in annual revenue from housing federal prisoners. But Sheriff Craig Apple said his facility will not accept ICE detainees — even if they are charged with a crime — and he has said he will not honor ICE’s requests to hold a migrant in custody under one of their detainee requests.

But even his department’s policies are murky. Last year, Apple’s department contacted federal immigration authorities to come to the county jail and take into custody a Turkish immigrant who was being released after serving time on charges of forcing a 15-year-old girl into his car and raping her in Albany’s South End in 2024. The man was not facing any additional criminal charges at the time he was turned over to ICE to be deported.

Affirmations attributed to multiple sheriffs in the federal lawsuit challenging New York’s law banning the agreements include statements from Madison County Sheriff Todd Hood and Broome County Sheriff Fred Akshar. They indicated that the primary reason for their now-rescinded 287(g) agreements with the U.S. Marshals Service had been so they could serve and execute federal warrants of arrest “for immigration violations on designated aliens in our jail at the time of scheduled release, so (their) custody could transfer to ICE.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Askhar, a former state senator, said in his affirmation that Broome County’s agreement with the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is part of what’s known as a Warrant Service Officer Program — which is one of the most limited forms of 287(g) agreements under the section of federal law that created the programs.

Like other sheriffs, he said their agreement had not resulted in the department assisting with any cases involving only civil immigration proceedings.

“It operates only inside the jail. Its purpose is to allow designated officers to serve immigration warrants and complete custodial transfers of people who are already in local criminal custody at the moment of scheduled release,” Akshar wrote in his affirmation. “Our designated officers did not make civil immigration arrests in the community, did not conduct traffic stops for immigration status, and did not question people on the street about their papers.”

Akshar, who along with many other county sheriffs cancelled their agreements with ICE under the state law that went into effect Tuesday, said that roughly eight members of his department had been trained and designated to take part in the program.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Madison County Sheriff Todd Hood, who is the Republican gubernatorial candidate for lieutenant governor, said that his department also signed a Warrant Service Officer Program agreement with ICE last year. Although those agreements fall under the umbrella of the types of agreements banned by New York’s law, he also said his department has not engaged in any civil immigration matters — which is what the law was intended to ban.

“In the past year, we have seen approximately seven deportations of individuals who offended in Madison County. The underlying local charges have included rape … assault, driving while intoxicated, and weapons possession, among others,” Hood said in his affirmation. “These are not theoretical cases. They are people who were arrested on local criminal charges, booked into our jail, and later removed.”

Hood added that his department does not “treat every foreign-born inmate as a threat.”

“I do treat every person already in our custody on a criminal charge as someone whose identity and warrants should be fully checked before we open the door,” he said. “When someone is arrested in Madison County on a local charge, the jail must be able to determine who that person is. Equally important, we must be able to determine whether another jurisdiction (including the federal government) wants them before they are released back into the community.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Under the agreement that Madison County has had with ICE for the past year, Hood said, the small department that employs about 187 people and has a jail with 150 beds did not detain any immigrants based solely on civil immigration violations.

“Each case began with a local criminal booking, not an immigration sweep,” Hood said. “That is the entire scope of what we did: people already in the jail on criminal charges, already subject to ordinary release procedures, and already of interest to federal authorities.”

But Hochul and other state officials have implied in their public statements that the agreements have led to local sheriff’s departments participating in ICE raids or helping round up migrants who may be facing only deportation proceedings. The governor also reiterated her position that she wants police to be able to help ICE deport someone convicted of a crime.

“We’ve worked hard to drive down crime … to record lows, and that includes working with ICE to track down and apprehend criminals,” Hochul said Tuesday. “Once they’re convicted and do their time, we work with ICE to ensure they’re deported. And I’ll repeat that New York state will never become a sanctuary for criminals. But at the same time, we’re not talking about criminals, and we will not sit idly by when ICE commits atrocities on our streets.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

But the sheriffs' lawsuit alleges that the only migrants they process or run background checks on are individuals who are being held in their jails for criminal charges.

The sheriffs' affirmations were filed as part of a motion in the federal lawsuit that seeks to suspend enforcement of the law pending the outcome of the case. The case was filed in U.S. District Court in Albany this week by an attorney with the Federation for American Immigration Reform in Washington, D.C. The sheriff’s departments listed as plaintiffs in the case are from St. Lawrence, Wayne, Broome, Madison, Cattaraugus, Orange, Jefferson, Saratoga, Lewis, Franklin, Delaware, Fulton, Oswego, Cayuga and Rensselaer counties.

'Less safe'

Nassau County Executive Bruce Blakeman, the GOP gubernatorial candidate, on Wednesday said that his county sheriff’s office had suspended its 287(g) agreement with ICE due to the new state law, but that the department would seek to join the lawsuit filed by 15 other sheriff’s departments.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Blakeman said the new state law “will completely restrict local law enforcement from cooperating with ICE and getting illegal migrants who have committed crimes out of our communities. This law has made New York state more dangerous and less safe. … We have a governor and a Legislature that every major criminal justice initiative makes it easier for criminals to prey on our communities.”

Hochul said Tuesday that two of New York’s 62 sheriff’s departments had not informed her administration about whether they would comply with the law.

However, Akshar, who is Broome County’s sheriff, said he his department had declined to respond to a July 24 letter from the state attorney general’s office inquiring about their plans to comply with the law.

“I did not respond to that letter because the attorney general had no statutory authority to ask me those questions, nor did I have any obligation to do so,” Akshar said during a news conference Wednesday.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

But the sheriff said he did reply to a second letter from a new unit within the attorney general’s office — the Office of Immigrant Trust — that he received on Aug. 19. He said he responded in writing the next day and affirmed that his 287(g) agreement was being terminated under the requirements of the new state law.

Akshar said Wednesday that his department stands to lose about $2.2 million a year in revenue from not housing ICE detainees.

“This lawsuit really is about the associated independence and the constitutional authority that is granted to the office of the sheriff,” he said. “This lawsuit is about the aggressive and gross overreach by state government, specifically the defendants in this case, Gov. Hochul and the attorney general.”

The sheriff’s lawsuit was filed as the state law is also being challenged in an ongoing federal lawsuit filed by the U.S. Department of Justice in June.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Newsletter

Sign up for the Capitol A.M. Roundup newsletter

Get a free roundup of New York government and political news, delivered weekdays to your inbox.

Sign up here

Last month, U.S. District Judge Mae A. D’Agostino rejected the Justice Department’s request for a temporary injunction to block the portion of the law that bans the 287(g) agreements that had been made between U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and 12 New York sheriffs' departments.

D’Agostino concluded that the law prohibiting those agreements does not impede federal immigration enforcement activities.

She said that portion of the law, known as the Termination Act, “seeks only to control whether New York and its localities voluntarily engage in certain cooperation with federal authorities. The United States has also failed to show, at this stage, that the Termination Act likely discriminates against the federal government.”

text:
The Department of Homeland Security sent its second deportation flight in a week to Haiti on Thursday, returning dozens of Haitians to the unstable Caribbean country, including several children born in the U.S.

The children were among several families aboard the Immigration and Customs Enforcement charter flight scheduled to land in Cap-Haïtien, Haiti’s second-largest city and the main gateway for international flights since gang violence prompted restrictions on U.S. carriers flying into Port-au-Prince.

The youngest person aboard the ICE Air flight was 1-year-old born in the U.S., according to information shared with Haitian authorities ahead of the plane’s arrival.

The ICE Air deportation charter flight GXA6196 originated in Alexandria, LA and departed Opa-locka Executive Airport at 10:04 a.m. for Cap-Haïtien, where it was scheduled to arrive at 11:33 a.m.

Until now, deportation flights to Haiti have taken place an average of once a month. The previous flight was last Thursday and had 161 deportees, including over a dozen individuals with criminal records that included sex crimes involving children.

Last month, however, U.S. officials warned Haitian authorities to expect an increase in deportations following the Supreme Court’s decision to allow President Donald Trump to end Haiti’s Temporary Protected Status designation even while litigation challenging the termination continues in the courts.

More than 300,000 Haitians were enrolled in the humanitarian program, which allowed them to legally live and work in the United States because of conditions in their homeland. Haitian immigrant-rights groups and others have argued that Haiti remains far too dangerous for large scale returns, while DHS has maintained that conditions have improved enough to send Haitians back.

Of Haiti’s nearly 12 million people more than half need humanitarian assistance because of surging gang violence while also facing deepening poverty. Meanwhile, nearly 1. 5million people have been displaced by gangs — the same number displaced by the 2010 earthquake, which prompted the Obama administration to designate Haiti for TPS.

“Following its mass de-legalization efforts, this administration is knowingly sending people, including children, back into danger in Haiti. There is no limit to its cruelty and disregard for human life,” said Savi Arvey, director of policy refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First. “This is the 9th flight this year and on average we’ve seen one flight per month since December 2023.”

The flight comes amid ongoing gang attacks in Haiti and a broader immigration crackdown by the Trump administration, which saw nearly 50,000 arrests in July. It is the highest single monthly arrest total by the Department of Homeland Security since Trump began his second term, according to the recently released government data provided by ICE to the Deportation Data Project based at U.C. Berkeley and UCLA.figures. Among them are over 7,000 arrests in Florida and 500 in Ohio, two states with populations of Haitians who previously had TPS and now are in danger of detention and deportation.

READ MORE: DHS boasts it returned gang leaders, sexual offenders to an unstable Haiti

In addition to being arrested at traffic stops, Haitians are also being outfitted with electronic ankle monitors by federal authorities in the Ohio-area. No one appears to be immune, not individuals with asylum applications pending or pastors, two of whom were recently arrested by ICE in Springfield.

This weekend, faith leaders are expected to travel to Springfield to request the immediate release of one of the pastors, Joubert Adrien, from immigration detention after he was detained while riding as a passenger in a car. A husband and father of two children, ages 15 and 7, he has lived in the United States for five years. Faith leaders also note that he has no criminal history, no prior immigration detention and no final order of removal. He also has not lived in Haiti for more than 20 years.

This week dozens of Haitian migrants for example, were brought to the Krome Detention Center in southwest Miami-Dade country after being arrested in front of grocery stores and shopping malls.

On Tuesday, the United States was among several foreign governments offering its “deepest condolences to the victims and their families” after armed gangs stormed the mountainside farming community of Kenscoff above the capital, killing dozens of people and kidnapping more than 50 others, including infants. The gang leader is threatening to kill them or use them as human shields, if police move against his fighters.

Some of the victims killed were massacred in a church that had become a place of refuge for those displaced by the repeated violence; others were shot as they fled or burned alive.

It was unclear where those aboard Thursday’s flight were from in Haiti or how long they had been in the U.S. As reflected in the birthplace of some of the younger passengers, some of those being deported had previously lived in Brazil, which is part of a broader migration route that had emerged after Haiti’s 2010 earthquake.

text:
As increasing numbers of migrants perish during the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum has vowed to ramp up pressure on U.S. authorities to investigate the deaths.

“There are too many cases,” Sheinbaum told reporters last week, referring to 17 Mexican citizens who have died while in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody or during ICE operations. “Our obligation is to always defend Mexicans who are in the United States or whatever part of the world.”

The growing toll prompted Sheinbaum last month to direct Mexican diplomats to file complaints with state attorneys general and district attorneys across the United States, demanding that prosecutors investigate deaths that occurred in their jurisdictions.

“We cannot turn a blind eye to the Mexicans who have died,” Sheinbaum said following the most recent fatal incident — the ICE shooting in Houston last month of Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, 52, a construction contractor from Mexico who had lived in the United States for three decades.

Mexico’s new strategy represents an escalation from the country’s traditional policy of filing protests through diplomatic channels while assisting families with legal advice, paperwork and shipping remains back to Mexico.

However, to date, Mexico’s stepped-up efforts have yielded few results.

There is no public confirmation of prosecutions in any of the 17 cases, despite the entreaties of the Mexican government to the U.S. Department of Justice, eight attorneys general and 12 district attorney’s offices.

“The Americans don’t seem to be paying much attention,” said Víctor Clark, a long-time human rights advocate in Tijuana. “What Mexico is doing is basically a bureaucratic step with no real response.”

From a legal standpoint, Mexico faces an uphill battle. Mexican authorities use the word denuncias (complaints) for their actions, but Mexico cannot directly file complaints in U.S. courts in these cases. U.S. prosecutors have no mandate to respond to Mexican inquiries.

“The reality of the matter is that the Mexican government has very little standing to file complaints in the United States,” said Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, a senior fellow at the American Immigration Council, a Washington-based research and advocacy group. “A request for investigation from the Mexican government probably has a little more of an impact than a request from a random private citizen.”

At least 52 migrants — including 14 Mexican citizens — have died while in ICE custody since the beginning of the second Trump administration, according to a report in June from Human Rights Watch and Physicians for Human Rights.

In addition, at least nine people have died during reported agency operations since 2025.

ICE says it thoroughly investigates all deaths of individuals in its custody or during agency actions. Critics charge that the Trump administration fails to pursue such cases adequately.

To date, Mexico has received partial or no responses to complaints sent to the eight states where the 17 deaths of Mexican citizens occurred, Roberto Velasco, Mexican’s foreign secretary, said last week.

Attorney generals in only four states — California, Texas, Florida and Illinois — even acknowledged receipt of Mexico’s demands, Velasco said.

The single definitive state reply came from Florida’s attorney general’s office, which concurred with ICE’s findings that the death of Royer Pérez Jiménez, 19, at the Glades County Detention Center was a “presumed suicide.”

According to Velasco, Ventura County was among only three of 12 local jurisdictions contacted — along with Cook County, Ill., and Harris Country, Texas — that said it was “evaluating” Mexico’s complaint.

But Joey Buttita, spokesperson for the Ventura County district attorney’s office, said the county had received no communication from Mexico.

Ventura was the site of one of ICE’s most sensational operations — the July 10, 2025, sweep at the Glass House Farms cannabis complex in Camarillo that resulted in hundreds of arrests as masked ICE agents descended on the facility.

One worker, Jaime Alanis García, 56, originally from Mexico’s Michoacán state, was fatally injured when he fell 30 feet from a greenhouse roof.

A flashpoint in the controversy is the private Adelanto ICE Processing Center in San Bernardino County, where some 1,500 detainees are held. At least four Mexican citizens have died at the Adelanto facility, which is operated by the Geo Group, a Florida-based company.

Representatives of detainees at Adelanto have filed a civil class-action lawsuit alleging widespread abuse — including systemic medical neglect, inadequate food and water and mold contamination.

In July, a federal judge ordered ICE to institute sweeping changes at the Adelanto center, mandating improvements in the provision of water, food, sanitation and medical care.

Both ICE and Geo Group have denied any abuse at the facility.

“For many illegal aliens this is the best healthcare they have received their entire lives,” according to a statement from Department of Homeland Security, ICE’s parent agency ,to The Times. “All detainees are provided with proper meals, water, medical treatment, and have opportunities to communicate with their family members and lawyers.”

In March, after the fourth death of a Mexican national at Adelanto , the Mexican government vowed that it would “exhaust every legal and diplomatic avenue to bring attention to conditions” at U.S. detention centers.

Mexican diplomats in Los Angeles presented relatives of José Guadalupe Ramos Solano, 52, who, according to an ICE statement, was found “unconscious and unresponsive” on March 25 at Adelanto. He had lived for 28 years in the United States and worked at an industrial laundromat, said his widow, Antonia Tovar.

“My husband was a good person, dedicated to his kids and to his wife,” Tovar said. “I just want justice and to fight for the people who are there. I want my husband’s case to be the last one.”

The San Bernardino County district attorney’s office has received three letters from the Mexican government about the deaths of at least two detainees at the Adelanto facility, said Jacquelyn Rodriguez, spokesperson for the district attorney’s office. But no criminal complaint has been filed.

Sixteen people were allegedly detained by federal immigration agents in Danbury on Monday, 10 on Tuesday and 25 on Wednesday, according to state officials. Lamont said the state is working to identify who was taken and why.

Lamont reiterated the following rights that residents of Connecticut hold, including the right to remain silent and the right to refuse a search. He said residents do not have to unlock their phones or give passwords without a warrant, and they can’t be detained without reasonable suspicion of unlawful presence or criminal activity.

“Record names, badge numbers, the time agents arrive and leave, and what areas they access,” Lamont stated. “Keep copies of any warrants or documents that are presented and take notes, photographs, or video of the interaction. Residents should never lie about citizenship or use false documents, Lamont said.

“In Connecticut, we respect the dignity and humanity of every person who calls our state home, and we value the contributions of our immigrant communities to our state,” Lamont said in a written statement.

“I am also grateful for the community advocates and volunteer lawyers assisting those who have been detained and those they leave behind,” the governor continued. “For those communities being targeted, know that we support you and we’re here for you.”
