In an unsigned statement, ICE's parent agency, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, declined to discuss the operation, citing "operational security and the safety of our officers."

"To be clear: ICE does not target schools, but we will not allow criminals to hide in our nation’s schools and put the safety of children at risk," the statement said.

DHS also sent CT Insider a list of five "public safety threats" it said ICE has arrested in Connecticut — including a man from Nicaragua the department said had been convicted of various assault and weapons charges; men from Ecuador and Guatemala it said had been convicted of sexual assault; a man from Guatemala it said had been convicted of child sex abuse; and a man from Mexico it said had been convicted of DUI. The agency previously sent CT Insider the same list twice before — once in February and once in July. Both times it said the men were arrested in Hartford, not Danbury.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

It's the second August in a row ICE has been prevalent in Danbury. The agency arrested some 65 people as part of Operation Broken Trust, a statewide operation last August that also focused heavily on Danbury. The agency has ramped up arrests nationally as the Trump administration advances on its promise of mass deportations of immigrants who entered the country illegally.

Elected officials and local activists addressed reporters Wednesday in front of a mural of the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr., former President John F. Kennedy and former U.S. Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bater Ginsberg in Kennedy Park, in downtown New Haven — the same location where activists say ICE has arrested several day laborers this week.

"ICE is here to put Danbury into a state of terror," said U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn. "And we know that because of what happened this morning. You couldn't design evil more effectively than ICE did this morning."

Juan Fonseca, a co-founder of DUFI who spoke at Wednesday's press conference, told CT Insider in an interview that ICE arrested four parents Wednesday morning while a school bus with their children on it was nearby. While Fonseca said he did not witness the arrests first-hand, he said that he arrived shortly after and spoke with eyewitnesses. Prominent state officials referenced the arrest during their comments at the press conference. Federal officials did not provide information about the incident.

It can be difficult to know who ICE arrests and for what reasons. The agency will occasionally release some details of individual arrests, as with the list it sent CT Insider, but it only does so voluntarily. ICE does not generally release arrest reports or other similar records. Unlike judicial warrants, the administrative warrants ICE often uses to make targeted arrests are not publicly available. And the people ICE arrests generally have their cases heard in immigration court, where case files and recordings of hearings are not open to the public.

Fonseca and other activists said they've been waking up before dawn to rush to the scene of ICE arrests or handle calls coming in from families, staying up late managing incoming information and media requests, then waking up the next day to do it over again.

Clementina Lunar with DUFI told reporters that volunteers are working with over 20 families to help them find relatives who have been arrested, get attorneys and stay afloat in the meantime.

"We are talking about mothers with babies and school-aged children who, unfortunately, had their breadwinner taken," she said.

Lunar said she spent part of Wednesday taking calls on DUFI's help line, trying to help families find relatives or how to find lawyers to help.

Celina Beatriz Curillo, an attorney with The American Immigrant Legal Clinic (TAILC), told reporters Wednesday that she and other attorneys witnessed ICE removing men from its Hartford office yesterday shackled to each other in leg and handcuffs.

There's no long-term, adult immigration detention facility in Connecticut, and ICE's policies only allow it to hold people in the Hartford office — located at the Abraham A. Ribicoff Federal Building downtown — for 72 hours or less. Because of that, the agency generally moves people it arrests to facilities out of state quickly.

Often, that means the Plymouth County Correctional Facility, in Plymouth, Massachusetts, or the Donald W. Wyatt Detention Facility, in Central Falls, Rhode Island. However, at least one woman who told CT Insider that ICE arrested her husband and his coworker in Stamford on Monday said the agency has taken both men to a facility in Colorado.

Speaking at the press conference Wednesday, Democratic Rep. Jahana Hayes of Connecticut, whose district includes Danbury, said she has requested a meeting with DHS' regional director to gather more information about why ICE has surged its operation in Danbury and how long it will last. Hayes faced blowback from the crowd for her initial comments, suggesting she was not going far enough.

"There are certain things that I have the ability to do," Hayes responded. "And this is what I can do. You elected me to go to Washington to pass laws. To vote on legislation. If I am not doing those things, then I cannot be the best representative for you."

Members of Congress have legal authority to make unannounced visit facilities where ICE hold detainees to conduct oversight — although the Trump administration has sought to place limits on those visits. After the press conference, Hayes told CT Insider she's waiting to see where ICE takes the people it's arresting in Danbury first.

"Once I have the location of these detainees, I'll request a visit," Hayes said.

The interruptions were a frequent theme during Wednesday's press conference, with a small group of activists shouting down Democratic elected officials over what they said was their inaction on immigration along with a host of related issues — including a recent meeting between U.S. House Minority Leader Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

Gov. Ned Lamont grew so frustrated with the shouting as he fielded a question about state laws that limit how ICE can operate in Connecticut — including a law passed earlier this year that makes it a misdemeanor offense for ICE agents to wear masks, outside of narrow exceptions — that he walked away from the podium.

A reporter had asked whether Lamont would support giving those laws "more teeth."

"Arrest ICE agents who wear masks," one activist chimed in. "Use our police to defend out communities."

"We've got a Trust Act," Lamont said. "It says no masks. Stay away from courthouses. Stay away from schools. But enforcing it ... "

"Alright," the governor finally relented. "Forget it."

House Minority Leader Vincent Candelora criticized Lamont and state Democrats later in the day.

"Connecticut has real problems tied to illegal immigration, and both the Governor and legislative Democrats keep pretending their sanctuary state policies and their refusal to work with federal officials have nothing to do with what is happening in Danbury," he said.

Many of the ICE agents captured on video in Danbury this week have been wearing masks, in apparent violation of the new state law. The Department of Justice has filed a lawsuit claiming the law is unconstitutional, and ICE has told CT Insider in the past that it "will not abide by this unconstitutional ban." There's a hearing in federal court next week on an injunction that would block enforcement of the ban.

Speaking at Wednesday's press conference, Danbury Mayor Roberto Alves said the ban is "damn near impossible to enforce," drawing more jeers from some activists.

As Lamont walked away from the presser, he told CT Insider he spoke with DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin shortly before the press conference. Trump nominated Mullin to replace former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem in March, in part because of growing discontent after DHS agents shot and killed two U.S. citizens who were protesting a high-profile ICE operation in Minnesota. Mullin took a more conciliatory tack at his confirmation hearing.

text:
WASHINGTON — A federal appeals court ruled Wednesday that the criminal case against Rep. LaMonica McIver (D-10th) can proceed, a setback for the New Jersey congresswoman who had argued that she was “selectively” and “vindictively” targeted by federal prosecutors.

She is accused of “assaulting, resisting, impeding and interfering with a federal officer” outside the immigration detention center Delaney Hall in Newark in 2025. A three-judge panel of the Third Circuit Court of Appeals ruled, 2-1, that two of the charges against McIver can proceed. A third charge was remanded to a lower court.

In November, the lower-court judge allowed the case to proceed.

“To protect the people, their elected representatives must be authorized to conduct oversight of the executive branch without fear of retaliation,” McIver said in a statement Wednesday to MS Now, the former MSNBC cable news channel. “Today’s decision chills that authority and emboldens the Trump administration to continue persecuting our most vulnerable communities.”

McIver argued she was shielded from prosecution because she was present at the detention center for an oversight inspection of the site, a legislative power of Congress.

The court disagreed. Writing for the majority, Cindy Chung, an appointee of Joe Biden, called McIver’s actions “unambiguously non-legislative” and said “they are not integral to the legislative process.” Trump appointee Stephanos Bibas joined Chung, while Thomas Ambro, an appointee of Bill Clinton, dissented in part.

A two-term Democrat, McIver is among several high-profile critics of President Trump facing criminal charges in his second term.

‘She will not be last’

In May 2025, after McIver, Reps. Rob Menendez (D-8th) and Bonnie Watson Coleman (D-12th), inspected the site, a scrum erupted among ICE agents, demonstrators, congressional staffers, the three lawmakers and Newark Mayor Ras Baraka outside the security perimeter.

In the indictment, prosecutors accused McIver of slamming “her forearm” into an immigration official and “using each of her forearms to forcibly strike” another official.

Charges against Baraka were dropped.

McIver, who is expecting her second child in the fall, faces up to 17 years in prison if convicted. She is running for reelection in the November midterms.

“The administration is using criminal charges to go after political opponents who dare conduct oversight of their activities—that is what was at stake in this appeal,” Hanna Rumsey, a McIver spokeswoman, said in a statement Wednesday. “Congresswoman McIver was first, but she will not be the last, and these protections are more critical than ever.”

Paul Fishman, the lead attorney for McIver, said the case is about political intimidation.

“The goal of the administration is clear: chill members of Congress from overseeing the actions of the Trump administration,” said Fishman, the former chief federal prosecutor in New Jersey. He said he was “evaluating all possible next steps.” McIver has the option to appeal the ruling to the circuit’s full panel of judges and even to the U.S. Supreme Court.

Ambro, the dissenting judge, cited the U.S Constitution’s speech or debate clause, a privilege extended to members of Congress in connection with their official work as lawmakers.

“The duty Congresswoman McIver sought to perform when she visited Delaney Hall on May 9, 2025 strikes at the heart of the Clause’s purpose: to oversee the Executive Branch,” Ambro wrote.

The charges against McIver were filed by Alina Habba, a former acting chief of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for New Jersey and a Trump loyalist and campaign surrogate.

text:
Immigration-related committals up 112%

The sharp rise in immigration‑related prison committals — up 112% in a single year to 444 cases – has been criticised by the Irish Penal Reform Trust (IPRT).

The IRPT stated that detention for immigration purposes should be exceptional, proportionate and decided on a case-by-case basis.

Overstretched

“Prison is not an appropriate environment for people to be held on an administrative basis, and this practice places unnecessary additional pressure on an already overstretched system,” said executive director Saoirse Brady (small picture).

Despite a modest increase in committals, the overall prison system is now operating well above its designed capacity, with overcrowding worsening and rehabilitation opportunities diminishing, the IPRT also stated.

It called for a more humane system of evidence‑based alternatives such as bail supports, supervised temporary release schemes and community sanctions.

Responding to publication of the Irish Prison Service's (IPS) annual report 2025, the body expressed its concern at the State's ongoing reliance on imprisonment for short sentences and remand and the continued rise in prison costs.

The continued use of prison for short sentences, 74% of all sentenced committals, highlights the need to shift towards evidence‑based, community‑based alternatives, the IRPT stated.

The report shows that the average annual cost of a staffed prison space has risen to €103,334, a 4.3% increase on 2024.

The IRPT said the escalating expenditure, driven by increased numbers of people detained, inflation and payroll pressures highlights, shows the need for a move away from prison towards effective community-based alternatives, particularly for those on remand or for those serving sentences of less than 12 months.

Saoirse Brady said the annual report paints a picture of a system under sustained and mounting pressure.

Although overall committals increased by just 1.1% in 2025, the daily average prison population rose by 9.6% she added.

And 74% of remand prisoners last year did not go on to serve a sentence, and the high number of short sentences are major contributors to overcrowding, she stated.

Last resort

Prison should be a sanction of last resort, Brady continued, and short sentences do little to reduce reoffending and come at enormous human and financial cost.

“Continuing to use prison for minor offending is neither effective nor sustainable,” she stated.

“The IPS has added 187 new spaces this year and plans a further 65 in 2026, but we cannot build our way out of this crisis.

“Overcrowding is undermining rehabilitation, safety and dignity. Some people continue to sleep on mattresses on the floor — a clear breach of basic human rights,” she stated.

text:
A federal judge in Texas on Wednesday denied the state of Minnesota’s extradition request of Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent Christian Castro, who is charged in the shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis in north Minneapolis in January.

The ruling means Castro is likely to be released from a Texas jail.

Hennepin County issued a warrant for Castro’s arrest on May 18, and he was arrested by Texas Rangers, a state law enforcement agency, on May 29. Since then, Castro has been incarcerated in a county jail and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott has declined to sign the paperwork ordering his extradition to Minnesota.

Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison sued Abbott on Aug. 18 under a federal law prohibiting law enforcement agencies from detaining fugitives awaiting extradition for longer than 90 days. Ellison asked the judge to require Abbott to sign the extradition papers, or at least block Castro’s release, ahead of the 90-day deadline on Thursday.

U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. of the Southern District of Texas did neither, denying Ellison’s request outright.

“This case should concern officials and citizens of every state,” Ellison said in a statement Wednesday. “If a governor can delay extraditions and cherry-pick cases according to their political tastes, then no state will be able to hold fugitive criminals accountable.”

Rodriguez Jr. ruled that Abbott has not violated the Constitution, the Extradition Act or the Uniform Criminal Extradition Act.

“Those statutes prescribe no deadline for a governor of the asylum state to complete an investigation and either sign a rendition warrant or deny the request,” Rodriguez Jr. wrote in his order.

Ellison had argued that governors have no discretion when it comes to facilitating extraditions.

A unanimous 1987 Supreme Court ruling said “the commands of the Extradition Clause are mandatory, and afford no discretion to the executive officers or courts of the asylum state.”

Rodriguez Jr. cited a section of the Uniform Criminal Extradition Act, a state law in Minnesota and Texas, which authorizes the governor of the asylum state to call on authorities in the demanding state to investigate the circumstances of the subject of the extradition request, and whether he ought to be surrendered.

The Extradition Act also allows governors to consider “whether the petitioner is a fugitive.”

Abbott’s office argued that Castro is not a fugitive because he didn’t flee Minnesota — he was reassigned to Texas by ICE.

AG Keith Ellison sues Texas governor for failure to extradite ICE agent charged with assault

Castro is charged with four counts of second-degree assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime. He is accused of firing his gun through the closed front door of a Minneapolis home, hitting Cesar-Solis in the leg. Three other people were inside the house, according to Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, and one of the bullets was found embedded in the wall of a child’s bedroom.

CHICAGO (WLS) -- Six children were ordered removed Wednesday by a federal immigration judge in Chicago.

The orders were handed down in a courtroom closed to cameras on the 15th floor of a downtown office building.

ABC7 Chicago is now streaming 24/7. Click here to watch

One by one, the children appeared before Judge Shawn Abraham for hearings that lasted a few minutes. All of the children have been legally deemed abandoned by their parents by the government.

"These children fled to the United States seeking safety and protections from the horrors that no (child) should have to endure," attorney Laura Smith told reporters after the hearings.

She says the deportation of children is speeding up in Chicago.

Wednesday's removal orders will send the children to countries including Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador.

In many cases, the children have been in the United States for years.

SEE ALSO: State Department preparing to cancel tens of thousands of visas held by asylum seekers: Officials

"These kids, some as young as 12 years old and younger, are now being deported from the United States," Sen. Dick Durbin said.

Durbin made a surprise appearance in court to witness the removal orders.

But the judge was not physically present and appeared virtually.

"He was somewhere in the cloud, appearing before us and ruling against these kids time after time after time," Durbin said.

Congress created a pathway for some children in the U.S. without legal authorization to obtain a green card. The program is backlogged, however, and judges are now ordering removals as applications are processed.

"All of this is brand new. Up until June of 2026, given a pending application for special immigrant status meant termination of removal proceedings," Smith said.

The removal orders come amid President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown.

New data analyzed by ABC News shows more U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrests in July than in nearly four years. In Chicago, there have been at least 1,200 apprehensions so far this year.

The president has repeatedly said violent criminals would be targeted first.

text:
A federal judge in Texas on Wednesday rejected a push from Minnesota officials to force the extradition of the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer accused of shooting a Venezuelan migrant in the leg during the height of Operation Metro Surge earlier this year.

Christian Castro, 52, has been jailed in Brownsville, Texas, since late May on charges related to the shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis, including that he lied about how it unfolded.

Because Castro cannot legally be held for longer than 90 days while awaiting extradition, Minnesota had sought a court order requiring Texas Gov. Greg Abbott (R) to sign the paperwork authorizing his transfer. Without it, he is set to be released Thursday.

U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. ruled Wednesday that Minnesota’s bid was not ripe for consideration because Abbott has not yet taken any action on the warrant.

“Minnesota alleges that Governor Abbott has ‘refused to sign’ and has ‘with[eld]’ the rendition warrant. But the record reflects only that Governor Abbott has neither agreed nor refused to sign the rendition warrant as to Castro,” Rodriguez wrote in a 13-page order.

The decision was a win for Abbott, who argued he was not obligated to hand Castro over to Minnesota authorities. The Texas secretary of State’s office is currently reviewing the request to determine whether Castro meets the definition of a “fugitive” under federal extradition law, the filing noted.

Minnesota officials also wanted Castro to remain in custody beyond the 90-day window over concerns that he is a flight risk and may try to leave the country. The state cited repeated jailhouse phone calls between the officer and a woman who lives in Mexico, during which he “expressed a desire to purchase property” in the country and “move there in the future.”

“We are a nation of laws. It’s incumbent on all of us to uphold them,” Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz (D) said in a statement to The Hill. “Texas has previously fulfilled every extradition—as has Minnesota—and this case should be no different.”

Castro is facing four counts of second-degree assault with a deadly weapon and one count of falsely reporting a crime in connection with the Jan. 14 scuffle that occurred during an immigration enforcement operation in the Twin Cities.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) claimed following the incident that an officer had fired a “defensive shot” after being attacked by three men with a snow shovel and broom handle. One of those men, Sosa-Celis, was hit in the thigh and taken to the hospital.

But DHS officials later said they were investigating what appeared to be “untruthful statements” made by the officers after reviewing video evidence.

The Justice Department is reportedly weighing whether to bring federal charges against Castro, according to CNN.

This story was updated at 9:32 p.m. on Aug. 26, 2026.

Delivering for Maryland and Preserving Our History Despite the dysfunction and chaos generated by the Trump Administration, I remain focused on delivering real results for communities across Maryland.
text:
Senate Update: Two Things at Once – Fighting a Lawless Trump Administration While Delivering for Maryland

As we continue to confront huge challenges at home and abroad, I want to update you on the work I am doing to stand up for Marylanders, defend our democracy, and hold the Trump Administration accountable.

Here at home, we continue to see the tragic consequences of an Administration that believes it is above the law. Last month, Trump’s Department of Homeland Security and ICE agents shot and killed two more people in a single week, bringing the total number of people killed by DHS and ICE agents since President Trump returned to office to ten – and that is in addition to the more than 50 people who have died in ICE custody in that same time.

A few weeks ago, I traveled to Minneapolis and visited the makeshift memorials for Renee Good and Alex Pretti. It was heartbreaking to see the teddy bears at the site for Renee Good, reminding us all that her children’s stuffed animals were on the passenger side of her car when she was gunned down. The Alex Pretti site displayed photos of the veterans he had cared for as a nurse at the local VA Hospital. Renee Good, Alex Pretti, and the eight others should all be alive today. And, to add insult to injury, Trump’s DHS and his Administration will lie to avoid accountability for those who gunned them down. In all of these killings, we need the truth, and we need accountability. I will continue working to ensure these shootings are independently investigated and that those responsible are held accountable. This killing spree must end.

These attacks are part of the Trump Administration’s broader assault on immigrant communities – which also includes stripping legal status from Temporary Protected Status (TPS) holders to fuel Trump’s mass deportation agenda. Congress established TPS decades ago, with bipartisan support, to ensure that when people cannot safely return to their countries of origin, we do not put their lives at risk by forcing them to go back. While in the United States, these TPS holders are subject to strict eligibility requirements, repeated vetting, and thorough background checks as part of maintaining their legal status. Many of them have lived in the United States for decades, started small businesses, and become part of the fabric of our communities. The fact that his Administration is seeking to end TPS protections puts a lie to Trump’s claim that he is focused on deporting “the worst of the worst.”

I joined Senate Democrats on the floor to fight to pass legislation that would redesignate Haiti for TPS through early 2029. That legislation would have protected Haitian TPS holders from being forced back into a country which our State Department’s own travel advisory warns is too dangerous to visit for any reason.

I also went to the Senate floor to bring up my SECURE Act, which would provide qualified TPS and Deferred Enforced Departure (DED) recipients with a pathway to lawful permanent residence after years of living and working legally in the United States. Republicans blocked us from moving forward on both efforts, putting these individuals’ lives at great risk.

We must not give up. I will continue pushing to redesignate TPS for Haiti, as well as Yemen and Syria, and restore these protections. We also understand that the Administration is planning to remove TPS for Salvadorans, who represent a large community within Maryland. I will continue fighting to uphold the once bipartisan principle that, in the United States of America, we do not send people directly into harm's way.

Meanwhile, the Trump Administration remains engaged in what a federal judge determined was a vindictive prosecution against Kilmar Abrego Garcia because he exercised his constitutional rights. The judge called the Administration’s attack “an abuse of prosecuting power.” The Justice Department has asked the federal appeals court to reinstate the charges against Kilmar Abrego Garcia that were already dismissed, as the Administration continues trying to deport him to Liberia. This is unacceptable. I will not stop fighting to uphold Kilmar’s constitutional rights – because when the rights of one of us are threatened, the rights of all of us are at risk.

Whether it is standing up for immigrant communities, defending our Constitution, or delivering for Maryland families, I will keep standing up and speaking out to hold this Administration accountable and deliver results for the people of our state. Here's the latest:

Pushing Back Against Trump’s Illegal War in Iran

President Trump declared victory in Iran months ago. But almost six months into this war, more Americans and civilians are being killed, the conflict is expanding, and American families are paying higher prices for everything from groceries to gas as a result.

In June, both chambers of Congress passed House Concurrent Resolution 86, directing the President to terminate hostilities against Iran. The passage of that resolution should have marked the end of this disastrous war. But time and again, President Trump has shown he has no respect for the Constitution or the rule of law. So, in July, I brought my War Powers Resolution to the Senate floor to end this senseless and illegal war and force every senator to go on the record. Republicans voted it down, even as they refuse to pass an affirmative resolution to authorize the Iran war. The Constitution is clear: the power to declare war belongs to Congress because our founders understood the danger of allowing any one person to send our service members into harm’s way.

Republicans have continued to duck their constitutional duties. If they had the courage of their convictions, they would vote to give President Trump the authorization to use military force. They have refused to do that. Yet, at the same time, they have voted against our effort to end these unauthorized hostilities. Meanwhile, the costs continue to mount.

The death toll among American service members is now eighteen, while hundreds more have been injured. Thousands of civilians have been killed across the region. The Strait of Hormuz is closed, gas prices have climbed to about $4 per gallon, and rising fuel costs continue to push up the prices of groceries and other necessities for families here at home.

President Trump told the American people this war would last only weeks. He later repeatedly claimed that we had won. But if we won in March, why were more Americans killed in July? Why is the Strait of Hormuz closed? And why are American families still paying the price?

I put those questions directly to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth when he appeared before the Senate Appropriations Committee last month. I asked him: What does winning this war look like? He had no clear answer.

He eventually said the mission was to prevent Iran from developing a nuclear weapon – even though he and President Trump previously claimed their bombing campaign last year had already “obliterated” Iran’s ability to do so. It is clear that this is a war in search of a mission.

Meanwhile, Trump and his Administration have demonstrated contempt for our soldiers on the front lines. Our Marines and members of the Navy have endured grueling conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln during its record-breaking deployment of more than eight months without a port of call. The Lincoln is finally headed home, but the Administration’s dismissive response to the serious concerns raised by those on board was shameful – including President Trump saying the deployment was “not nearly long enough.”

Instead of confronting these failures, the Administration continues to attack the journalists who bring them to light. The Administration wants a press that will spout their propaganda, rather than the facts. They even recently fired the head of the Stars and Stripes – the independent Department of Defense newspaper funded by taxpayer dollars – yet another blatant crackdown on free speech and a free press.

While they mislead the public about the costs of the war, the Trump Administration is asking Congress for approximately $70 billion more to fund it and replenish depleted weapons stocks. That request comes on top of a proposed $1.5 trillion defense budget, despite the fact that the Pentagon has never passed a clean audit.

Congress should not hand the President a blank check to continue a war that it refuses to authorize. But that’s what Republicans want to do. I have been clear: I will not vote to support this illegal, senseless war or add billions to a bloated Pentagon budget that serves as a de facto authorization for it. I will keep fighting to end this war, reassert Congress’s constitutional authority, and stop the Trump Administration from sacrificing more American lives and taxpayer dollars for this strategic blunder of epic proportions.

Fighting Trump’s Crypto Corruption

The power of the presidency should be used to serve the American people, not to enrich the person who holds the office. Unfortunately, we are seeing the opposite under Donald Trump. He has turned the presidency into a vehicle for personal enrichment schemes, using the power of the office to benefit himself, his family, and his political allies.

The Trump and Melania “meme coins” are among the clearest examples of this corruption. Nearly one million people who bought Trump’s meme coin have lost money, with combined losses totaling $3.8 billion.

At the same time, Donald Trump has made approximately $1.4 billion from his family’s crypto schemes. In 2025 alone, he raked in $636 million from his crypto coin as part of at least $2.2 billion amassed through all of his business ventures, while the American people pay the price.

And it is not just the meme coin. His family’s World Liberty Financial venture brought in $799 million last year alone. This is all while the Trump Administration leverages its power over agencies to expand this venture’s reach. Earlier this month, the Trump Administration approved a bank charter for World Liberty Financial. The company, the deal, and the entire process are corrupt to the core. I warned this would happen.

That’s why I joined Senator Warren and our colleagues in introducing a bill to ensure that no President, Vice President, their immediate families, or other senior government officials can exploit their positions to own or control a bank, which could serve as a major vehicle for corrupt dealings.

We saw the potential for corruption last year when Trump held a special dinner for the largest holders of his meme coin, including foreign investors who spent millions of dollars to gain access to the President of the United States. We’ve also seen foreign investors from the United Arab Emirates (UAE) make massive investments in World Liberty Financial while the President relaxed export controls on very sensitive chip technology to the UAE.

The American people should never have to wonder whether a policy decision was made in the public interest or to increase the value of an asset owned by the President and his family.

Congress is currently considering the CLARITY Act, legislation that would establish a new regulatory framework for digital assets. I’ve said repeatedly that any such legislation must protect consumers, safeguard our financial system, protect our national security, crack down on illicit finance, AND establish real, enforceable protections against corruption, including guardrails against self-dealing and conflicts of interest by the President and Members of Congress.

But the CLARITY Act fails all those tests.

When the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee considered the bill in May, I offered amendments to crack down on public officials – including the President and Members of Congress – using digital assets for personal enrichment and to strengthen protections against illicit finance, self-dealing, and other abuses. Republicans blocked those amendments. Without critical changes, the CLARITY Act risks opening the door to more corruption and abuse while failing to provide the protections Americans deserve.

The American people see what is happening. They see a President using the power of his office to enrich himself while ordinary people are left holding the bag. They see a system where the people at the top make money and everyone else takes the risk. They deserve better.

The presidency is not supposed to be a pathway to owning a pay-to-play casino, and I will keep fighting to ensure that our laws will never allow elected officials to use public office as a vehicle for personal profit.

Delivering for Maryland and Preserving Our History

Despite the dysfunction and chaos generated by the Trump Administration, I remain focused on delivering real results for communities across Maryland.

In Baltimore, Team Maryland celebrated a major milestone with the completion of the Howard Street Tunnel project. Thanks to $125 million in federal funding we secured for the project, the expanded tunnel can now accommodate double-stacked rail containers. That will allow more cargo to move efficiently through the Port of Baltimore and along the East Coast, increase the Port’s container business by an estimated 160,000 containers annually, and support more than 13,000 jobs.

I also joined Congressman Mfume and Beloved Community Services Corporation to celebrate the restoration of the historic Juanita Jackson Mitchell Law Office. Juanita Jackson Mitchell was a trailblazing civil rights leader and the first Black woman admitted to practice law in Maryland. The building will now serve as the home of the University of Maryland, Baltimore’s ROAR Center, which provides holistic services to survivors of crime. We secured $1.75 million in federal funding to help restore this important civil rights landmark and give it a new life serving Baltimore residents.

And in Baltimore County, I joined local leaders at AfriThrive Inc.’s community food center to announce $800,000 secured in federal funding for facility renovations that will increase AfriThrive’s ability to help immigrant and low-income families across Baltimore County and Baltimore City put food on the table.

In Southern Maryland, I joined local leaders for the public launch of the Management Plan for the Southern Maryland National Heritage Area. I was proud to help secure the region’s designation as a National Heritage Area in 2023, recognizing its extraordinary contributions to our state and nation. This new plan will help preserve Southern Maryland’s history and environment, strengthen local tourism, and support economic opportunity throughout the region.

In Montgomery County, I joined the community to celebrate the reopening of the Pleasant View Historic Site. Founded in 1868 by formerly enslaved Maryland families, Pleasant View served as a school, place of worship, and community gathering space at a time when Black Marylanders were denied their most basic rights. We secured $943,000 in federal funding to support its restoration so future generations can learn from this history.

Earlier this month, I traveled to the Eastern Shore to speak with local leaders at the Maryland Association of Counties annual conference and to highlight two federal investments that Senator Alsobrooks and I secured for Shore communities. In Berlin, we fought to deliver $1.4 million that will help transform the historic Flower Street School site into a new community center that will house the SHORE UP! Head Start Center, recreational spaces, and a museum honoring the history of the Flower Street School. In Ocean City, we secured $20 million to support the Army Corps of Engineers’ work to replenish the beach, protecting the shoreline, homes, and businesses against storms and erosion.

And last week, I spent the day in Western Maryland with Congresswoman McClain Delaney, highlighting $6.25 million in federal investments we secured in Garrett and Allegany Counties. At Frostburg State University, we delivered over $3.5 million to expand STEM education opportunities, and in Westernport, we delivered $675,000 for the Potomac Fire Company to replace its 35-year-old fire engine. We also highlighted $1 million we secured to support the Garrett Regional Medical Center’s new radiation department that will provide treatment for cancer patients across the region, and another $1 million we secured for the Town of Oakland to help replace their aging water infrastructure.

I also recently wrote about the lessons Maryland’s history holds for us as our nation commemorated its 250th anniversary. From the sacrifice of the Maryland 400 and George Washington’s decision to surrender power by resigning his military commission in Annapolis to the courage of Frederick Douglass, Harriet Tubman, and Thurgood Marshall, Marylanders have repeatedly challenged our country to live up to its democratic ideals.

At a moment when the Trump Administration is attacking our history and democratic institutions, their examples remind us that preserving our democracy requires active participation from all of us.

title: Forty children reported missing from UK asylum hotels still not found - The Guardian
description:
Forty children who went missing from hotels housing asylum seekers in the UK have still not been found, according to a parliamentary report.
The cross-party committee has been told by a witness that 40 of the cohort of missing children have still not been found.
The high court ruled in 2023 that the Home Office’s routine use of hotels to house lone child asylum seekers was unlawful.
The government also revoked its legal duty to support asylum seekers at risk of destitution this year, the watchdog said.
But our human rights only work when they protect each and every one of us, including migrants and asylum seekers.
text:
Forty children who went missing from hotels housing asylum seekers in the UK have still not been found, according to a parliamentary report.

Ministers are facing calls from MPs and peers to explain what they are doing to locate the group, two of whom are believed to still be under 18. The figure emerged in a report on Thursday by the joint committee on human rights on how the social care system is failing young adults.

In 2023, it emerged that more than 440 unaccompanied asylum-seeking children had gone missing from Home Office hotels, some of whom were reported to be as young as 12. The cross-party committee has been told by a witness that 40 of the cohort of missing children have still not been found.

Helen Waite, a director of children’s social care at the Department for Education, told the committee in June that 472 children had gone missing in total and 432 had since been located.

“Guidance was issued to police from the Home Office, to be shared with local networks, to ensure that we continue to look for those children and that we can surface whether they have been found, and information can be updated to provide more reassurance,” she said.

The high court ruled in 2023 that the Home Office’s routine use of hotels to house lone child asylum seekers was unlawful. At the time, the Conservative government said: “Due to the unsustainable rise in illegal Channel crossings, the government has had no option but to accommodate young people in hotels on a temporary basis while placements with local authorities are urgently found.”

Angela Eagle, in a letter to the committee last year when she was the border security and asylum minister, said some of those found were “located in exploitative situations and may have been trafficked or victims of other forms of exploitation”.

The committee, which published a wider report on children’s social care on Thursday, said: “We welcome the fact that the majority of missing children have now been found. However, we continue to be extremely concerned about the fact that some children who went missing from asylum hotels in previous years remain missing.”

The committee called on the Home Office to “make clear what specific action is being taken to locate these children, to investigate the causes for them going missing, and to avoid unaccompanied asylum-seeking children going missing in the future”.

It asked the Home Office to provide an update to the committee every three months “with details of efforts to locate the children who remain missing”.

Patricia Durr, the chief executive of Every Child Protected Against Trafficking UK, said: “The government cannot allow the disappearance [of children] to fade from public scrutiny. It is a significant child protection failure and we strongly support the committee’s call for regular public reporting and greater transparency about what is being done to find those who remain missing, understand why so many children disappeared, and ensure this can never happen again.”

In a further development, a watchdog on Thursday gave the UK government its lowest ranking for failing to uphold asylum seekers’ rights in line with UN recommendations.

The Equality and Human Rights Commission said an assessment found “gaps in social security provisions” and “failures to provide protection from poverty and destitution” in how new arrivals were treated.

Officials criticised the government’s decision to end a programme designed to help refugees with CV writing and interview skills after just two years. The government also revoked its legal duty to support asylum seekers at risk of destitution this year, the watchdog said.

Dr Mary-Ann Stephenson, the EHRC chair, said: “Everyone in the UK is covered by its human rights framework, regardless of their citizenship or immigration status. But our human rights only work when they protect each and every one of us, including migrants and asylum seekers. When the government fail to protect the rights of one group, it puts everyone’s rights at risk.”

This month it was announced that a further 13 hotels housing asylum seekers had closed, after Labour’s pledge to stop using asylum hotels completely by the next election.

Ministers are increasing their use of more “basic” sites including former military barracks, and the most recent closures are expected to save taxpayers £51m and bring the total number of asylum hotels below 160, down from a peak of about 400 under the Conservatives.

A government spokesperson said: “Police forces are responsible for investigating missing children cases and we continue to review our records, share relevant information with them and work closely with local authorities and safeguarding partners to support those investigations.”

text:
COLUMBUS, Ohio — Democratic candidate for Ohio governor Dr. Amy Acton is breaking from her party to support local police in working with federal immigration enforcement. This comes as Republican candidate Vivek Ramaswamy raises concerns about mass surveillance due to Flock cameras.

"It's an honor to fight for the people who are first responders," Acton said at a news conference Tuesday.

She had just been endorsed by the Ohio Patrolmen’s Benevolent Association, a police union representing about 8,000 officers.

Now, Acton is breaking from her colleagues.

"We always work with the federal law enforcement, and we will do so — whatever it takes to keep Ohioans safe," Acton said when specifically asked about federal immigration officers, or ICE.

Unlike other liberal leaders, she said she wouldn’t prevent local law enforcement from helping out with immigration raids. However, she expects ICE to follow laws.

"We need to hold anyone who comes to our state to the same standards of professionalism that we expect of our public safety officers, and I will always fight for that," she said.

RELATED: Democrat Amy Acton breaks with party to support Issue 3

ICE has been utilizing Flock Safety cameras amid growing distrust over privacy concerns. The devices are typically, and supposed to be, used as license plate readers. Some Ohioans have chopped the cameras down.

"I absolutely know that we have had, as Governor DeWine said, many crimes solved due to the use of technology," Acton said. "When I come in, we'll be doing a very comprehensive overview of all our public safety and emergency response."

Following this story being published, the Acton Campaign reached out to provide additional thoughts on Flock.

"As Governor, she would push for strict guardrails around this technology and work to prevent the abuse of AI surveillance,” spokesperson Addie Bullock said. “Dr. Acton’s number one priority is keeping Ohioans safe, but it cannot come at the expense of our First Amendment rights.”

Republican candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, in July, warned the tech could lead to government overreach.

"I do not want to see an authoritarian surveillance state that ultimately threatens what this country was built on," Ramaswamy said during a local county fair event.

He said he shares the same concerns as worried citizens.

"If the government is able to, and does, map out every movement you make, we're ultimately living eventually; it's not there now, but eventually — you skate to where the puck is going," Ramaswamy continued. "It's not hard to imagine a Chinese-style surveillance state."

But when it came to working with ICE, he went further than Acton. The Fraternal Order of Police of Ohio, which has 23,000 members, has endorsed him.

"Our cities are no longer going to get away with being so-called sanctuary cities, where even the federal government says that you can't engage in certain illegal behavior, crossing the border illegally," Ramaswamy said during an event in the spring. "Somehow Cincinnati declared itself a sanctuary city. That's wrong."

RELATED: Ohio candidates for governor weigh in on how to fight corruption

Unlike the other two candidates, Libertarian Don Kissick and running mate James Mills oppose both Flock and how ICE is currently operating.

"We should investigate suspects, not surveil entire communities," Mills said Wednesday. "The Fourth Amendment should not become obsolete simply because technology makes mass surveillance easier."

Just because someone doesn't follow the U.S.'s immigration policies doesn't mean they automatically need to be treated like "dangerous criminals," he added.

"I also strongly oppose the way ICE is currently operating and would not use Ohio’s resources to enable indiscriminate enforcement that disregards due process or basic human dignity," Mills added. "While a governor and lieutenant governor cannot rewrite federal immigration law, we can refuse to give federal agencies a blank check to exercise unchecked power in our communities, and we can speak out against executive overreach regardless of which party controls Washington."

Enforcement on immigration crimes should be proportional, constitutional and humane, the Libertarian said.

"Just because someone is undocumented doesn’t mean we should treat them with any less dignity," he added.

text:
An immigration court judge in Chicago on Wednesday ordered six children to be deported after they were deemed abandoned by state courts.

Judge Shawn Abraham was not in court for Wednesday's hearings. He appeared virtually while requiring kids to be there in person.

Ten children appeared for hearings without their parents, having been deemed abandoned by the state. Six were ordered removed from the country. Their ages ranged from 12 to 17 years old.

All of them had been designated abandoned by a state family court, meaning they were without one or both of their parents.

U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois) attended the hearing to observe the proceedings, and criticized the Trump administration's efforts to deport the children.

"You remember how they explained it? We're going after the worst of the worst, the terrorists, the rapists, the murderers, the child predators, and we were going to once and forever remove them from America and make our streets safer. I wish the people who made those statements could see what we saw this morning," Durbin said.

Attorneys for each child argued they should legally be eligible to stay in the U.S., because of a federal classification called special immigrant juvenile status, which is designed to help kids who are neglected, abused, or abandoned. Each had a pending application for that status.

"Let's just be clear that all of this is brand new. So, up until June of 2026, even a pending application for special immigrant juvenile status meant termination of removal proceedings," said Laura Smith, an attorney and executive director of the Chicago-based Children's Legal Center.

Abraham ordered them removed anyway, arguing the time it would take for them to acquire valid visas was too long to justify them staying in the U.S.

"When the Trump administration said that they were going to target people who were criminals or people who didn't have a right to be here in the United States, they were lying," said Keren Zwick, executive director of the National Immigrant Justice Center.

Critics also have raised concerns about the speed of these proceedings. Previously, there might be months between court dates, but for the four children who were not ordered removed on Wednesday, they were scheduled to be back in court in as little as two weeks, which experts said is an unheard-of turnaround time, especially for kids in these situations.

Abraham was appointed as an immigration judge by the Justice Department in May. Before that, he spent more than 12 years as a prosecutor at the Cook County State's Attorney's Office, and most recently as an attorney for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

CBS News Chicago is told there are at least 20,000 unaccompanied immigrant children in the U.S. currently working their way through the legal system, including approximately 1,000 in the Chicago area without a parent or guardian, who are represented by organizations around the city.

Diaz said he and Godoy had been planning their future together before she was detained.

"We were planning to get married. Start our life. To see all that crashing down... it's a nightmare," Diaz said.

Diaz said he is fighting for Godoy's release and is increasingly concerned about her health. He shared photos showing injuries to the 24-year-old's leg, which he said have been worsened by diabetes and a fractured foot that has gone untreated for eight months.

"She doesn't even get a cast. It's just unbelievable what I'm seeing, what I have to see her go through," Diaz said. "If she doesn't get surgery on her foot, it's going to get to a point where it'll have to be amputated."

According to Diaz, Godoy is now confined to a wheelchair and unable to walk.

Godoy is being held at an ICE detention facility in Tacoma, Washington, after being detained during an immigration appointment in Los Angeles in November 2025.

Originally from El Salvador, Godoy arrived in Los Angeles in August 2024 on a tourist visa and later applied for asylum, citing political persecution.

"Couple months later we found out she had an Interpol red alert, which is clearly politically motivated," Diaz said. "Her dad used to be the attorney for [ El Salvador President ] Nayib Bukele."

According to Diaz, Godoy left El Salvador before the country's president imprisoned her mother and father on fraud allegations after her father discovered discrepancies in a case.

Diaz said Godoy fears for her safety if she is deported.

"Her fear is that if she's deported, that she'll be tortured, sexually assaulted, possibly even killed," he said.

Attorneys are appealing Godoy's deportation order and seeking her release so she can receive surgery for the fracture before she loses her limb, according to Diaz.

"If I do get her back, she's going to be in such an unhealthy state, possibly without her foot... It's just not right," he said.

Diaz said the facility has been treating Karla's wounds and giving her pain medication but has not done anything for the fracture.

Eyewitness News reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for comment and are waiting to hear back.

text:
A judge has denied an attempt by Minnesota officials to block the release of the ICE agent charged in a January shooting in Minneapolis as the state battles with Texas Governor Greg Abbott over the agent's extradition.

Restraining order denied

What we know:

Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. denied Attorney General Keith Ellison's petition for a temporary restraining order that would have kept ICE agent Christian Castro in Cameron County Jail amid an extradition battle between Texas and Minnesota.

Minnesota is trying to force Texas Governor Greg Abbott to move forward with the extradition process. Gov. Abbott argued in court documents he is awaiting a determination from his Secretary of State and doesn't want to move forward with the extradition until he receives that.

What's next:

Castro is expected to be released from Cameron County Jail on Thursday. Under Texas law, people being held for extradition can only be detained for 90 days. Castro has been in Cameron County Jail since late May.

Minnesota officials have worried that Castro could be a flight risk, saying he has been speaking with a woman in Mexico.

Big picture view:

The judge did not make a decision on whether Castro should ultimately be extradited to Minnesota.

MN Attorney General Ellison, Hennepin Co. Attorney Moriarty respond

What they're saying:

Minnesota's attorney general shared the following statement:

"I respectfully but strongly disagree with the court’s order, which nonetheless acknowledges that Christian Castro is a flight risk, that Minnesota will be harmed if he is allowed to flee to Mexico, and that Governor Abbott’s consideration of Minnesota’s extradition request is of ‘an atypically long duration’ — to say the least. We will continue litigating this case and do everything in our power to ensure Castro is returned to Minnesota to face his criminal charges.

"Minnesota should never have had to file this lawsuit or this motion. Greg Abbott has a black-letter legal and constitutional duty to sign the rendition warrant to return the fugitive Castro to Minnesota — full stop — and we are only here because Abbott is playing with constitutional fire.

"This case should concern officials and citizens of every state. If a governor can delay extraditions and cherry-pick cases according to their political tastes, then no state will be able to hold fugitive criminals accountable.

"Greg Abbott is turning Texas into a sanctuary state for violent criminals. But regardless of today's ruling, Christian Castro will not escape justice in Minnesota. "

Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moiarty spoke during a news conference on Wednesday speaking out against the judge's decision.

"What this means is that Christian Castro, the ICE agent who shot Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis through the door of his home in Minneapolis in January, will walk out of jail in Texas tomorrow because Governor Abbott is, so far, refusing to sign the extradition paperwork," Moriarty said. "I want to be clear about what's happening here: Castro is a fugitive in Minnesota. According to the federal government, he lied. He lied about what happened that night on Jan. 14."

She later shared a written statement that said the following:

"Gov. Abbott still has the ability to prevent Christian Castro from walking out of jail. He can choose to stop harboring a fugitive by simply signing the extradition paperwork today. If Castro walks out of jail tomorrow and disappears into Mexico, it will be the fault of one person – Greg Abbott."

Texas Governor Abbott responds

The other side:

Below is a statement from Texas Governor Abbott's press secretary:

"The court was right to reject Governor Walz’s absurd claim. The Constitution requires deliberate consideration of extradition requests and tasks Governor Abbott to ‘decide, upon such evidence as he may deem satisfactory’ whether ‘the person demanded is a fugitive.’ Today’s order rebuffs Minnesota’s efforts to conscript federal courts into commandeering the authority of Governor Abbott’s office."

Castro charged in Minneapolis shooting

Local perspective:

Christian Castro is charged with shooting and injuring a man in Minneapolis during Operation Metro Surge. He faces four counts of second-degree assault and one count of falsely reporting a crime in connection with the on-duty shooting that wounded a man back in January.

Castro initially claimed that he was attacked with a shovel and broom before he fired his service weapon. However, video evidence underlined Castro's story.

After surveillance video showing the shooting became public, the U.S. Attorney's Office said it was investigating the matter and DHS officials condemned the false statements.

"Lying under oath is a serious federal offense," a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson said at the time. "Violations of this sacred sworn oath will not be tolerated."

Big picture view:

On Tuesday morning, CNN reported that the Justice Department was now considering its own charges against Castro for the shooting.

The CNN report cited a "source familiar with the deliberations and a DOJ spokeswoman." However, in an official statement, a DOJ spokesperson said no decision had been made. The spokesperson did confirm "conversations" about the case had been held between the DOJ's civil rights division and Minnesota prosecutors.

text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has arrested more people in the state so far in 2026 than in the previous two years combined, and those arrests have overwhelmingly been people who did not have criminal convictions.

These are takeaways from the latest data obtained by the Deportation Data Project through a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit, analyzed by Maine Morning Star.

The new data from March 3 to Aug. 6 provide an updated look at every ICE encounter, detainer request, arrest, book-in to detention, and removal since October 2022, though it has some limitations. For example, around 5% of arrests do not show where they were made.

Of 491 ICE arrests that led to detentions in Maine through Aug. 6 of this year, nearly 89% were people who did not have criminal convictions.

ICE apprehended 56 people convicted of a crime — but only one person with a violent criminal conviction — and 97 people with pending criminal charges. Comparatively, the agency detained 338 people this year with no criminal conviction or charge.

“When you look at the data, there’s no public safety risk justification that can be found,” said Ruben Torres, advocacy and policy manager for the Maine Immigrant Rights Coalition.

The highest monthly arrests this year was 208 in January, when ICE launched a large-scale operation in the state. There was another spike of 74 arrests in June.

Most of these arrests were of people originally from Angola, followed by Ecuador, Guatemala and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, respectively.

On Saturday, ICE arrested a Cumberland County Jail corrections officer originally from Angola. He is at least the fourth jail officer in Maine arrested during President Donald Trump’s second term so far.

Looking at all arrests, including those that did not result in detention stays, there were 497 in Maine this year.

The data also confirm ICE’s operations are happening across the state, with apprehensions reported in 50 different towns so far in 2026.

The Trump administration has indicated that federal operations are expected to ramp up.

Border czar Tom Homan recently told state Rep. Mike Soboleski, R-Phillips, “You’re going to see a lot more enforcement action in Maine,” which he noted was because of the recent U.S. Supreme Court ruling allowing the Trump administration to end Temporary Protected Status for immigrants from Haiti and Syria.

authors: Gisela Salomon, Matthew Lee, apnews.com, gisela-salomon, matthew-lee

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration has trained much of its immigration crackdown on people who entered the United States illegally from Mexico and elsewhere, but it is intensifying another battle, this time with people who come legally.

The State Department has paused all immigrant visa applications while it briefs consular officials around the world on a new policy that aims to keep out people who are considered potential drains on public coffers.

The administration is also preparing to revoke the business and tourism visas of up to 200,000 foreigners who applied for asylum, which The Associated Press first reported this week. It would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in U.S. history and would likely face legal challenges.

“The thing linking them is a general philosophy that immigration is bad for the United States and that the Trump administration is looking for all of the ways it can to button down our immigration system to allow in fewer people,” said Julia Gelatt, associate director of the U.S. immigration policy program at the Migration Policy Institute.

The pause in issuing immigrant visas is expected to be temporary

The pause is related entirely to new rules about a “public charge” requirement that numerous consular officers in U.S. embassies around the world had questions about, according to a State Department official who was not authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.

It began in early August and is not expected to last beyond early to mid-September, the official said, noting that most people affected by the pause had interviews scheduled for August but that none of them had been canceled. Those interviews will be rescheduled for September, October and November.

Anybody applying for an immigrant visa outside the U.S. could be affected by the pause, experts said, mainly those seeking to come on family grounds, including parents, spouses, children or siblings of U.S. citizens.

Gelatt cautioned, though, that rescheduling a visa appointment may not be easy. “They’re hard to get, and so having to reschedule is a big challenge for people,” she said.

Other types of immigrant visas, like those for workers who have an employer sponsoring them, are not affected because they can demonstrate earnings and would not be a “public charge.”

“We need to see how long this pause lasts. It sounded like it would be short, just to make time for training, but if it does last longer, I imagine we’ll see litigation,” Gelatt said.

A policy that halted the issuance of visas to immigrants from 75 countries was in place from January to mid-August, when a court struck it down. It could be seen as a precedent.

In tightening the public charge rules, U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, which is part of the Department of Homeland Security, revived a rule that could deny green cards to immigrants who use public benefits such as food stamps, Medicaid and housing vouchers.

Revoking tourism and business visas will ‘send a message’

Unless the decision is challenged or revised, the State Department is expected to announce in the coming weeks the revocation of so-called B1 and B2 visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum, according to State Department documents obtained by The Associated Press and two U.S. officials. The action will be taken in coordination with DHS.

The State Department has not said how many visas will be revoked, but some experts and immigration lawyers point out that the measure will have no consequences for those already in the United States who have applied for asylum.

“The goal is instead to send a message that this administration is focused on enforcement and that people who want to live in the United States should not think about coming on a tourist visa and then seeking asylum,” Gelatt said. “For people who already have a tourist visa that’s being revoked, it really is not going to affect them because they already have lodged their asylum application and are waiting in line for that asylum adjudication. The temporary visa really doesn’t matter anymore.”

Asylum claims can take years to decide. Tourist and business visas, on the other hand, allowed stays of about six months. If the visa holders request asylum, their ability to stay in the U.S. depends on their open asylum cases and not on their visas, according to experts.

For years, people who apply for tourist or business visas have had to demonstrate to U.S. officials that they plan to return home when their time expires. Any indication that they wish to stay permanently is grounds for denying their visa.

Plans to revoke visas are consistent with Trump’s long-held belief that asylum is largely a sham.

“People in the U.S. and all over the world are fed up with bogus asylum claims. Asylum isn’t supposed to be a loophole to circumvent immigration laws,” Christopher Landau, a deputy secretary of state, said Monday.

In April, the administration said consulates would deny visas to applicants who indicate they were afraid to go home.

___

Salomon reported from Miami

text:
A second witness to a fatal shooting in Houston by a federal immigration agent has been ordered released from custody after more than a month in detention.

Daniel Tirado Pantoja was one of three passengers riding in a work van when the driver, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a Mexican national who ran a homebuilding business, was shot July 7. The Department of Homeland Security has said Salgado Araujo, who had lived without legal status in the U.S. for 35 years, had “weaponized his vehicle” and that the officer fired on him in self-defense.

U.S. District Judge Alfred Bennett in Houston ordered Tirado Pantoja released after finding that he had no criminal record and was neither a flight risk nor a danger to the community, according to court records.

“We’re very glad that Mr. Tirado is going to be reunited with his family,” said Ross Miller, an attorney for Tirado Pantoja.

Tirado Pantoja and another passenger, Jose Trinidad Rojas Pliego, have disputed accounts given by DHS about the confrontation with agents with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

They said the agents were never in front of the ICE vehicle and that Salgado Araujo had put the vehicle in park as the agents were shooting. Tirado Pantoja also has said the agents’ vehicle hit them from behind and then again on the driver’s side.

Rojas Pliego was already released from detention last month. DHS did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment Tuesday about the judge’s ruling.

Victor Salgado, the brother of the man killed, was also in the van and remains in custody. He also has asked a judge to order his release.

Ronaldo Salgado, Salgado Araujo’s son, had said on social media after the shooting that his father was on his way to work, picking up his workers, when the shooting occurred. He said his father was a hardworking man and was in the process of getting a work permit.

text:
WASHINGTON, Aug 25 - President Donald Trump's administration has issued a pause on immigrant visa appointments for applicants around the world during an ongoing immigration crackdown by the U.S. government in the Republican leader's second term in the White House.

A U.S. State Department spokesperson said on Tuesday that it launched a global training initiative at all U.S. embassies and consulates worldwide and that appointments for visa services will be adjusted to accommodate the training.

Trump has pursued an aggressive deportation drive and immigration crackdown that includes revocations of visas and green cards and rejection of applications over a range of reasons like political opinions and pro-Palestinian protests against U.S. ally Israel's assault on Gaza.

He says the crackdown aims to improve domestic security.

The crackdown has faced some legal setbacks. A U.S. judge on Friday struck down a Trump administration policy suspending the issuance of immigrant visas to ​applicants from 75 countries, saying that the policy exceeded Secretary of ‌State Marco Rubio's statutory authority.

The State Department did not specify details on the training and its timeline, beyond saying the training aimed to help consular officers screen out applicants deemed likely to become dependent on U.S. public benefits and to ensure evaluation of visa applicants "comprehensively and consistently."

The pause on visa appointments was reported earlier by the Financial Times, which said immigrant visa applicants with scheduled interviews at U.S. embassies and consulates have received emails that their appointments were being rescheduled and that they would receive future notice of a new date.

Trump's immigration crackdown has been widely condemned by human rights groups as being discriminatory and in violation of free speech and due process rights. Rights groups also say the crackdown has created an unsafe environment in the U.S., especially for ethnic minorities who have raised concerns about racial profiling.

While Trump campaigned in 2024 on a ​platform of stopping illegal immigration, his administration has also made legal immigration more difficult - for example, by imposing new and expensive ​fees for applicants of certain work visas.

(Reporting by Kanishka Singh in Washington; Editing by Stephen Coates)

text:
The Trump administration has deported a former lieutenant colonel in Venezuela’s National Guard who has been accused of torturing political dissenters and spearheading a violent crackdown on protests against the Venezuelan government.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement in Miami confirmed on Wednesday that Rafael José Quero Silva had been returned to Venezuela after a judge ordered him deported. ICE had first arrested the Venezuelan national in February 2025.

READ MORE: Venezuelan military commander accused of torturing Maduro’s opponents is at Krome

Five Venezuelans — who supported and participated in mass protests after the death of Hugo Chavez and the election of Nicolas Maduro over a decade ago — sued Quero Silva in Miami federal court in December. They accused him of torturing them or directing his underlings to do so while he was a top official in the Bolivarian National Guard, a military force tasked with internal security.

Quero Silva is the latest target of the federal government’s crackdown on South Florida residents with ties to the Cuban and Venezuelan governments or accused of committing human rights violations in their home countries before immigrating to the United States.

In April 2025, the agency arrested 57-year-old Daniel Morejon Garcia, for failing to disclose he was a government official and a member of Cuba’s communist party. And earlier this year, ICE picked up Adys Lastres Morera, the sister of the official in charge of GAESA, the military conglomerate that runs most of Cuba’s economy.

READ MORE: ICE detains in Miami sister of head of GAESA, the military firm that runs Cuba’s economy

“ICE officers continue to remove human rights violators to their home countries,” said Miami Field Office Director Matthew Elliston. “We are committed to public safety and national security, and to ensuring the United States does not become a safe haven for individuals who participated in persecution, torture or other serious human rights abuses.”

Homeland Security Investigations and the FBI in Miami were both involved in Quero Silva’s detention and deportation, as was the Human Rights Violators and War Crimes Center.

Quero Silva arrived in the United States in 2016 at Miami International Airport, but overstayed his visa, according to ICE. The plaintiffs who sued him realized that Quero Silva was in the U.S. when he appeared as an extra in a Spanish-language soap opera in 2018.

The lawsuit claims that Quero Silva, as the top military authority in Barquisimeto, a city in central-western Venezuela, oversaw their torture in the headquarters of the National Guard in the region.

“He used his authority to orchestrate a violent crackdown on political dissent, targeting Venezuelan civilians who protested the contentious election of Nicolás Maduro in 2013 or who opposed the Venezuelan government,” the lawsuit states.

The five Venezuelans filed suit under the Torture Victim Protection Act in December 2025 in Miami. U.S District Judge Michael Moore, a veteran jurist appointed by President George H.W. Bush., is presiding over the case.

Quero Silva filed a motion to dismiss the case, claiming that the people accusing him had not properly served him at Krome, that the claims were time-limited, and that they had not pursued remedies under local courts. He asked the court to stay the matter until his release from immigration custody.

His lawyer told the Herald in February that he had “consistently maintained that he had never persecuted anyone and never authorized abuse. To the contrary, when he learned of misconduct, he castigated those responsible and sought to stop it.”

Quero Silva had applied for asylum in the United States, but was found ineligible because he had been a national guard member.

One plaintiff, a green card holder who lives in Chicago, said that he had been shot in the abdomen by officials under Quero Silva, an injury that left him with psychological scars and nerve damage. Another plaintiff, a woman living in Atlanta, says that Quero Silva and a group of his officers arrested her at home after she had sheltered protesters.

She was imprisoned for four months in different facilities, where she was deprived of her medications, forced to stay awake, and convicted of falsified charges, according to the lawsuit. Female guards “used the pretext of searching for drugs to molest her,” the lawsuit states.
