title: Human Rights at Sea and Spain's 2026 Migration Paradox - Opinio Juris
description:
Latest figures published by Spain’s Ministry of Interior show that maritime arrivals to the Canary Islands plummeted in the first half of 2026.
The interaction between this strategy and the 2026 regularization must be made explicit, because it is structural, not coincidental.
Maritime migration is frequently framed as a border-security issue, a smuggling-prevention problem or a matter of migration management.
This is an important lesson for international lawyers: maritime migration control cannot be evaluated only at the moment of arrival.
A serious human rights approach to maritime migration should therefore measure success differently.
text:
[Francisco Javier Rozas Porras is a Spanish lawyer and PhD researcher in international law of the sea at the DEHUKAM Institute / Ankara University. He holds an LL.M. in Maritime Law from ICADE University in Madrid, Spain.]

Introduction

In 2026, Spain’s migration policy features a striking paradox. The Government has launched one of the most ambitious regularization processes in Europe on land, defining migration as a matter of rights, an integration process and an economic reality. At sea, though, a steep decline in arrivals to the Canary Islands illustrates a different logic: prevention, containment and cooperation with third States before migrants reach Spanish or European territory. This shift raises one pressing question for the discipline of international law: when the regulation of maritime migration is taken farther away from the coast, do human rights obligations vanish or do they simply harden into something less apparent? The Spanish case is particularly current. Latest figures published by Spain’s Ministry of Interior show that maritime arrivals to the Canary Islands plummeted in the first half of 2026. Between 1 January and 15 June 2026, 3,267 people reached the islands by sea, against 11,284 in the same period during 2025. This is a reduction of over 70 per cent. Politically, such a reduction can be presented as a signal of effective migration management. Legally, though, it should prompt a more difficult question: What occurs before people vanish from the statistics of arrivals? Yet Spain has simultaneously shown an entirely different kind of receptiveness toward those already present on its territory. In Spain the extraordinary regularization process for migrants already living in Spain was approved by the Government in April 2026. By mid-June, hundreds of thousands of applications had reportedly been made, and international media subsequently reported that the final number of applications could exceed one million. The effort was framed not just as an administrative step, but as a right, social inclusion and demographic imperative. Spain has thus made relatively clear its message on land: living and working migrants should be legal rather than condemned to irreversible invisibility.

This post is concerned, above all, with State responsibility for human rights at sea. It examines the 2026 regularization not for its own sake, but for what it reveals when read alongside Spain’s maritime strategy: a State treating territorial presence as the threshold at which rights begin. Therein lies the paradox, and it is worth stating precisely. It does not consist in the mere coexistence of a generous policy on land and a restrictive one at sea; States combine openness and control routinely. It consists in their mutual dependence. The regularization rewards presence; the maritime strategy prevents it; and the first is made politically and practically possible by the second. Spain’s most rights-protective migration measure in two decades thus rests upon a practice that withholds comparable protection from the same category of persons at an earlier point on the same journey. A policy premised on the harm of legal invisibility on land is sustained by the production of legal invisibility at sea. The argument proceeds in three steps. It first situates the regularization and its logic of presence. It then turns to the maritime strategy that determines who attains presence, and shows that the two policies operate not as parallel tracks but as a single system. It concludes by drawing out the consequence for State responsibility: under the law of the sea and international human rights law, a State’s obligations toward migrants cannot be made contingent on the very presence it acts to prevent.

Presence Rewarded: The 2026 Regularization in Context

The scale and design of the regularization deserve closer attention, because they explain why the Spanish case is so compelling. Royal Decree 316/2026, approved by the Council of Ministers on 14 April 2026 and in force since 16 April, opened a single application window running until 30 June 2026. Applicants had to prove presence in Spain before 1 January 2026, at least five months of continuous residence and the absence of a criminal record; successful applicants receive a one-year residence and work permit. The Government estimated that around half a million people could benefit, and the process is the first extraordinary regularization Spain has undertaken in more than two decades, since the 2005 process aimed at irregular workers. In numbers alone, it is one of the largest legalization exercises in recent European history.

The political significance of the measure is also notable. It did not come only from the Government. It responds to a popular legislative initiative promoted by migrant associations, trade unions and civil-society organizations, backed by hundreds of thousands of signatures and admitted for consideration by the Spanish Congress with cross-party support. The Government has presented the decree as the first milestone of a broader plan for integration and intercultural coexistence, and has defended it on three grounds: human rights and social inclusion, demography, and the needs of the labour market. It also builds upon the 2024 reform of the Immigration Regulation, which eased the ordinary arraigo pathways to legal residence. Regularization in Spain is therefore not an isolated administrative gesture. It is part of a deliberate and publicly argued model of migration governance, built on legality and presence.

Seen from a European perspective, this choice runs against the prevailing current. The EU’s Pact on Migration and Asylum, adopted in 2024, prioritizes screening, accelerated border procedures and returns; several Member States have recently restricted, rather than expanded, avenues to legal status; and recent large-scale regularizations elsewhere in Europe have been either sector-specific or discontinued. Spain is thus doing something genuinely distinctive: legalizing presence on a mass scale at the very moment when the Union’s centre of gravity is shifting toward containment. Yet the same Spain converges fully with that restrictive current at sea. The sections that follow show that these two positions are not merely simultaneous; they are structurally linked.

Presence Prevented: Fewer Arrivals, Harder Legal Questions

If the regularization rewards presence, the maritime strategy examined in this section determines who attains it. It is not as though Spain is the only country to have to confront this dilemma. Throughout Europe and beyond, coastal states as a whole show more and more efforts to prevent maritime arrivals with respect to monitoring, interdiction, information-sharing, patrol cooperation and with agreements with third states. The aim is often to prevent departures rather than simply handle arrivals. Within a Spanish context, the Canary Islands route has seen cross-border cooperation with countries like Morocco, Mauritania and Senegal be the cornerstone of migration control. This architecture is not new. It was forged during the so-called cayuco crisis of 2006, when more than 31,000 people reached the Canary Islands in a single year, prompting the first Plan África, a network of bilateral cooperation and readmission agreements with West African States, the permanent deployment of Spanish officers in Mauritania and Senegal, and the first joint maritime operations coordinated by Frontex off the West African coast. Two decades later, the model has been progressively Europeanized: after record arrivals to the Canary Islands in 2024, the European Union and Mauritania signed a Joint Declaration establishing a migration partnership backed by €210 million, negotiated with the active involvement of Spain. The sharp decline recorded in 2026 is therefore not an isolated outcome. It is the intensified product of a twenty-year-old strategy of anticipatory, delegated border control. The practical consequence could be fewer vessels reaching the Spanish shores. But a smaller number of arrivals does not necessarily mean fewer people are left in danger or shielded from the abuse of violence or shunted into more remote routes. This poses one of the most difficult questions in modern migration governance: does a decline in arrivals signal more protection, or only greater control at a distance? This is where the law of the sea and human rights law have to be read in unison.

The interaction between this strategy and the 2026 regularization must be made explicit, because it is structural, not coincidental. First, externalization is what makes mass regularization politically possible: the Government can present the legalization of half a million people as responsible governance precisely because arrivals are falling and the maritime border appears to be under control. Second, the two policies operate sequentially on the same population: cooperation at sea filters who becomes present on Spanish territory, and regularization then legalizes those who passed the filter. Third, the regularization’s own eligibility rules embed this logic: because applicants must prove presence in Spain before 1 January 2026, a person intercepted, diverted or deterred at sea during 2026 is excluded from the process by the very policy that prevented their arrival. Regularization and externalization are thus not competing philosophies. They are two faces of the same system: a system of selective legality.

Presence as the Threshold of Rights: Externalization and State Responsibility

At this point the analysis must move from policy to law, because the system just described rests on an assumption that international law does not share: that a State’s obligations begin where its territory does. Maritime migration is frequently framed as a border-security issue, a smuggling-prevention problem or a matter of migration management. Those frames are not wrong. States certainly have a legitimate interest in restricting borders and combating criminal networks that prey on those without power. But the sea is not a legal vacuum. It is a regulated space where overlapping legal duties apply for states, ships and rescue authorities. UNCLOS Article 98 mandates States to provide aid for persons in distress at sea. The SAR Convention and SOLAS have duties in the area of search and rescue coordination and assistance. International human rights law, including the principle of non-refoulement, restricts the return or transfer of persons to places where they may face persecution, torture, inhuman treatment or other serious harm. In European legal terms, a further layer complicates the picture: the European Convention on Human Rights, which applies wherever State agents exercise authority or control over persons, vessels or maritime operations.

The central legal problem is not merely whether Spain rescues people once they are within Spanish waters. The harder question concerns practices that take place before that point: cooperation with third States, remote surveillance, operational support, shared intelligence and coordinated prevention of departures.

If a State contributes to a system designed to stop boats before they reach its jurisdiction, can it avoid responsibility by pointing to geography? If migrants are intercepted, diverted or prevented from leaving by third-country authorities with European support, where should legal responsibility begin and end?

International law has not fully resolved these questions, but it has made one principle clear: formal distance cannot automatically erase responsibility. The relevant issue is not only territory, but control, influence, knowledge and foreseeable consequences. Human rights obligations are most clearly triggered when a State exercises effective control over persons or operations. Yet modern externalization policies often operate precisely in the grey zone below direct custody: funding, training, equipment, intelligence, diplomatic pressure and operational coordination. This makes responsibility harder to prove, but not conceptually irrelevant.

Spain’s 2026 paradox illustrates this problem with unusual clarity. On land, the State recognizes that irregularity produces vulnerability, exclusion and legal invisibility. At sea, however, the policy goal often appears to be preventing irregular migrants from becoming visible in the first place. Regularization responds to the human reality of people already present. Externalization, by contrast, may prevent that reality from entering the legal and political field of view. This is why the paradox, as defined at the outset, is more uncomfortable than a simple contradiction. The two policies are, in fact, coherent: both treat territorial presence as the switch that activates rights. Regularization rewards presence; externalization prevents it. What looks like contradiction is better understood as a filter: the State keeps its generosity for those who are inside, and delegates exclusion to actors and spaces beyond its formal jurisdiction. The legal problem is that human rights law does not treat jurisdiction as a purely territorial fact to be managed strategically: where a State exercises control, influence or a decisive contribution over what happens to people at sea, obligations may follow it there.

The Human Cost of Non-Arrival

If presence is the threshold at which rights begin, then the decisive facts concern those who never attain it — facts that arrival statistics are structurally unable to record. On migration routes in 2025, at least 7,667 people died or went missing globally, according to the International Organization for Migration. UN/IOM data also recorded thousands of deaths and disappearances across the Mediterranean and the Atlantic route toward the Canary Islands. These numbers matter because they challenge a purely statistical reading of success.

Fewer arrivals may indeed reflect safer, more orderly migration. But it can also be a function of deterrence, containment, rerouting, underreporting or deaths that don’t make it legally visible.

Seen in this light, the Canary Islands route must be regarded not just as a Spanish or European problem, but as part of a broader case study in maritime governance. The same pattern holds in other countries: Italy and Libya, Greece and Türkiye, the United Kingdom and France, Australia and its offshore processing arrangements. Each is a national variant of the same filter: rights conditioned upon a presence that the State labours to prevent. In each case, States are trying to reconcile a set of three goals that are often competing and in opposition to one another — reducing irregular arrivals, avoiding deaths at sea and limiting legal responsibility. Externalization promises to deliver all three. In practice, however, pursuing the first can obscure the second and dilute the third.

This is an important lesson for international lawyers: maritime migration control cannot be evaluated only at the moment of arrival. Legal analysis should instead trace the process outwards: from disembarkation decisions, to coordination of rescue missions, to interception, to surveillance, to inter-State collaboration, to building capacity in third States. The further migration control is shifted away from European shores, the more important it is to ask who knew what, who enabled what, and who benefited from the arrivals that never took place.

Conclusion: Responsibility Beyond the Shoreline

Spain’s regularization process shows that irregular migration can be addressed through legality, inclusion and institutional recognition. That makes the maritime side of the policy more legally uncomfortable. If the State accepts that invisibility is harmful on land, it should not rely on invisibility at sea as a tool of governance. The 2026 experience shows, moreover, that the two policies are not parallel tracks but one system: regularization legalizes those whom externalization has allowed to arrive, and excludes those it has kept away. That is the paradox in its final form: a humanitarian achievement inseparable from the machinery of exclusion that makes it possible.

The point is not that Spain has no right to manage its maritime borders. Nor is it that every form of cooperation with third States is unlawful. Rather, the point is that border control cannot be used to transform human beings into legal absences. Search and rescue duties, non-refoulement and human rights obligations cannot depend solely on whether a boat manages to reach the beach.

A serious human rights approach to maritime migration should therefore measure success differently. Not only by how many boats arrive. Not only by how many departures are prevented. But by what happens to those who are intercepted, rescued, diverted, returned, stranded or deterred.

The real legal question is not whether Spain has reduced arrivals to the Canary Islands. The question is whether the reduction has been achieved in a way that preserves access to rescue, protection and accountability.

title: ICE agent charged with shooting in Minnesota could be released from Texas jail - AP News
description:
BROWNSVILLE, Texas (AP) — An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer charged with shooting and wounding a man during the crackdown in Minneapolis then lying about it, could walk free from a Texas jail if a federal judge does not intervene.
Christian Castro is charged in Minnesota with assault and falsely reporting a crime in the Jan. 14 shooting of 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis.
Minnesota authorities have sought Castro’s extradition since his arrest, but he remains in custody in Brownsville, Texas, a city bordering Mexico.
Castro is accused of firing a gun through the front door of a Minneapolis home, shooting Sosa-Celis in the leg.
“There’s nothing legally left for them to investigate,” Kimberly Ann Svendsen, an attorney representing the Minnesota attorney general, told the judge.
text:
BROWNSVILLE, Texas (AP) — An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer charged with shooting and wounding a man during the crackdown in Minneapolis then lying about it, could walk free from a Texas jail if a federal judge does not intervene.

Christian Castro is charged in Minnesota with assault and falsely reporting a crime in the Jan. 14 shooting of 24-year-old Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis. Minnesota authorities have sought Castro’s extradition since his arrest, but he remains in custody in Brownsville, Texas, a city bordering Mexico.

A judge said he would announce Wednesday whether he would order Texas to extradite Castro to Minnesota or allow his release.

Texas law says he must be released after 90 days of detention, which is Thursday. Minnesota’s governor and attorney general filed a lawsuit asking a judge to compel Texas to extradite Castro and to prevent the sheriff in Cameron County, Texas, from releasing him.

Castro is accused of firing a gun through the front door of a Minneapolis home, shooting Sosa-Celis in the leg. Prosecutors say Castro also falsely accused Sosa-Celis and another man of attacking an ICE officer with a broom handle and a snow shovel.

At a federal hearing in Brownsville on Tuesday, attorneys with the Minnesota Attorney General’s Office argued it would be hard to compel Castro to face charges in their state if he is released, and they fear Castro may flee the country, citing his phone conversations with a woman who lives in Mexico.

U.S. District Judge Fernando Rodriguez Jr. said he was inclined not to stop the sheriff from releasing Castro, but that he would respond to the temporary restraining order on Wednesday.

Attorneys representing Texas Gov. Greg Abbott’s office said he had not decided whether to deny or grant Minnesota’s extradition request and therefore the lawsuit is premature.

“I think ripeness is a significant issue,” Rodriguez told attorneys.

Abbott ordered an internal state investigation to determine if Castro can be legally considered a “fugitive.” Trevor W. Ezell, Abbott’s general counsel, also questioned whether the court could impose a deadline for the governor to respond to an extradition request.

“There’s nothing legally left for them to investigate,” Kimberly Ann Svendsen, an attorney representing the Minnesota attorney general, told the judge.

title: New Country Guidance case for Albanian male victims of trafficking - Free Movement
description:
The Upper Tribunal has published new country guidance on Albanian male victims of trafficking, in the highly anticipated case of LR (Male VOTs) (CG) [2026] UKUT 315 (IAC).
No typical profile of Albania male victims of trafficking There are common themes among trafficking victims: they are often young, from marginalised backgrounds, with limited education, and may have experienced domestic violence.
Risk on return The risk to male victims may come from their original traffickers, other traffickers, or both.
Aid and obstacles to reintegration The decision confirms that there are no shelters for individual adult male victims of trafficking.
Convention reason: particular social group The new guidance confirms that Albanian male victims of trafficking can rely on the Refugee Convention, as members of a particular social group.
text:
The Upper Tribunal has published new country guidance on Albanian male victims of trafficking, in the highly anticipated case of LR (Male VOTs) (CG) [2026] UKUT 315 (IAC). The decision runs to 403 paragraphs, with the headnote alone spanning 25. We set out key points from the decision below, but this is only a summary; anyone handling protection claims involving Albanian male victims of trafficking should read the decision in full.

No typical profile of Albania male victims of trafficking

There are common themes among trafficking victims: they are often young, from marginalised backgrounds, with limited education, and may have experienced domestic violence. Yet male victims come from all over Albania and from varied social backgrounds, so there is no typical profile. This reflects the position for female victims as previously set out in the case of TD and AD (Trafficked women) (CG) [2016] UKUT 92 (covered here).

Men might become vulnerable to trafficking in various ways. They may be lured by offers of well-paid employment, or receive threats to their safety or family, to then be forced to work in exploitative conditions in the UK. Recruitment increasingly happens through social media, though abduction remains uncommon.

Risk factors

The risk factors are varied and non-exhaustive. Practitioners working in this area will recognise similar – though not identical – risk factors outlined in TD and AD. Factors include:

low socio-economic status or homelessness

limited education and difficulty in securing legitimate work

ill health or addiction

originating from Northern Albania or a rural area

age (younger men and teenagers are more vulnerable)

lack of family or other support, due to a blood feud, criminality or adverse childhood experiences

belonging to a minority ethnic group, or identifying as LGBT

The decision emphasises that one risk factor alone may be sufficient to make a person a victim, and multiple factors may increase the risk.

Risk on return

The risk to male victims may come from their original traffickers, other traffickers, or both. It is not possible to quantify the risk of re-trafficking in any given case, but past persecution is a strong indicator of future risk. This is unless there are good reasons to consider that it will not be repeated – a familiar principle from paragraph 339K of the Immigration Rules.

The risk from original traffickers requires an assessment of the particular circumstances and vulnerabilities of the appellant. This includes the re-integration assistance that they would likely be able to benefit from. Information relating to the original traffickers must also be considered, for example, the size and scale of the trafficking group (though the decision explicitly acknowledges the power imbalance between the trafficker and victim which may mean that the victim has very little knowledge of these matters).

Aid and obstacles to reintegration

The decision confirms that there are no shelters for individual adult male victims of trafficking. Victims will therefore need to rely on rental accommodation provided by NGOs if they are unable or unwilling to return to their family. This accommodation support is usually only provided for six months, though victims can access longer-term support if required.

After leaving rented accommodation, a victim will need to obtain a formal declaration of trafficking status to access state support. There is a comprehensive framework of support for recognised victims of trafficking, but there are overlapping obstacles which may make it difficult to access.

One obstacle is prevailing societal attitudes. A victim may be deterred from seeking support by society’s patriarchal ideas on masculinity. He may fear discrimination, stigma and shame. Mental health difficulties, disability or minority ethnicity exacerbate this. A victim’s subjective fear will also make his reintegration more challenging, even where it is not objectively well-founded.

Corruption is another obstacle. It is a widespread and consistent problem in Albania, and there is evidence of complicity between local police and officials and traffickers, something already recognised in TD and AD.

Paragraphs 257 to 279 set out the full discussion of the overlapping obstacles to re-integration, and are essential reading.

In general, a male victim of trafficking can reasonably be expected to identify himself as such on return and access the support available. However, this depends on the individual. Some victims may be able to establish that it would be unreasonable to access the support due to particular vulnerabilities, such as mental health problems.

Sufficiency of protection

There is sufficient protection generally for adult male victims of trafficking, but this will not be effective in every case (again, in line with TD and AD). The framework of protection has improved since TD and AD. Male victims still face specific challenges which distinguish them from female victims, including difficulties with identification as a victim and the absence of any adult male shelters.

Decision-makers should assess whether only shelter accommodation will remove a real risk of ill-treatment or re-trafficking. When doing so, they must carefully consider the individual’s particular circumstances. This includes any vulnerability to re-trafficking, for example, age, disability or lower social status. They must also assess the information available relating to the traffickers, such as their size, intent and determination to locate the victim.

Victims will not be able to obtain sufficient protection if they have established a clear need for 24-hour shelter accommodation to obviate a real risk of re-trafficking or reprisal. Where rented accommodation and NGO support are adequate to meet the level of risk and vulnerabilities, there will in general be sufficient protection.

The individualised and fact-specific assessment of both a victim’s vulnerabilities and the information relating to the traffickers is therefore key.

Internal relocation

Decision-makers must consider all relevant circumstances, including any vulnerabilities, when assessing safety and reasonableness of internal relocation. A victim’s vulnerabilities impact his ability to access rehabilitation and support.

Generally, victims who are not at risk of reprisal or re-trafficking will be able to relocate internally. A victim who requires a shelter to be safe in his home area is unlikely to be able to safely relocate elsewhere.

Where rehabilitation is not possible or unlikely, the risk of re-trafficking increases.

Internal relocation to anywhere outside of the bigger cities, such as Tirana, Durres, Vlore, Elbasan and Shkoder, is unlikely to be safe if the victim is not at such risk as to require a shelter, but is still being pursued by his traffickers. Whether these cities would be safe will depend on how actively the victim is being sought, the reach and intent of the traffickers, any connections with the authorities in that area, and the victim’s vulnerabilities. In addition, re-integration is more accessible in Tirana, as other areas lack available social housing or rental support.

Convention reason: particular social group

The new guidance confirms that Albanian male victims of trafficking can rely on the Refugee Convention, as members of a particular social group. This is because they share a common background. Crucially, male victims are perceived as different from the rest of society.

The judgment highlights that prevailing patriarchal attitudes are likely to lead society to stigmatise male victims. Victims face stigma for being weak or having failed as men, whereas other male members of society are generally seen as being strong.

This aspect of the judgment is unlikely to alter the way in which these types of cases are presented, because subsidiary protection remains available as an alternative. At the very least, it will mean that appeal hearings can proceed more efficiently without lengthy argument about whether or not the Refugee Convention is engaged.

Comment

LR endorses a fact-sensitive, nuanced assessment of a male victim of trafficking’s particular circumstances when assessing these types of protection claims. Success on appeal will depend on the particular facts of the case.

While certain aspects of LR are welcome, for example, the much-needed confirmation that male victims are members of a particular social group, other aspects of the judgment are not so positive for appellants. In particular, the scrutiny required of the trafficking gang may prove difficult for appellants who have limited knowledge of their traffickers’ operations or organisational networks.

Practitioners who have previously acted in Albanian male trafficking cases are unlikely to be surprised by this new guidance, particularly since much of it reflects well-established principles from TD and AD. Practitioners and judges alike will be familiar with applying the TD and AD factors by analogy to cases of male victims.

In reality, therefore, it is unlikely that LR will dramatically increase the overall success rate of claims brought by this cohort, though there will hopefully be greater consistency in decision-making.

They’re certainly not murderers and rapists.” Both Jen and Glenda confirmed they are unpaid volunteers.
And these are U.S. citizen children,” Jen said.
text:
LEE COUNTY, Fla. —

Immigration and Customs Enforcement arrested nearly 50,000 people in July, marking the highest single-month total during the second Trump administration, with Florida and Texas accounting for nearly 20,000 of those arrests, according to data from the University of California, Berkeley.

On Palm Beach Boulevard, ICE operations have been particularly active this week, with agents seen pulling people over and taking nearly all of them into custody. Videos captured by two local ICE observers, Jen and Glenda, show agents breaking the driver’s side window of a vehicle off U.S.-41 and forcibly removing the driver.

“They’re absolutely terrified,” Jen said.

Jen and Glenda, who asked for their identities to be shielded for safety reasons, document ICE arrests by taking pictures and videos, which they send to the American Civil Liberties Union for review.

“They don’t even necessarily ask for your identification. They get out of the car, they snatch and grab,” Jen said.

Glenda emphasized their role as observers.

“We are there to document what is happening. Not engage. Not impede,” she said.

The pair have documented dozens of cases, describing the emotional toll of witnessing vulnerable individuals being taken into custody.

“It’s the worst thing I’ve ever seen in my life. It’s hard. It exhausts us and angers us to see these vulnerable innocent people being often brutalized,” Jen said.

ICE issued a statement Monday, saying, “Every day, DHS is conducting law enforcement activities across the country to keep Americans safe. DHS does not discuss ongoing or future operations.”

When asked about the perception that those arrested are criminals, Jen said, “A lot of them do have papers and are productive citizens, and most are not criminals. They’re certainly not murderers and rapists.”

Both Jen and Glenda confirmed they are unpaid volunteers.

“We’re both volunteers. This is fully volunteer work,” Jen said.

Responding to ICE labeling them as agitators, Glenda said, “We are the most peaceful, respectful, calm white middle-aged women you could probably meet.”

The observers shared stories of families being separated, with U.S. citizen children left alone after their parents were taken into custody.

“Even if we don’t witness it, we get word from families that the parent has been taken and the children are all alone and fending for themselves. And these are U.S. citizen children,” Jen said.

Both women admitted the emotional toll of their work.

“We cry. We cry a lot. I pray it will [end] because it can’t go on like this,” Jen said.

ICE has not disclosed how many people have been taken into custody during these operations.

text:
Emergency motion seeks to halt August 25 voiding of 287(g) and federal housing agreements

WASHINGTON—Today, representing fifteen New York county Sheriffs, the Federation for American Immigration Reform (FAIR) filed a lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of New York challenging the State’s so-called “Local Cops, Local Crimes Act” and the newly created Office of Immigrant Trust. The Sheriffs simultaneously filed an emergency motion seeking a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction to stop the State from voiding existing 287(g) agreements on August 25, 2026, and from forcing the termination of federal housing agreements by November 25, 2026.

The lawsuit argues that New York is tearing up valid contracts the sheriffs already signed with the federal government, coercing independent elected officials into a statewide policy of non-cooperation, and overriding the constitutional authority of the Office of Sheriff. Several of the plaintiff sheriffs maintain long-standing 287(g) agreements and federal housing contracts that let them identify and transfer criminal aliens already in their jails. Albany has now declared those agreements illegal, set hard deadlines to kill them, and created a new investigative office to police any sheriff who refuses to comply.

“New York’s law does not merely decline to cooperate with immigration enforcement priorities. It actively dismantles existing, congressionally authorized partnerships that sheriffs lawfully entered to protect their communities,” said Dale L. Wilcox, executive director and general counsel of FAIR. “Independently elected sheriffs should not be forced by Albany to abandon tools that keep dangerous criminal aliens from walking back onto their streets. This lawsuit seeks to restore the status quo and vindicate the independence of the Office of Sheriff.”

“These sheriffs are not asking for new powers. They are asking to keep the agreements they already have,” said Mateo Forero, counsel for the plaintiffs. “The State has declared those contracts void, set a hard deadline of August 25, and stood up an investigative office to force compliance. That is a direct impairment of existing contractual rights and a clear intrusion on the independent authority the New York Constitution gives to elected sheriffs.”

description:

text:
GRAND FORKS — The University of North Dakota Immigration Law Clinic recently won a federal lawsuit that helped release a client from detention.

While it was the first win of its kind for the clinic, which opened in February 2025, cases like these have been successful across the U.S.

According to Erick Resek, director of the clinic, it recently filed a habeas petition in the District of North Dakota federal court for a client who he said “was detained, in my opinion, for absolutely no good reason.”

The goal of the lawsuit is to grant the individual a bond hearing in immigration court. In this type of case, the federal judge doesn't order the release of the detained individual. According to Resek, his client wasn’t initially offered a bond hearing due to the Trump administration’s reinterpretation of a long-standing immigration statute.

The change was issued in February, according to the American Immigration Council. It said that individuals who entered the U.S. without inspection would be subject to no-bond detention. The statute was originally interpreted to only apply to immigrants seeking admission at ports of entry, according to the council. It can now apply to people who have lived in the U.S. for years.

In response, immigration practitioners across the country have been filing thousands of habeas corpus petitions. Resek said judges have been overwhelmingly disagreeing with the Trump administration’s interpretation of the law and granting people bond hearings.

“The overwhelming majority of judges, and that’s including judges who were appointed by Trump himself, are saying the way that you’re reading a law doesn’t make any sense,” said Resek, who recently was interviewed by NBC about his work at the clinic.

Resek, along with UND Immigration Law Clinic students, went before Judge Peter Welte, the chief U.S. District Court judge for North Dakota, who was nominated by President Donald Trump in 2019. In August, Welte granted their client a bond hearing in immigration court. She was then granted bond and has since paid it and been released. She was detained for five months and 27 days.

But this was one win among what he says have been multiple similar cases for the clinic. Resek said a large portion of the clinic's clients get detained after it begins representing them or they apply for immigration.

“It would be one thing if they had entered unlawfully, and they were committing crimes,” he said, “but the clinic does not take cases from people who have entered unlawfully or have committed crimes.”

The clinic was created by a bill passed in February 2025 with the purpose of addressing the statewide labor and attorney shortages , but has since had to pivot.

Resek said with the new administration, it has become increasingly difficult to use foreign workers to fill open jobs. He also said cases in immigration court have gotten much harder to win. He doesn't have exact numbers, but he estimates denial rates from immigration judges were really high compared to previous administrations.

“It’s really hard to practice law when you feel like the whole system is rigged against you,” he said. “If you don’t see a path to winning a case, that’s really demoralizing.”

Resek also said it can be difficult being realistic with clients. The clinic takes cases pro bono, so clients aren’t “losing thousands and thousands of dollars if their case gets denied,” he said. But he said private practices either have to lower their rates or tell the client that their case might not win and they won’t get a refund.

“Right now, everything is getting denied and delayed and rejected,” he said. “So you might be paying me all of this money for no reason.”

The delays he’s been seeing could make a case last for years. Resek has one client whose final hearing, scheduled in 2025, is set for 2029.

According to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse, or TRAC, there were nearly 3.2 million pending cases in immigration courts across the U.S. as of June.

Starting in 2012, the immigration backlog has been on the rise. It peaked in 2024 at over 3.7 million pending cases. There were over 10 times more pending cases at the end of fiscal year 2025 than there were at the end of fiscal year 2012, according to the data from TRAC.

“We’re doing our best at the immigration clinic to meet the goals that the state Legislature set for us despite the challenges,” Resek said.

text:
Flanked by police chiefs, Gov. Kathy Hochul touted how New York’s ban on 287(g) agreements makes the state safer.

“Local police, local crimes, not conducting civil immigration enforcement, not chasing Stephen Miller's inane deportation quotas," Hochul said.

287(g) agreements allow local police to assist or function as federal civil immigration enforcement officers. According to the governor, prior to 2025, just one county, Rensselaer, had this agreement with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Fifty-three counties have never had one, and seven of those are among the 25 safest in America, per U.S. News & World Report.

“Trust directly impacts public safety," said Albany Police Chief Brendan Cox. "When that trust is broken, when residents fear calling the police, when victims stay silent, when witnesses refuse to come forward, we all become less safe.”

But not all officials say they’ll follow this law.

Nassau County, whose executive Bruce Blakeman is the Republican gubernatorial candidate running against Hochul, won’t comply. Rensselaer County Executive Steve McLaughlin won't either. He says Rensselaer's program is focused on background checks, not raids.

“We'll see you in court, governor," McLaughlin said. "Because of the governor and the AG's actions, we're not left feeling safer.”

Following Hochul’s announcement, 15 New York state sheriffs sued the state to try and get this 287(g) ban struck down. According to their suit, they allege that this law nullifies “the ability of independently elected constitutional officers to enter into contracts authorized by federal law.”

New York is also banning counties from using their local jails to hold people that ICE detains. Clinton County exited their agreement with ICE this March but not because of this law.

“What they're willing to reimburse us right now at $109 a night doesn't cover our costs to be able to do that," said Clinton County Sheriff David Favro. "I refuse to have our local taxpayers bear the burden of having to house federal detainees.”

Orange County used its jail to hold people detained by ICE and according to their contract, received twice what Clinton County did. A statement from a spokesperson for Orange County Executive Steve Neuhaus said that, "according to the County Attorney the County terminated its contract with the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, Immigration Customs Enforcement to house ICE detainees at the Orange Jail. ICE is responsible for the transfer of these detainees out of the Jail to a new location. The County has no information regarding where any of the detainees will be transferred.”

However, Orange County Sheriff Paul Arteta is one of the sheriffs suing the state over the ban.

Attorney General Letitia James responded to the lawsuit with a statement, saying in part that, "Many of the 12 entities with these agreements have complied without incident, and the vast majority of New York’s law enforcement agencies were already successfully protecting their communities without any collaboration with ICE. The claim that these sheriffs cannot do the same says more about them than it does about the law."

text:
The Trump administration arrested and deported a record number of immigrants in July, according to newly released government data – apprehending an average of 1,500 people and removing 1,100 people daily.

This latest data confirms what attorneys and immigrant advocates have been seeing across the US – although the administration has moved away from the high-profile, militarized raids that came to define its immigration enforcement approach last year, it is quietly ramping up its operations.

“The way that people are being detained is far less flashy, but we are still continuing to see arrests,” said Melissa Shepard, director of legal services at the southern California-based immigrant services group ImmDef. “It’s just on a quieter scale instead of, you know, 10, 12 officers making one arrest, you have a handful of officers pulling someone over.”

Overall, 49,571 people were arrested last month, according to government data obtained by the Deportation Data Project – the highest number since October 2022, and a 15% increase from the previous record set in June of this year.

Despite the administration’s insistence that it is targeting criminals, a record number of people caught in the surge of arrests in July had no prior criminal history. July was the first month during the second Trump administration that the majority of people – 51% of arrestees — had no criminal convictions or charges, according to the Guardian’s analysis.

Removals were also at a record high in July. Nearly 34,000 people were removed from the US last month, the most since the start of the second Trump administration.

Boosted by a $70bn funding surge, the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) – the agency that oversees ICE and the border patrol – has been working to ramp up to the White House goal of 2,000 arrests every day. Immigrants are being arrested when they report to mandated appointments at ICE offices, at traffic stops, outside their homes and, increasingly, at US airports.

“I think it’s just they’re looking for any way to be able to continue to detain people,” said Shepard. “They are being creative.” In recent weeks, she said, ImmDef has advised even clients with pending or valid immigration statuses, who are legally cleared for travel, to avoid flying due to the uptick of enforcement.

Attorneys are also advising clients with temporary protected status (TPS) to make sure they apply for different forms of immigration relief after the supreme court cleared the way for the administration to strip the designation from 50,000 Haitians and 6,100 Syrians.

Detentions in ICE custody have also been rising this summer since a drop following a January peak.

In the past month, the administration has been particularly focused on enforcement in the Springfield, Ohio, area, where a large group of Haitians with TPS had settled in recent years. Advocacy groups in Springfield said that Haitians were being called in to ICE offices and fitted with ankle monitors.

The first deportation flight to Haiti since the supreme court decision landed last week. TPS for Salvadorans is set to expire in September – ending protections for 170,000 people.

“I am anticipating and a little afraid for what it’s going to look like with the end of TPS,” said Shepard. “I think we are at the precipice.”

ICE’s enforcement powers have also been boosted by the rapidly expanding 287(g) program – which deputizes local law enforcement agencies to carry out immigration enforcement. Markwayne Mullin, the DHS secretary, called the program “the greatest partnership we can have” – and said it was a key part of his goal to conduct enforcement in a “more quiet way”.

text:
A New York law barring local police from helping federal agents carry out civil immigration operations took effect on Tuesday, after passing earlier this year under the state’s budget. Local police need to focus on local crime, not aiding and abetting an out-of-control federal agency, Gov. Kathy Hochul said at a Tuesday press conference.

Hochul underscored the difference between migrants with what she characterized as real criminal charges and migrants with civil infractions. New York supported Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s past operations against criminals, but the state will not allow local police to continue being converted into ICE agents to carry out federal civil enforcement, she said.

The law only applied to civil immigration matters, meaning local police would continue supporting ICE in criminal immigration operations. New York will never be a sanctuary for criminals, and state police will support ICE only when a real crime has been committed, Hochul said. Any police or sheriff departments that continued supporting ICE’s civil operations would face legal action, she said. Hochul said she welcomed any legal challenges, noting that courts have already ruled to uphold the law.

The New York Immigration Coalition released a Tuesday statement celebrating the law’s enforcement. Every resident deserved to feel safe interacting with police without fearing that their immigration status may be reported to authorities, according to the coalition’s president, Murad Awawdeh. This life-saving law sends a powerful message that New York will not be an extension of the Trump administration's mass deportation agenda, Awawdeh added.

Lansdowne constable signed collaboration agreement with ICE a year ago

Borough officials initiated the process to pass the ordinance and codify its opposition to voluntarily working with ICE even as an independently elected constable in the borough is one of just two local law enforcement departments in Philadelphia’s collar counties to have an active collaboration agreement with ICE.

Jerome Fletcher, the Lansdowne constable, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Fletcher signed a memorandum of agreement with ICE in the summer of 2025.

In Pennsylvania, constables are elected to six-year terms. The law enforcement officers have the power to make arrests without a warrant for a disturbance of peace. They also work with magistrate district judges and can serve civil papers, among other duties.

The Lansdowne constable’s agreement is under the program’s task force model, which provides training and funds to local law enforcement agencies and deputizes officers to carry out certain immigration enforcement duties.

As of Aug. 21, the agreement is active, according to ICE records.

According to U.S. Census data, immigrants make up 12.7% of the population of the tiny borough that spans just 1.2 square miles — more than 1.5 times the percentage of foreign-born residents in Pennsylvania.

Jessica M. Pointer, president of the Lansdowne Borough Council, told WHYY News that the constable “is in no way associated with our governing body” and works under the county, not the borough. But borough officials, she said, absorbed “the brunt of concerns” for residents who were opposed to collaborating with ICE and the constable’s participation in the 287(g) program.

“Although people understood it was no association, they still were concerned about their neighbors, their friends, whoever had to deal with ICE as an immigrant,” Pointer said. “This ordinance … says that our staff, our police department, or anybody a part of volunteering or governing or leading in this municipality could not offer our resources, or there will be some sort of … disciplinary action.”

Ordinance is ‘legally binding’

The borough had passed a resolution outlining officials’ stance on collaboration with ICE earlier this year but wanted to enact legislation that was “legally binding” and not just “performative,” Pointer said.

“People live in fear every day of what immigration officers will do to their family, breaking up their family and not being able to sustain their household,”she said. “This sends a clear message that these individuals that live in our town know that council, the governing body staff are looking out for their best interests as best as they can within their authority.”

The ordinance does not apply to the constable because that position works for the county, not the borough.

Other municipalities throughout the Philadelphia area have passed both resolutions and ordinances stipulating non-cooperation with ICE, with Montgomery County codifying its position in March that it would not enter into any 287(g) agreements.

title: Twin Falls ICE flight observers record more than 500 detainees flown out of Magic Valley airport
description:
The McDaniels have recorded more than 500 detainees being flown out of the airport since flights began in early April.
Idaho lawmaker says operations enforce ‘rule of law’ Karen Stroder has lived in Twin Falls nearly 30 years and in Idaho her entire life, she said.
She got involved in watching the ICE flights through a local chapter of the group Indivisible, a progressive advocacy organization.
Muth said she and others in the group have since learned these operations previously took place out of the Twin Falls airport, but stopped until operations started in April.
She and other observers contribute to a volunteer network that tracks ICE flights called Habeas Flight Watch.
text:
Around mid-day on a recent Tuesday in Twin Falls, a small plane landed on the tarmac at the Magic Valley Regional Airport but never taxied to the terminal.

Outside the fence surrounding the airport runway area, a group of five people watched through telescopes and binoculars as three white vans drove onto the tarmac. Around 20 men got out of the vans and boarded the plane as law enforcement oversaw the process, which took just over 30 minutes.

One man was escorted back off the plane and into a van.

According to a flight tracker, the plane then traveled to King County International Airport, or Boeing Field, which is located south of Seattle.

Similar flights, operated by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, or ICE, happen every Tuesday and Thursday at the Magic Valley airport.

Shelly McDaniel and her husband Tim McDaniel, who live about 30 minutes outside of Twin Falls, have watched every flight since they became involved in efforts to observe them on May 12. The McDaniels have recorded more than 500 detainees being flown out of the airport since flights began in early April.

An ICE spokesperson told the Idaho Capital Sun the air operations provide “a network of air transportation to Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) 25 field offices to facilitate the movement of illegal aliens within the United States and their removal to destinations worldwide via air charter and commercial charter services.”

“ICE is committed to the safety and welfare of those in custody throughout the entire transfer and removal process,” the spokesperson, who did not provide a name, said in an email.

The spokesperson said in the Aug. 12 email that the agency had conducted 20 missions at the Magic Valley airport, also called Joslin Field. The agency’s Salt Lake City Field Office, which oversees Idaho, requests the flights “to support their operations which include the Magic Valley Region.”

The Human Rights First ICE flight monitor has recorded 33 flights out of Twin Falls in 2026, and three flights out of the Boise airport. No other Idaho cities are listed.

The federal immigration agency has a $1.8 billion contract with CSI Aviation, a private charter and cargo air transportation company, to operate the flights nationwide, according to federal spending data.

Airport Manager Matt Barnes told the Sun in an email that the local airport does not have any formal agreement with ICE or CSI Aviation.

“We are a public use airport that accepts federal grant funds, so we may not discriminate against aircraft operators who can safely operate at our facility,” Barnes said.

‘I think it’s wrong’; observers watch ICE flights because of due process concerns. Idaho lawmaker says operations enforce ‘rule of law’

Karen Stroder has lived in Twin Falls nearly 30 years and in Idaho her entire life, she said. She got involved in watching the ICE flights through a local chapter of the group Indivisible, a progressive advocacy organization.

“I think it’s wrong,” Stroder said of the flights. “I don’t think people are getting due process. I think everybody deserves their day in court.”

Twin Falls resident Heather Muth, who helped found the local Indivisible group, learned from an Indiana chapter member that these flights were happening and that various groups tracked and recorded them. She and other members connected with these groups to learn about monitoring the flights.

Muth said she and others in the group have since learned these operations previously took place out of the Twin Falls airport, but stopped until operations started in April.

“What’s new in the last couple of years is just the fact that … these people aren’t getting their due process,” Muth said.

Maureen Newton of the Burley/Rupert area recently went to the airport to watch a flight for the first time. She said she’d read about the flights and had concerns about it.

“This is my taxpaying dollars here I’m watching go down the garbage can,” she said, keeping her eyes on the plane as detainees with their hands bound in front of them boarded the plane one at a time.

Shelly McDaniel records a video of the boarding process for each flight and later takes a screenshot of each person who boards. She and other observers contribute to a volunteer network that tracks ICE flights called Habeas Flight Watch. The goal is to make the information available to attorneys so they can find their clients.

McDaniel and her husband told the Sun they are supportive of people with criminal convictions being deported, but their concern is that the detentions and deportations happen too quickly for the court process to finish. Shelly McDaniel said she

“I know of people that have been taken on a Sunday, and on Tuesday they’re on a plane,” Shelly McDaniel said. “… there’s just no way they’re even able to present their case in court.”

Twin Falls Republican state Rep. Clint Hostetler told the Sun in an email he’s supportive of the flights and argued that due process is being followed.

He said he supports “the rule of law, and that includes enforcing our nation’s immigration laws.”

“My understanding is these operations prioritize individuals who have already gone through the legal process and received a final order of removal, it also includes people with criminal convictions, public safety concerns, or no valid legal status to remain in the country,” Hostetler said. “This isn’t a new or extraordinary policy, it’s the law being applied.”

He said he understood that the flights could be “unsettling to some in our community, but failing to enforce the law isn’t fair to the people who came here the right way, or to Idaho taxpayers.”

“My focus as a representative is on what’s best for Idaho families and communities,” he said, “and that includes a secure, lawfully enforced immigration system.”

Attorneys must file a Habeas petition in court with jurisdiction before detainee is moved

If an attorney is going to be able to stop a detention before someone is deported and get a chance to argue their client’s case in court, they often must obtain what is called a habeas corpus petition.

Habeas petitions allow people to challenge their detention in court.

Twin Falls attorney Brian Tanner said attorneys for detainees must file for a habeas in a court with jurisdiction over where the detainee is located.

“You have to know immediately where they are, because you have to provide notice to the district court that you are filing habeas so that they don’t send them out, or you have to get them before they leave,” Tanner said.

If the petition is filed in time and someone is flown out anyway, that person has to be returned, Tanner said.

Shelly McDaniel said she’s seen at least one person leave on a plane and return later.

Prior to 2025, those who were apprehended by federal immigration authorities in the interior of the United States and who hadn’t committed a separate crime typically had the ability to get a bond hearing and avoid detention.

Tanner said before the flights began, a bus with the area’s detainees would leave on Wednesdays and eventually take them to an immigration court in Utah. Tanner could often secure his clients’ release before they left.

However, the U.S. Department of Justice under the Trump administration has changed its policy and began using a federal law typically only used for people who are caught while crossing the border or who just crossed the border, which allows them to be held without bond.

He said the no-bond policy reinterprets how immigration has been enforced for “decades and decades and decades.”

This new policy has been challenged and, at the end of July, a Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals panel of judges ruled that the government couldn’t withhold bail. Other circuit courts in other regions have had mixed rulings regarding this policy, with some upholding it and others blocking it, Stateline reported.

Tanner’s frustration with the recent major changes in the system have led him to limit how many immigration cases he’s taken. He’d previously practiced immigration law for nearly 20 years.

“Immigration is constantly changing in so many different ways. The president has an influence. The courts are basically interpreting laws in different ways. It’s always moving,” Tanner said. “So we get a different president, but I’ve never seen anything like this.”

ICE flight observers helped someone find detained family member, hope to help more

McDaniel said she recently saw a post on social media about someone trying to find their family member after he was detained in Idaho Falls. McDaniel reached out to ask her what he was wearing when he was detained and shared some photos with the person that matched the description.

McDaniel used the screenshots of detainees boarding flights and was able to help to find the family member near Tacoma. The person who posted was then able to try and find a lawyer in the area.

“It was very nice to know we were able to help them,” McDaniel said.

Muth, the Indivisible leader, said the plan is to try and keep monitoring and let people know what’s happening at their local airport.

“I think it’s always good to hear what everyone thinks about them, and to be able to have civil discourse, to talk about it,” Muth said. “… we do notice people are either one way or another. So they’re either for the flights and they’re happy that it’s happening, or they’re just extremely upset. And there can be a lot of emotion on both sides.”

text:
A federal judge in the Eastern District of Michigan on Friday dismissed a lawsuit alleging that Washtenaw County’s “sanctuary policies” were illegal.

In her opinion, Judge F. Kay Behm stated that “neither the federal government nor the President may conscript local officials to enforce their will,” adding that “the government cannot otherwise compel localities to enforce the President’s priorities in the manner it wishes.”

She wrote that the federal government cannot compel states or local governments to enact or administer a federal program, and cannot “conscript state or local officers directly.”

Three county policies were at issue in the lawsuit, Behm laid out in her decision. First, the county prosecutor’s office directed prosecutors to consider immigration consequences when making charging decisions, as well as not to share information with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement beyond what would be required by federal law. Second, the county sheriff’s office instructed officers not to ask about immigration status and determined that the office would not detain individuals for ICE without a judicial warrant or court order. Finally, the county’s Board of Commissioners decided not to allow federal immigration officers onto county property if they did not have a judicial warrant or court order.

The federal government’s initial complaint alleged that the county “insists on obstructing federal immigration enforcement operations and shielding criminal offenders from apprehension by federal law enforcement. Washtenaw County’s policies aim to obstruct federal law enforcement and celebrate thwarting the constitutional obligation of the President of the United States to take care that federal immigration law be faithfully executed.”

The supremacy clause of the U.S. Constitution has complicated local and state level responses to federal immigration enforcement for communities around the country that do not want ICE to have a presence.

One aspect of that legal doctrine is ‘obstacle preemption,” when state law serves as an obstacle to the purposes and objectives embodied in a federal law. The federal government argued Washtenaw County’s policies fit that definition. However, a high threshold must be met to prove that preemption.

Behm wrote that a refusal to cooperate with immigration enforcement “does not constitute discrimination against the federal government,” and therefore is not constitutionally prohibited.

Quoting from another court ruling, Behm added that a “healthy balance of power between the States and the Federal Government [reduces] the risk of tyranny and abuse from either front,” concluding that Washtenaw County had done nothing more than “exercise its constitutional authority under the Tenth Amendment.”

title: Deported to Equatorial Guinea with a large abdominal hernia: 'I'm not worth a dime'
description:

“I’m not worth a dime,” Sánchez says, appearing on a video call with EL PAÍS from a room at the Bamy Hotel in the city of Malabo.
Savi Arvey, director of policy for refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First, a rights organization that has tracked these deportations, says they are “deeply concerned” about the situation in Equatorial Guinea.
Pietro Lima, a 56-year-old Brazilian also deported to Equatorial Guinea, needs medication after losing 30% of his intestine and a kidney because of gunshot wounds sustained in his home country.
The plane changed course and almost three hours later they were in Equatorial Guinea — an unprecedented incident, the first time a group of deportees has refused to disembark from an ICE plane and ended up somewhere else.
text:
Faces have blurred with the days, as they slowly sank into the reality of waking up in America and suddenly finding themselves in Africa. On board an ICE Air flight that left Alexandria, Louisiana, on August 20, there was a man who, nevertheless, almost everyone will remember. “He’s Cuban, yes, a Cuban whose insides were bulging out of his belly,” says a young Colombian who cannot precisely identify what he saw. A Honduran on the same plane also noticed the protrusion showing through the other passenger’s stomach, “like it was intestine, everything was open, his belly sticking out.” When that man and four others refused to get off the plane in Liberia and were taken on to Equatorial Guinea, no one cared that he was ill and fell face-first onto the tarmac as he was shoved.

The man’s mother, Caridad, hasn’t been able to eat at home in Lehigh Acres, Florida. His sister, Dorty Sánchez, is desperate. One day they went on Facebook and watched a video from Equatorial Guinea. One of the people deported there reported that someone traveling with him was in very poor health. “He said there was a young man with an open belly and that his name was Leonardo Sánchez. And if he has an open belly and his name is Leonardo, then that’s my brother, it can’t be anyone else.”

That is how the family learned that Sánchez, who until now had been held in Texas, was even farther away from them despite being a lawful permanent U.S. resident. They say he had been arrested for drug possession and had been doing community service hours. Last year, at a gas station, he was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents and initially taken to the Alligator Alcatraz facility. Since then, his mother and sister have done everything they could to get him out of detention. “We had hired a lawyer from the Wannamaker firm and, supposedly, there were options because of his medical condition.” But that lawyer, they say, scammed them, and now Sánchez is in a faraway place, his body aching, not knowing whether he will be able to have the surgery — his tenth — that is scheduled at Jackson Memorial Hospital.

“I’m not worth a dime,” Sánchez says, appearing on a video call with EL PAÍS from a room at the Bamy Hotel in the city of Malabo. The hotel is owned by the family of Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo, the country’s president, who has been in power for almost half a century. This month, several reports said some people were threatened at gunpoint in that hotel, where the government was also housing Ebola patients. For some time, the facility has also been hosting deportees who have arrived in the country as part of a $7.5 million agreement with the administration of Donald Trump.

Sánchez strokes his beard; he hasn’t been able to shave. They haven’t even given him a toothbrush, toothpaste, or clothes. Four days after his arrival, he was still wearing the same gray pants he left the United States in on the more than 36-hour flight alongside about 20 other deportees who were never told they were bound for Africa. During the trip they were given sandwiches and water they could barely bring to their mouths while remaining handcuffed and shackled. Sánchez says he wasn’t allowed to go to the bathroom the entire time. “I wet my pants three times,” he says.

As soon as he reached the hotel he washed his pants and the binder — the only one he has to support the bulge in his abdomen. Sánchez clutches his stomach constantly, as if holding himself together to stop his body from spilling apart. Nearly 10 years ago, in Hialeah, he was stabbed several times. “His intestine was damaged, he was in a coma for 40 days. The skin was left open and they had to graft it and put the colon to the side,” his sister says. Later, when he fell into ICE custody, he found his attackers had also been detained, but they were released. “They put the man who stabbed me in my same unit and then released him. I told the judge that,” he says.

That lump everyone notices on his stomach is a large abdominal hernia. Ever since he developed it, Sánchez has been unable to lift more than 20 pounds, has trouble finding work, and suffers from pain he finds unbearable. At the hotel — which is guarded by armed personnel and which they are not allowed to leave — he has only been given paracetamol to relieve the discomfort.

They also took him to a local hospital. “But at the hospital, they said that if I didn’t have any documents, the doctors wouldn’t take responsibility for me. They asked the officer who brought me there if he was responsible, and he said no, that he’d just been sent there. The doctor said, ‘If you won’t take responsibility, how are we supposed to?’” Sánchez recounts.

At a time when the U.S. government has signed deportation agreements with more than a dozen African countries, concern centers not only on the danger and legal limbo these people face but also on the medical care they receive. Savi Arvey, director of policy for refugee and immigrant rights at Human Rights First, a rights organization that has tracked these deportations, says they are “deeply concerned” about the situation in Equatorial Guinea. “People held in the hotel are deprived of access to essential medical care and subjected to conditions that further endanger their health and well-being, while suffering physical abuses by guards and being pressured to return precisely to the countries they fled to escape persecution or torture,” she says.

Over weeks of speaking with migrants of various nationalities sent to the Central African Republic, Liberia, and Equatorial Guinea, this newspaper confirmed that not only are they not receiving adequate medical care, but they can barely communicate with doctors in places where most people speak French. Some have reported stomach problems and allergies from the water or food. Others have experienced malarial episodes.

Pietro Lima, a 56-year-old Brazilian also deported to Equatorial Guinea, needs medication after losing 30% of his intestine and a kidney because of gunshot wounds sustained in his home country. “ICE had my medication on hand and I’ve been without it for five days; I need to take it. I spoke to people here and they know nothing about it,” he says.

When asked about Sánchez’s health and that of other migrants deported to Africa, a Department of Homeland Security spokesman told El PAÍS that “all of these undocumented migrants were deported to a safe third country.” “We are enforcing the law as written. If a judge determines an undocumented immigrant has no right to remain in this country, we will remove them. Period. The Trump administration is using every legal option to carry out the largest deportation operation in history, as President Trump promised,” the spokesman said. The State Department has not yet responded to this newspaper’s questions.

“This is human trafficking”

The flight that left Louisiana on August 20 made a refueling stop in Dakar, Senegal. It then continued to Monrovia, the capital of Liberia, a country that agreed to receive migrants under a $5 million deal with Washington. Pietro Lima, the Brazilian, never thought he would end up there. “Three days earlier, at the detention center, they tried to force me to sign a paper saying whether I wanted to go to Liberia and I didn’t sign it,” he says.

In Liberia, some migrants disembarked, but a small group refused to get off the plane. Pietro and the Cubans Darwin Hernández, Emilio Destrade, Carlos Rodríguez, and Leonardo Sánchez were prepared to do anything to avoid stepping into a territory they did not know. Through the plane windows they could see a large police deployment. “We told them we didn’t feel safe, but they forced us to get off. They carried me between four people and beat me while I was handcuffed,” Rodríguez says. Leonardo Sánchez was thrown down the aircraft stairs and landed on the tarmac with his hernia exposed.

The Cubans and the Brazilian began to protest. “We are not from Africa, we’re from another part of the world,” Rodríguez told them. Because of the commotion, they were returned to the plane, and ICE officers told them to remain calm, that they would take them back to the United States. The plane changed course and almost three hours later they were in Equatorial Guinea — an unprecedented incident, the first time a group of deportees has refused to disembark from an ICE plane and ended up somewhere else.

“How can a government, in the space of a few hours, send us to another country, and that country accept us?” Rodríguez asks. “This is human trafficking, they trafficked us on a plane.”

The government of Equatorial Guinea, which has been receiving deportees since late 2025, issued a statement saying it would treat “any national of a third country transferred by the Government of the United States of America to Equatorial Guinea consistently with its international legal obligations” and that they would not be “subjected to persecution on grounds of race, religion, nationality, membership of a particular social group or political opinion, nor to torture.”

Finally, the migrants arrived at Malabo International Airport, shortly after 8:00 p.m. According to Lima, they were taken down a rear part of the terminal, in the dark, away from the public eye. “To hide from people what was happening,” he says. “When the plane landed we asked ourselves: what place is this? Nobody told us anything. They asked us to get off and we still refused. But we saw more than 30 hooded police officers with weapons below. We were scared.”

Still handcuffed, they were taken by van to the Bamy Hotel, just a couple miles from the airport, about a 10-minute drive. “We are the only Latinos here,” Rodríguez says. “We are prisoners here. If we are free, as they say, why can’t we cook our food or go to the market to buy it?” To this day they have no identification, no passports or legal documents provided by Liberian or Equatorial Guinean authorities. They do not know what will happen to them.

Michael Flynn, executive director of the Global Detention Project, an organization that researches and documents the detention of migrants, asylum seekers, and refugees worldwide, told this newspaper that Equatorial Guinea “lacks an asylum framework to properly process refugee claims.” “Testimonies from detainees indicate they are not receiving safe or adequate food, that they are not being provided necessary medical treatment and that they have no clear idea what is happening to them or what their fate will be. The uncertainty must be truly agonizing,” he says. “The detention of these people is part of a deeply troubling trend in which migrants are deported from the United States to countries with which they have no significant ties, and then subjected to detention, often with little or no access to legal assistance or effective remedies.”
